rep.ov: Philosophy 1 introduces philosophy through its four branches (ontology/metaphysics, epistemology, logic, values) and Socrates as the model critical thinker (elenchus, Socratic ignorance, the Euthyphro dilemma, rhetoric vs philosophy). It then builds a critical-thinking toolkit: argument reconstruction, deductive vs inductive, validity and soundness, the ARS criteria, and informal fallacies and argument schemes (ad hominem, correlation/cause, slippery slope, appeal to authority). Normative ethics (utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics) is then applied to capital punishment, drone warfare and AI in education (Rundell). Each block supplies tools for the next: Socratic questioning motivates argument analysis, which is then used to evaluate ethical and applied cases.
must: Argument structure: premises, conclusion, sub-conclusions and implicit premises; reconstruct in standard form (P1, P2, C) using the principle of charity, with the conclusion last

Validity vs soundness: valid = if the premises are true the conclusion must be true; sound = valid AND all premises true. A valid argument can have false premises (e.g. 'All fish can fly...'). Distinguish deductive from inductive (probable, not certain)
ARS criteria: acceptability, relevance, sufficiency. A valid but unsound argument fails acceptability; an inductive argument never fully meets sufficiency
Valid forms (modus ponens, disjunctive syllogism) vs the invalid form affirming the consequent; necessary vs sufficient conditions

Fallacies as defined by Govier (a typical, deceptive error); straw man, weak analogy, hasty generalisation, equivocation, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to popular opinion, conflating morality with legality

Ad hominem: abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque, guilt by association; fallacious only when the personal attack replaces assessment of the claim. Ethotic arguments, and Brinton's person/advocacy/claim distinction
Causal reasoning: post hoc ergo propter hoc, common cause, reversed cause, necessary vs sufficient cause, critical questions for correlation-to-cause, and Argument from Consequences
Appeal to authority (ad verecundiam): not always fallacious; the critical questions on genuine expertise, relevance, bias/vested interest, consensus and verifiability; Willard's problem of authority

Socrates: elenchus, midwife analogy, Socratic ignorance, gadfly, the Socratic problem (only known via Plato/Xenophon), the charges (impiety, corrupting youth), the Euthyphro dilemma with both horns, and the Apology episodes (oracle, denial of being a paid teacher)

Normative ethics: utilitarianism (Greatest Happiness Principle; objections: overriding rights, scapegoat), deontology (ends in themselves, Rawls' veil of ignorance and maximin, negative vs positive duties), virtue ethics (character, eudaimonia, universality of virtues via Peterson & Seligman and Nussbaum)

Applied ethics: capital punishment through retributivism, deterrence and wrongful conviction; killer drones (RPAS, human-in-the-loop, paradox of precision, jus in bello, supreme emergency, lower threshold for war)

Branches of philosophy: classify questions by what they are about (ontology vs epistemology vs logic vs values); Rundell's cognitive offloading vs surrender and analysis of her argument via analogy and fallacies
conn: Validity/soundness and ARS: every evaluation of a reconstructed argument (e.g. the seminar arguments) asks whether it is valid, then which of acceptability, relevance or sufficiency fails
Socrates, rhetoric and fallacies: Socrates' contrast with the Sophists leads to Aristotle's logos/pathos/ethos, and ethos links directly to ethotic and ad hominem arguments
Rundell's AI article: reconstruct it, assess the Olympic/bus analogy, identify straw man, equivocation and anecdote, and relate it to Socrates' Phaedrus critique of writing
Euthyphro dilemma and normative ethics: whether goodness is independent of authority links to utilitarian, deontological and virtue accounts of what grounds morality

Ethical theories applied: capital punishment and drones can be run through utilitarian (consequences, deterrence), deontological (rights, retribution, distinction) and virtue lenses, and slippery slope or consequence arguments about autonomous weapons combine causal reasoning with ethics
exq: Reconstruct the following passage in standard form, supply any implicit premise, and assess it using acceptability, relevance and sufficiency. State whether it is deductive or inductive.
Explain the difference between validity and soundness. Give an example of a valid but unsound argument and say which ARS criterion it fails.
Explain the Euthyphro dilemma, setting out both horns and the problem each creates for the claim that piety is what the gods love.
Apply utilitarianism, deontology and virtue ethics to the case for capital punishment, and say which objection is most damaging to each theory.
When is an ad hominem or appeal to authority fallacious and when is it legitimate? Use the critical questions to assess a given example.
Evaluate Rundell's argument that AI undermines learning: identify the analogy, assess its similarities and dissimilarities, and name two fallacies, with quotes.
weak: Validity vs soundness vs ARS: students conflate truth with validity, or forget that a valid argument with a false premise fails acceptability rather than validity, and that inductive arguments are judged by strength, not validity

Fallacies that are only sometimes fallacious (ad hominem, authority, slippery slope, post hoc): the marks come from applying critical questions rather than just labelling, which is hard because it requires judging context

Rawls and deontology, and the Euthyphro dilemma: hypothetical consent, maximin and the veil of ignorance are easily confused with actual consent or total utility, and the two horns of Euthyphro are abstract and often muddled

units.name: correlation cause, Walton
units.ov: This material covers how to evaluate causal claims based on correlation or temporal sequence, using Walton's argumentation schemes. It treats the Argument from Correlation to Cause and the post hoc fallacy, the main ways a cause gets misidentified (coincidence, common cause, reverse causation, reporting effects), and the Argument from Consequences, which predicts causal outcomes of actions. The common thread is that a causal claim must be tested with critical questions, never assumed from co-occurrence.
must: Correlation does not by itself establish causation: the Argument from Correlation to Cause is reasonable only when its conditions are met, and is otherwise fallacious.
Post hoc ergo propter hoc ('after this, therefore because of this'): inferring that A caused B just because A came first. Succession alone is insufficient.
Post hoc reasoning is not always fallacious: it is acceptable when some inference beyond the bare sequence or correlation is shown.

Three critical questions for a causal claim: (1) Is there a correlation supporting it? (2) Could coincidence explain the apparent link? (3) Is the causal claim credible, with a common cause ruled out?
Ways of misidentifying a cause: coincidence, common cause (a third factor Z produces both X and Y), reverse causation (Y causes X), and hasty conclusions.
Reporting effects: a change in recording can be mistaken for a change in events (e.g. a shelter or safe venue increasing reported assaults without increasing actual assaults).

Necessary vs sufficient cause: a necessary cause must be present for the effect, while a sufficient cause can produce it alone. An effect may occur through another sufficient cause when the first is absent.
Argument from Consequences: reasons from the predicted positive or negative consequences of a policy to adopting or rejecting it. A negative prediction is also a causal claim.
Evaluating a consequence argument means assessing both the likelihood that the consequence will be caused by the proposal and the strength of the reasons given, not just whether it is good or bad.
Post hoc has two varieties: a one-off sequence of two events, and a pattern of occurrences across examples (correlation). Each needs its own supporting evidence.
conn: Correlation to cause and misidentifying the cause: each misidentification (common cause, reverse causation, reporting effect, coincidence) is a way the correlation-to-cause scheme fails its critical questions.
Post hoc fallacy and the correlation scheme: both infer cause from association (sequence or co-occurrence), and both become legitimate when additional supporting inference is supplied.

Argument from Consequences and causal reasoning: a policy argument depends on a causal prediction, so a poorly grounded causal link (post hoc, hidden common cause) undermines the policy recommendation.
Necessary and sufficient causes with common causes: ruling out alternative sufficient causes or a third factor is needed before a claimed cause can be treated as the cause.
exq: A town reports that after a new shelter opened, recorded assaults rose. Evaluate the claim that the shelter caused more assaults, using reporting effects, common cause and the critical questions.

Explain the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy and state when post hoc reasoning is not fallacious. Illustrate with a sustainable development example, such as a policy introduced before an improvement in an indicator.

Apply the three critical questions of the Argument from Correlation to Cause to the claim that higher national income causes better health outcomes. Identify possible common causes and reverse causation.
Distinguish a necessary cause from a sufficient cause, and explain why confusing them can lead to misidentifying the cause of an effect.

Analyse an Argument from Consequences for a proposed carbon tax. What must be established about the likelihood of the predicted consequences and the reasons for them before the argument is reasonable?

notes.t: Correlation and Causal Reasoning
pts: Chapter 9 opens by building on Case 8E, which drew a correlation between two things; the key task is deciding whether that correlation supports a causal claim.
A correlation between two things does not by itself show that one causes the other; the causal claim must be tested rather than assumed.
The Argument from Correlation to Cause is a reasonable argumentation scheme only when its correct conditions are met; otherwise it is a fallacious reasoning occurring.
The chapter concentrates on three types of causal reasoning that can prove problematic, including confusing a correlation or mere temporal sequence with a causal relation.
Causal reasoning about a proposal or action predicts an expected causal outcome, and a negative prediction can also be a causal claim.
defs: Argument from Correlation to Cause
A scheme in which a correlation between two factors is used to infer that one causally influences the other; reasonable only when its correct conditions are satisfied.
tips: Do not treat correlation as proof of causation; check the conditions of the argumentation scheme before accepting the causal claim.
Distinguishing a mere temporal sequence from a genuine causal relation is a frequent source of error.
rq: Why can a strong correlation between two things still be insufficient to conclude that one causes the other?
Because the correlation may arise from a third factor, coincidence, or reversed causation; a causal claim needs the conditions of the argumentation scheme to be met.
In the busy social life and colds example, what alternative explanation must be ruled out before accepting the causal claim?
That colds cause a busy social life, or that a common third factor influences both, so the causal direction is not established.

notes.t: The Post Hoc Fallacy
pts: Post hoc reasoning infers a causal link from temporal sequence alone: an earlier event is wrongly taken to cause a later one.
Aristotle's discussion of post hoc does not restrict the fallacy to cases where one event precedes another; succession alone is insufficient.
Correlation (co-occurrence) is also treated under the post hoc heading; a correlation alone does not establish a causal claim.
Causal arguments can be fallacious even when a correlation is present, so a correlation cannot by itself lend support to a causal hypothesis.
Post hoc reasoning need not be fallacious when some inference beyond the mere sequence is shown.
defs: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
Latin for 'after this, therefore because of this': the fallacy of inferring that because event B followed event A, A caused B.
tips: Do not treat a correlation or temporal order as proof of cause; state what extra evidence would be needed.
Distinguish the fallacious form (sequence taken as proof) from legitimate causal reasoning that adds supporting inference.
rq: Why is temporal succession alone insufficient to establish causation?
Because two events can occur in sequence or together by coincidence or through a common cause, so a further causal justification is needed.
What would make a post hoc inference non-fallacious?
Some independent inference or evidence showing a causal mechanism linking the events, beyond their order or co-occurrence.

notes.t: Correlation, Cause and the Post Hoc Fallacy
pts: Temporal sequence alone does not establish a causal connection; coincidence can account for events that follow one another.
Post hoc reasoning concludes causation from one event merely preceding another; it is a serious reasoning error.
A correlation shows that two things occur together but does not indicate that they are causally related.
Accounts of the second variety of post hoc fallacy rely on a pattern of occurrences across examples, unlike a one-off situation.
Background context and other causal factors must be considered before judging a causal claim unwarranted.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
Inferring that A caused B simply because A occurred before B in time, without adequate evidence of a causal link.
Correlation
A statistical association in which two things tend to occur together; it does not by itself establish causation.
tips: Do not confuse correlation with causation: co-occurrence or temporal order alone is not proof of a cause.
Check for alternative causal factors and background context before accepting a causal claim.
rq: Why is a temporal sequence insufficient evidence for causation?
Because coincidence can produce events that follow one another; the sequence must be backed by a plausible causal mechanism and rule out alternative explanations.
What background information could make a post hoc inference about Stone unwarranted?
Knowing that other causal factors, such as the police surveillance of the foreign novelist, explain the arrest better than the lunch does.

notes.t: Correlation and Cause; Misidentifying the Cause
pts: Reasoning from an alleged correlation to a causal claim rests on assumptions, e.g. that the first correlated event causes the second.
Two correlated events may be linked only by coincidence; the causal link must be tested, not assumed.
The post hoc fallacy assumes that because X precedes Y, X caused Y.
A common cause Z may produce both X and Y, so X and Y are correlated without causing each other.
Reverse causation: the causal arrow may point the opposite way from the one suggested.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
Mistakenly inferring that because event X occurred before event Y, X caused Y.
Necessary cause
A cause that must be present for the effect to occur; absent it, the effect does not occur (distinguished from sufficient causes).
tips: Do not confuse a necessary cause with a sufficient cause; an effect may occur through another sufficient cause when the first is absent.
Temporal precedence (X before Y) is not proof of causation; always check for a third factor or reverse direction.
rq: Why is a correlation between two variables not enough to establish that one causes the other?
Because coincidence, a common third cause Z, or reverse causation could produce the same correlation without a direct causal link.
What would you need to test to move from a suspected cause to a confirmed one?
A causal hypothesis that is tested, e.g. by controlled checks or analysis of background conditions, rather than assumed from the correlation.

notes.t: Correlation, cause and misidentifying the cause
pts: Correlation between two factors does not by itself establish that one causes the other; a common cause may explain both.
Misidentifying a cause can happen when the causal relation is reversed, so that effect is taken as cause.
A safe-venue effect can be confused with a reporting effect: more reported assaults may reflect the shelter, not more assaults.
Hasty conclusions and a failure to think through likely causal relations can produce misidentified causes.
defs: Misidentifying the cause
Error of taking a factor to be the cause of an effect when the real causal relation is different (reversed, common cause, or mistaken source).
Common cause
A third factor that independently produces both of two correlated phenomena, so their correlation does not show one causes the other.
tips: Do not infer causation from correlation alone; check for reversed causation, common causes and reporting effects.
Distinguish actual change in events from change in how events are recorded.
rq: Why can a correlation between shelter presence and assault counts mislead us?
Because the shelter may increase reporting of assaults; the rise in reported assaults does not mean assaults actually increased, and the true causal relation may be missed.
What might explain the fall in birthrates alongside more women choosing careers, without one causing the other?
A common cause such as widely available contraception, which allowed women to choose careers over motherhood and also reduced births.

notes.t: Correlation and Cause: Critical Questions and the Argument from Consequences
pts: Three critical questions test a causal claim: is there a correlation supporting it, can the move from correlation to cause be explained by coincidence, and is the causal claim itself credible with its common cause ruled out?
A correlation alone does not establish causation; the post hoc fallacy arises when a causal link is assumed without an accepted plausible inference.
The Argument from Consequences reasons from predicted positive or negative consequences of an action or policy to whether it should be adopted or rejected.
Evaluating a consequence argument requires assessing the likelihood that consequences will be caused by what is proposed, and the reasons given for believing so.
Hidden common causes (A and B both caused by a third factor) must be considered before concluding that A causes B.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
The mistaken inference that because B followed A, A caused B, without a plausible causal link being established.
Argument from Consequences
A scheme of practical reasoning that projects the likely consequences of an action or policy and recommends or rejects it according to whether those consequences are positive or negative.
tips: Do not treat a correlation as proof of causation; always check for coincidence or a hidden common cause.
In consequence arguments, evaluate both the likelihood of the consequence and the strength of the reasons for it, not just whether it is positive or negative.
rq: Why does a strong correlation alone not justify a causal claim?
Because the correlation may be due to coincidence, a hidden common cause, or reverse causation; a plausible causal link must also be shown.
What would make a consequence-based argument for a policy weak?
If the consequences are unlikely to be caused by the policy, or if the reasons given for believing they will occur are poor.

units.name: CT AI moodle
units.ov: This material uses critical thinking tools, especially assessing arguments from analogy, to evaluate generative AI (LLMs) in education. It covers what LLMs are (the Chinese Room, the tool vs agent distinction), their benefits, limits and threats (hallucination, jagged frontier, cognitive surrender, intensification, ethics), and the problems they pose for understanding and learning. It ends with mitigation strategies and Illingworth's four criteria for using AI well. The ideas connect because the analogy argument (AI essay = bus shortcut) rests on the premise that learning, not the product, is the point, and the later criteria test when offloading respects that premise.
must: Argument from analogy: infer a conclusion about Y from its similarity to X; assess acceptability, relevance of similarities, sufficiency of dissimilarities, counter-analogies, and whether the conclusion's strength matches the comparison
Key premise of the bus/essay analogy: the essay's product is not the point, the learning from reading and writing is; the dissimilarity is that AI may legitimately offload some cognition
Illingworth's four criteria for using AI well: bounded task; a human with judgement downstream; honest comparison class; the thinking stays yours (do not confuse them with the mitigation strategies)

LLMs find patterns in vast data and make probabilistic, context-sensitive guesses about what comes next; they are creative, not fully understood by their designers, and behave more like agents than tools (self-improving, unpredictable)
Searle's Chinese Room (1980): symbol manipulation can look like understanding without comprehension, so 'appears to understand' is not 'understands'; the risk is the illusion of a person

Limitations: hallucination (false output delivered with confident plausibility); checking costs time and undercuts speed; speed can bypass judgement; skills erode with reliance; the jagged frontier is uneven, varies by profession and moves with each model release

Cognitive offloading (acceptable delegation) vs cognitive surrender (uncritical acceptance, loss of reasoning); related risks are the illusion of knowing and confirmation bias, since AI does not push back by default

Understanding means being able to explain, apply, and analyse or evaluate; it needs struggle and virtues (persistence, courage) and phronesis (Aristotle's wise judgement), so having an AI answer is not understanding

Mitigations: bans are weak; AI detection fails technically (false positives), ethically (hits international and first-generation students) and pedagogically (default suspicion); better options are AI literacy, teacher training, and AI-proof assessment such as vivas

Wider threats: environmental costs (electricity and water), unequal access (private schools ban it while other schools adopt it to save money), intensification of work, lack of empathy in simulated communication, concentrated ownership and corporate power, and job losses
conn: The analogy argument and Illingworth's criteria: the 'thinking stays yours' and 'honest comparison class' criteria are the test of whether the bus/essay dissimilarities defeat the analogy

Chinese Room, hallucination and cognitive surrender: because LLMs only appear to understand and can be confidently wrong, uncritical acceptance is dangerous, which is why expertise downstream (criterion 2) matters

Expertise paradox: AI is best used by experts who can judge output, but students still building expertise need the struggle that offloading bypasses, linking understanding and virtues to the second criterion and to vivas
Speed vs checking vs intensification: faster outputs need verification, and any time saved may be absorbed by more demanding work, so the net benefit is smaller than it first appears
exq: Evaluate the argument that using AI to write an essay is like taking the bus to Balham. Apply all five tests for analogical arguments and give one counter-analogy.
Explain Searle's Chinese Room and assess whether it shows that LLMs lack understanding. Why does this matter for how students should treat AI output?
Distinguish cognitive offloading from cognitive surrender with examples, and apply Illingworth's four criteria to a student using AI to (a) tidy grammar and (b) generate ideas on an unfamiliar topic.
Give three reasons (technical, ethical, pedagogical) against AI-detection software and argue which mitigation (AI literacy, vivas, ban) is most defensible.
Discuss the 'jagged frontier' and hallucination: why do they make generalisations about AI's usefulness unreliable, and how do they affect the claim that AI saves time?

notes.t: Critical Thinking, Education & AI: Analogy-based argument assessment and the nature of gen
pts: The seminar argument uses an analogy: taking the bus to Balham is like using AI to write an essay, both being shortcuts that bypass the real purpose of training or learning.

Analogical arguments are assessed by checking acceptability, relevance of similarities, sufficiency of dissimilarities, availability of counter-analogies, and whether the conclusion's strength matches the comparison.
Generative AI (LLMs) finds patterns in vast amounts of data and, unlike earlier AI, is sensitive to context, so it makes probabilistic guesses about what comes next.
The argument's key premise is that the product of an essay is not the point; the learning gained through reading and writing is.
defs: Argument from analogy

An argument that infers a conclusion about one case (Y) from its similarity to another case (X), assessed by the acceptability of Y's claim, the relevance of similarities, the sufficiency of dissimilarities, and the existence of counter-analogies.
Generative AI (LLM)
A system that identifies patterns in large datasets and, sensitive to linguistic context, produces probabilistic predictions of plausible language.
tips: Do not treat an analogy's conclusion as proven; check whether the dissimilarities (e.g. AI may legitimately offload cognition) undermine the similarities.
Distinguish the product of an essay from the learning process, since the argument depends on this premise.
rq: Why does the analogy between the Olympic runner taking the bus and a student using AI fail or succeed? Which premise would you challenge first?

It succeeds if training and essay-writing share the same purpose (building capacity); it may fail because AI could support legitimate cognitive offloading, a dissimilarity that undermines the similarity (Sufficiency).
What is the difference between checking relevance and checking sufficiency in an analogy?
Relevance asks whether the shared features actually bear on the conclusion; sufficiency asks whether dissimilarities undermine those shared features or whether counter-analogies exist.

notes.t: The nature of generative AI (LLMs)
pts: Generative AI is a creative system that recombines learned patterns to produce new outputs, and its designers do not fully understand how it works internally.
Unlike earlier technologies, generative AI behaves more like an agent than a tool: it can be self-improving and unpredictable.
John Searle's Chinese Room argues that symbol manipulation can look like understanding without any genuine comprehension or consciousness.
Generative AI can produce the illusion of being a person, which is a risk because humans instinctively treat fluent conversation as a sign of a mind.
Used well, generative AI offers clear benefits: fast data processing, efficient summarising, idea generation, and acting as a sparring partner that can counter confirmation bias.
defs: Chinese Room

Searle's thought experiment (1980) arguing that a system can produce correct outputs by following rules for manipulating symbols without understanding their meaning, so syntactic processing alone does not amount to a mind.
Large Language Model (LLM)
A generative AI system trained on vast text data to predict and produce plausible language, which can appear to understand without doing so.
Confirmation bias
The tendency to seek out or favour information that supports existing beliefs; generative AI can be prompted to challenge such bias.
Groupthink
A pattern in group decision-making where consensus pressure suppresses critical evaluation of alternatives.
tips: Do not conflate 'appears to understand' with 'understands': the Chinese Room is about the difference between behaviour and consciousness/meaning.
Distinguish 'tool' from 'agent' carefully; the lecture's claim is that generative AI's self-improving unpredictability sets it apart from earlier technologies.
rq: Why does Searle's Chinese Room suggest that fluent AI output does not prove understanding?

Because the person in the room can produce correct Chinese replies by following symbol-manipulation rules without knowing what the symbols mean, so correct behaviour can occur without comprehension or consciousness.
Why might a system designed to keep users engaged be a problem for learning and decision-making?
It can encourage dependency and reduce independent thinking, and because it is not a neutral friend, users may over-trust its fluent answers.
How could using AI as a 'sparring partner' improve decisions compared with simply asking it for agreement?
Prompting it to challenge your arguments exposes weak reasoning and counters confirmation bias and groupthink, whereas asking for agreement reinforces existing views.

notes.t: Limitations & threats of AI (technical, cognitive, ethical)
pts: AI systems can hallucinate knowledge, presenting false information with the same plausibility and confidence as genuine information, so important outputs must be checked, which can cost time and undo the speed benefit.
Speed can bypass judgement: a fast AI answer arrives before one's own judgement, and a machine-written draft skips the thinking the draft was meant to produce.
Over time, growing reliance on AI may erode human knowledge and skills, raising the question of what happens when the AI fails.
AI capability is uneven (a 'jagged frontier'): it performs well on some tasks and poorly on others, and the boundary differs by profession and shifts with each model release.

Ethical concerns include who owns AI, the risk of economic imperialism and anti-democratic corporate power if states do not regulate it, and job losses that may matter even if wealth is fairly distributed.
defs: Jagged (technological) frontier
The uneven boundary between tasks AI performs well and tasks it performs poorly; it is not a smooth line and varies across occupations and over time.
Hallucination
When an AI system generates false information while expressing it with the same confidence and plausibility as correct information.
tips: Do not confuse AI's speed with reliability: fast outputs still require checking, and checking time reduces the net speed benefit.
The 'jagged frontier' is not a fixed line; the boundary differs by profession and moves with each model release, so generalisations across all tasks are a common error.
rq: Why might a fast, confident AI answer be more dangerous to a learner than a slow, uncertain one?
A confident answer can short-circuit the learner's own judgement and checking, so errors pass unnoticed because they look as plausible as correct content.
If AI does most of a task for you, how would you ever notice that it has gone wrong?
You would only notice if you retain enough domain skill to judge the output from the inside; losing that capacity removes the ability to detect errors.
Even if AI-generated wealth were distributed fairly, what might still be lost if jobs disappear?
Work may be intrinsically valuable beyond income, so job loss could cost people meaning and purpose, not just money.

notes.t: Limitations & threats of AI: ethics, relationships, and guidance for using AI well
pts: AI carries environmental costs, since electricity and water are needed to run data centres.
AI can widen inequalities, as some private schools ban it while normal schools adopt it to save money.
AI can intensify work, so time saved may be transferred to more demanding tasks rather than returned to workers.
Gen AI mimics human communication without empathy or communicative intent, offering a thin substitute for authentic human connection.
Four properties define constructive AI use: the task is bounded, a human with judgement stands downstream, the comparison class is honest, and the thinking stays yours.
defs: Intensification
The process by which time saved through technology is not returned to workers but is instead filled with more demanding tasks, increasing workload.
Cognitive offloading
Delegating mental tasks such as memory or reasoning to an external tool, which can be beneficial but may reduce independent thinking if overused.
Cognitive surrender
Uncritically accepting an AI's output and abandoning one's own reasoning, leading to erosion of critical thinking skills.
Comparison class
The honest alternative against which an AI use should be judged; the relevant question is whether the alternative to using AI is actually worse.
tips: Do not confuse cognitive offloading (acceptable delegation) with cognitive surrender (uncritical abandonment of reasoning).
The 'comparison class is honest' property requires comparing AI against the real alternative, not an idealised one.
rq: Why might a tool that saves time at work still leave workers no better off?
Because of intensification: the time saved is transferred to more demanding tasks rather than given back to workers.
Why is Therabot's use of AI considered constructive when judged against the four properties?

It is bounded to a distinct set of disorders and timeframe, has human experts monitoring it, compares favourably to no therapy while on a waiting list, and does nothing more than a human therapist would, so the user's thinking stays theirs.
What is the risk when an AI user is not already an expert in the domain?
The 'human with judgement stands downstream' property implies AI is best used by someone already expert, so a novice cannot reliably evaluate or correct its output.

notes.t: Problems with AI in education: understanding, virtues and Socratic dialogue
pts: Heavy reliance on AI for cognitive tasks is correlated with reduced critical thinking skills and virtues, such as accepting factual errors and practising less reasoning.
Understanding means being able to explain, apply, and analyse or evaluate a concept, not merely possessing answers.

Understanding is implied by commitment to truth, and involves thinking through ideas, testing them through dialogue, and making informed judgements; Aristotle saw wise judgement (phronesis) as the primary virtue.
Learning is a struggle; relevant virtues for it include persistence and courage, which AI shortcuts can bypass.
AI dialogue can challenge arguments, but by default it is not programmed to push back, risking confirmation bias and misleading confidence.
defs: Cognitive offloading
Delegating mental tasks such as reasoning or recall to an external tool, which may reduce practice of critical thinking skills.
Illusion of knowing
Over-confidence in one's own understanding that is not matched by actual ability to explain or apply the concept.
Understanding
The ability to explain, apply, and analyse or evaluate a concept.
Phronesis
Aristotle's virtue of wise judgement, regarded as the primary virtue, grounding informed decision-making.
Confirmation bias
Tendency to favour information that supports existing beliefs; AI that does not push back can reinforce it.
tips: Do not equate having an AI-generated answer with understanding; understanding requires explaining, applying and evaluating.
Remember that AI does not challenge you by default, so ask explicitly for counter-arguments when testing your reasoning.
rq: Why might using AI to produce answers weaken critical thinking over time?
Because offloading reasoning to AI reduces practice in reasoning skills, and correlates with accepting factual errors and over-confidence.
How does thinking through ideas in dialogue help build understanding, compared with simply receiving an answer?
Testing ideas through dialogue requires explaining, applying and evaluating them, which allows informed judgement and reveals gaps in understanding.
What might be lost when feedback comes from AI rather than a person?
A tutor understands your personal context and how it affects learning, and interaction brings benefits such as being respected and a meeting of minds.

notes.t: Problems with AI in education: mitigation strategies and applying Illingworth's criteria
pts: Banning AI is weak because students will use it anyway and it does not prepare them for the world.

AI-detection software is unreliable (false positives), ethically problematic (flags grammar help, hitting international and first-generation students), and pedagogically damaging because it makes suspicion the default in teacher-student relations.
Asking students to show their AI process unfairly casts suspicion on those who never used AI at all.
Better mitigations: teach AI literacy (its dangers and good use), train teachers to use it well, and design AI-proof assessments such as vivas.
Illingworth's criteria for using AI well: the task is bounded, a human with judgement stands downstream, the comparison class is honest, and the thinking stays the student's own.
defs: AI literacy
Teaching students about the dangers of AI and how to use it well, as a mitigation for its problems in education.
Viva
An oral examination in which the student defends their work in person; proposed as an AI-proof form of assessment.
False positive (in AI detection)
When detection software wrongly flags human-written work as AI-generated or plagiarised; a technical reason not to rely on detectors.
Bounded task
A task with a clear scope indicating what AI will and will not be used for, as set out in the assignment remit.
Honest comparison class
Asking what the realistic alternative to using AI is, and whether that alternative is really worse.
tips: Give all three reasons against detection software (technical, ethical, pedagogical) and note that each is sufficient alone but none is necessary.
Do not confuse the four Illingworth criteria with the mitigation strategies; the criteria apply to using AI well, while detection and bans are separate responses.
rq: Why is an AI-detection tool not sufficient on its own, even if it were technically accurate?

Ethically it misclassifies grammar tidying as plagiarism, disproportionately affecting international and first-generation students; pedagogically it makes suspicion the default in teacher-student relationships.
What is the problem with requiring every student to show their AI process?
Students who never used AI are immediately put under suspicion, so the requirement punishes honesty and shifts the burden onto them.
Why might assessments like vivas be AI-proof?
A viva requires the student to explain and defend their reasoning live, which is hard to outsource to AI and so tests genuine understanding.

notes.t: Applying Illingworth's criteria to academic work: expertise, comparison and thinking owner
pts: Illingworth's second criterion implies AI is best used by someone who is already an expert, who can judge its output.
Asking students who are still learning a discipline to critique AI output may bypass the struggle through which expertise is built.
Checking AI-generated work is slow and unsatisfying, so it may not be faster than writing it yourself.
Illingworth's third criterion asks whether the comparison class is honest, i.e. whether the alternative to using AI is really worse.
The fourth criterion, 'the thinking stays yours', distinguishes using AI to tidy grammar from using it to generate ideas and text on unfamiliar topics.
tips: Do not confuse Illingworth's criteria: 'a human with judgement stands downstream' concerns expertise, while 'the thinking stays yours' concerns who does the intellectual work.
Using AI to tidy grammar is treated differently from using it to generate ideas and text on a topic you do not yet understand.
rq: Why might asking a novice to critique an AI-generated essay fail to build the skills the course aims for?

Learning a discipline comes through one's own effort, including getting things wrong; critiquing AI output presupposes the expertise that the effort is supposed to produce, so it skips the stage where expertise is built.
Why might checking AI output take longer than writing the work yourself?
Verifying content you did not produce requires reading it closely against your own knowledge, which is slow and tedious, so the time saved in generation can be lost in checking.
What is the difference between using AI for grammar and using it to generate ideas?
Grammar help leaves the intellectual content and reasoning with the student, whereas generating ideas and text on an unfamiliar topic outsources the thinking itself.

notes.t: References for AI, misinformation and the mind (Philosophy 1 / CT AI)
pts: Dialogue with AI can reduce belief in misinformation, but does not build lasting discernment skills.
Searle's 1980 paper argues about whether programs alone can constitute minds (the Chinese Room argument).
Commentary on AI's effects on young people's minds and happiness, from a classroom perspective.
Critique of AI hype meeting an immovable fact, from a New York Times opinion piece.
tips: Do not treat a reference list as evidence of content: cite the specific claim each source supports, not just the title.
Distinguish the study's finding (reduced belief in misinformation) from the stronger claim (improved discernment), which the reference title explicitly denies.
rq: Why might a study showing AI reduces belief in misinformation still not show that people become better at spotting misinformation themselves?
Reduced belief reflects the AI's corrections in the moment, whereas lasting discernment is a transferable skill the study found was not built.
What is the core claim Searle defends in 'Minds, brains, and programs', and why does it matter for evaluating AI?
That running a program, even one that passes as understanding, is not sufficient for genuine understanding or a mind, so behavioural success alone doesn't show AI understands.

units.name: 1.1 What philosophy is: the four branches
units.ov: Philosophy splits into metaphysics (reality), epistemology (knowledge), ethics/values (how to live) and logic (good reasoning).
must: Metaphysics = what exists; epistemology = knowledge; ethics = values; logic = reasoning.
Be ready to classify example questions into a branch.

notes.t: The branches of philosophy
pts: Philosophy asks fundamental questions and answers them with reasoned argument rather than authority.
Metaphysics asks what exists and what reality is like (e.g. mind and body, free will, God).
Epistemology asks what knowledge is and how we can justify our beliefs.
Ethics (values) asks how we ought to live and what makes actions right or wrong.
Logic studies what makes reasoning good: how premises support conclusions.
defs: Metaphysics
The branch of philosophy about the nature of reality and what exists.
Epistemology
The branch of philosophy about knowledge, belief and justification.
Ethics
The branch of philosophy about values: right and wrong, good and bad, how to live.
Logic
The study of correct reasoning: when premises really support a conclusion.
tips: Classify a question by what it is ABOUT: "Do we have free will?" is metaphysics; "How do I know my senses are reliable?" is epistemology.
rq: Which branch does "Is it ever right to lie?" belong to, and why?
Ethics — it asks what we ought to do, a question about values.
Which branch does "Can we know anything for certain?" belong to?
Epistemology — it is about knowledge and justification.
What does logic contribute to the other branches?
The tools to test whether arguments in any branch actually support their conclusions.

units.name: 1.2 Socrates: the examined life
units.ov: Socrates championed the examined life, intellectual humility and truth over reputation; he challenged Athens publicly and was executed for it.
must: Examined life; Socratic ignorance (knowing you don't know).
Gadfly role and why it made him dangerous to Athens.
We only know him through Plato.

notes.t: Who Socrates was and what he stood for
pts: Socrates (Athens, 5th century BC) wrote nothing; we know him mainly through Plato, so how much is really Socrates is debated.
"The unexamined life is not worth living" (Apology): he valued truth and virtue over reputation, wealth or safety.
The oracle said no one was wiser; he concluded his wisdom was knowing that he did not know — intellectual humility.
He called himself the "gadfly" stinging Athens awake, and was executed (399 BC) for impiety and corrupting the youth.
defs: Examined life
Socrates' ideal of constantly questioning your beliefs and values instead of accepting them unthinkingly.
Gadfly
Socrates' image of himself as an irritating insect that stings the lazy horse of Athens into self-reflection.
Socratic ignorance
Knowing that you do not know — the starting point of wisdom in the Apology.
tips: Name the primary texts: Apology (trial and defence), Meno (midwife / slave boy), Euthyphro (piety), Phaedrus (critique of writing).
We only know Socrates through Plato — a classic point to raise when evaluating him.
rq: What does Socrates mean by saying he is wise only because he knows he does not know?
Others think they know things they don't; he is aware of his ignorance, which makes him open to learning — intellectual humility.
Why did Socrates call himself a gadfly?
He saw his role as irritating Athens with questions so the city would wake up and examine itself, like a fly stinging a sluggish horse.
Why is Plato's authorship a problem for studying Socrates?
Socrates wrote nothing, so his views come filtered through Plato, who may have used him to voice his own ideas.

notes.t: His character and political role
pts: Ironic: often claimed ignorance while dismantling others' views.
Persistent and morally courageous — refused to stop philosophising even facing death.
Publicly tested politicians, poets and "experts", which embarrassed powerful people.
Seen as a threat to Athenian democracy after the defeat by Sparta; associates like Alcibiades and Critias harmed Athens.
defs: Socratic irony
Pretending ignorance to draw out and expose the weaknesses in someone else's position.
tips: A "modern Socrates" answer: whistleblowers, investigative journalists, or MLK, who cited Socrates and "creative tension" in Letter from Birmingham Jail.
rq: Give two personal characteristics of Socrates with an example of each.
Ironic (claiming ignorance while exposing others), morally courageous (refusing to stop questioning even when facing death).
Who might count as a modern Socrates, and why?
e.g. Martin Luther King Jr. — he deliberately created "creative tension" to force society to examine injustice, and cited Socrates.

units.name: 1.3 The Socratic method, Euthyphro & AI
units.ov: The elenchus tests definitions through questioning; the Euthyphro dilemma and the Phaedrus critique of writing are favourite exam material.
must: Elenchus + midwife analogy (Meno).
Euthyphro dilemma and both horns.
Phaedrus: writing (and AI) gives the appearance of wisdom without understanding.

notes.t: The Socratic method (elenchus)
pts: He asks for a definition (e.g. "What is piety?"), tests it with questions, and exposes contradictions.
He does not hand over answers; the learner discovers the gaps in their own thinking.
In the Meno he calls himself a midwife who helps others "give birth" to ideas already in them (the slave-boy geometry example).
defs: Elenchus
Socrates' question-and-answer method of testing a definition until it is shown to be inconsistent.
Midwife analogy
Socrates helps others bring out knowledge already within them rather than teaching it directly (Meno).
tips: If asked for the method, give the 3 steps: definition → test with questions → expose contradiction → revise.
rq: Describe the Socratic method in three steps.
Ask for a definition; test it with probing questions/counterexamples; expose the contradiction so the person revises their view.
Why does Socrates compare himself to a midwife?
He doesn't give people ideas; he helps them bring out understanding they already have, like the slave boy in the Meno.

notes.t: The Euthyphro dilemma
pts: Is something pious because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is pious?
Horn 1: if it is good because the gods love it, morality seems arbitrary.
Horn 2: if the gods love it because it is good, goodness is independent of the gods.
defs: Euthyphro dilemma
Is something good because God/the gods command it, or do they command it because it is good?
tips: Show both horns and the problem each creates — that is where the marks are.
rq: State the Euthyphro dilemma and explain the problem with each horn.
Good because gods love it → arbitrary; gods love it because good → goodness doesn't depend on the gods.

notes.t: What Socrates would think of generative AI
pts: In the Phaedrus, Socrates criticises writing: it gives the appearance of wisdom without understanding, and a text cannot answer back.
He would likely worry that AI answers let you skip the struggle where real learning happens.
He might accept AI used as a questioner that challenges you, not as an oracle that answers for you.
tips: Link AI to the Phaedrus critique of writing — the strongest textual support.
rq: Using the Phaedrus, what would Socrates say about ChatGPT?
Like writing, it gives the appearance of wisdom without understanding and can't be questioned properly; he'd prefer AI that asks you questions.

units.name: 2.1 Building arguments: premises and conclusions
units.ov: Arguments are premises supporting a conclusion; write them in standard form and make hidden premises explicit.
must: Standard form P1/P2/C.
Conclusion and premise indicator words.
Have a ready-made example (climate responsibility, misogyny education).

notes.t: Argument structure (P1, P2, C)
pts: An argument = premises (reasons) offered in support of a conclusion.
Write it in standard form: P1, P2, … C. Make hidden assumptions explicit as premises.
Indicator words: "therefore", "so", "hence" introduce conclusions; "because", "since", "given that" introduce premises.
Morrow & Weston's workbook: identify premises and conclusion, put ideas in a natural order, use clear consistent terms, start from reliable premises.
defs: Premise
A statement offered as a reason to accept the conclusion.
Conclusion
The claim the premises are meant to support.
Standard form
Writing an argument as numbered premises followed by the conclusion.
tips: When reconstructing an argument, add any unstated premise the reasoning depends on.
rq: What is the difference between a premise and a conclusion?
Premises are the reasons; the conclusion is what they are meant to support.
Reconstruct: "Schools should teach about misogyny because harmful attitudes learned in childhood are best challenged at school."
P1: If a harmful attitude is learned in childhood, schools are among the best places to challenge it. P2: Misogyny is learned in childhood. C: Schools are among the best places to challenge misogyny.

notes.t: Example arguments to reuse
pts: Climate responsibility: P1 If an activity causes long-term harm future generations inherit, we must limit it. P2 Burning fossil fuels does that. C We must limit burning fossil fuels.
Objection to P1: the non-identity problem (Derek Parfit) — can we owe duties to people who don't exist yet?
A news-style argument (e.g. BBC report → "national emergency") is usually inductive: the conclusion adds claims the premises don't guarantee.
defs: Non-identity problem
Parfit's puzzle: our choices determine which future people exist, so it's unclear how we can harm or owe duties to them.
rq: Give a valid argument for climate responsibility and one objection to it.
P1/P2/C as above (modus ponens); object to P1 using Parfit's non-identity problem.

units.name: 2.2 Deductive vs inductive; valid vs sound
units.ov: Validity is about structure, soundness adds true premises; know modus ponens, disjunctive syllogism and the fallacy of affirming the consequent.
must: Valid vs sound (with the flying shark example).
Deductive vs inductive.
Modus ponens, disjunctive syllogism; affirming the consequent is invalid.

notes.t: Validity and soundness
pts: Deductive: if the premises are true, the conclusion MUST be true. Inductive: premises make the conclusion probable.
Valid = the structure guarantees the conclusion IF the premises are true; the premises may actually be false.
Sound = valid AND all premises actually true. Every sound argument is valid, not every valid argument is sound.
Example valid but unsound: All fish can fly; a shark is a fish; so a shark can fly.
defs: Valid
An argument whose form guarantees that if the premises are true, the conclusion is true.
Sound
A valid argument whose premises are all actually true.
Deductive argument
An argument intended to make its conclusion certain given the premises.
Inductive argument
An argument whose premises make the conclusion probable but not certain.
tips: Can a valid argument have a false premise? YES — validity is only about structure.
rq: Can a valid deductive argument have a false premise? Give an example.
Yes: "All fish can fly; a shark is a fish; so a shark can fly" is valid but has a false premise (so it is unsound).
Explain the difference between valid and sound.
Valid = good structure; sound = good structure plus true premises.

notes.t: Argument forms: valid and invalid
pts: Modus ponens (valid): If A then B. A. Therefore B.
Disjunctive syllogism (valid): Either A or B. Not A. Therefore B.
Affirming the consequent (INVALID): If P then Q. Q. Therefore P.
Example of affirming the consequent: If there is an epidemic, the government acts. The government is acting on obesity. So obesity is an epidemic — but the government may act for other reasons.
defs: Modus ponens
If A then B; A; therefore B — a valid form.
Disjunctive syllogism
Either A or B; not A; therefore B — a valid form.
Affirming the consequent
The invalid form: if P then Q; Q; therefore P.
tips: To show an argument is invalid, describe a case where the premises are true and the conclusion false.
rq: Why is affirming the consequent invalid?
Q could be true for some other reason, so the premises can be true while P is false.
Name the form: "If it rains the ground is wet. It rains. So the ground is wet."
Modus ponens (valid).

units.name: 2.3 Evaluating arguments: acceptability, relevance, sufficiency
units.ov: Evaluate arguments by acceptability, relevance and sufficiency (ARS).
must: ARS definitions.
Inductive → fails full sufficiency; valid-but-unsound → fails acceptability.

notes.t: The ARS criteria
pts: Acceptability: are the premises true or reasonable to believe?
Relevance: do the premises actually bear on the conclusion?
Sufficiency: do the premises give enough support for the conclusion?
An inductive argument never fully meets sufficiency — its premises make the conclusion probable, never guaranteed.
A valid but unsound argument fails acceptability (structure is fine, a premise is false).
defs: Acceptability
Whether the premises are true or reasonable to accept.
Relevance
Whether the premises are actually connected to the conclusion.
Sufficiency
Whether the premises provide enough support to establish the conclusion.
tips: Two classic questions: "Which criterion does an inductive argument not fulfil?" → sufficiency. "Which does a valid but unsound argument fail?" → acceptability.
rq: Which criterion will an inductive argument never fully fulfil, and why?
Sufficiency — its premises only make the conclusion probable.
Which criterion does a valid but unsound argument fail?
Acceptability — at least one premise is false.

units.name: 2.4 Informal fallacies
units.ov: Know the common informal fallacies with a definition and example each, and when slippery slopes and dilemmas are legitimate.
must: Straw man, weak analogy, hasty generalisation, equivocation, appeal to emotion.
Slippery slope (causal vs conceptual) and false dilemma — and when they are not fallacies.

notes.t: Common fallacies
pts: Straw man: misrepresenting an opponent's view as weaker or more extreme, then attacking that version.
Weak analogy: arguing two things are alike in one respect because they share irrelevant or weak similarities ("employees are like nails").
Hasty generalisation / anecdotal evidence: generalising from one or a few cases (e.g. "my goddaughter says everyone in her class uses ChatGPT").
Equivocation: a word shifts meaning mid-argument ("efficient learning" → "an efficient childhood").
Appeal to emotion / rhetorical questions: persuading by feelings instead of reasons.
defs: Straw man
Attacking a distorted, weaker version of someone's argument instead of the real one.
Weak analogy
Drawing a conclusion from a comparison whose similarities are not relevant or strong enough.
Hasty generalisation
Drawing a general conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases.
Equivocation
Using a word in two different senses within one argument.
tips: For each fallacy: name it, define it, and give a short example — that is a full answer.
rq: Define the straw man fallacy with an example.
Misrepresenting someone's view then attacking it: "She wants stricter gun checks, so she wants to ban all guns."
What is wrong with "Employees are like nails; nails need hitting on the head, so employees do too"?
Weak analogy — the similarity between employees and nails is irrelevant to how people should be treated.
Which fallacy: "my goddaughter says almost everyone in her class uses ChatGPT, so all students cheat"?
Hasty generalisation / anecdotal evidence.

notes.t: Slippery slope and false dilemma
pts: Slippery slope: a small first step will supposedly lead through a chain to an extreme outcome; each link is asserted, not shown, and probabilities multiply (five 70% links ≈ 17%).
Causal vs conceptual slippery slopes: the conceptual version (accepting A commits you to B by consistency) can be strong, e.g. euthanasia debates.
False dilemma: "Either A or B" when other options exist. The form (disjunctive syllogism) is valid; the first premise is false.
Respond to a slope by attacking the weakest link or showing where a line can be drawn; to a dilemma by naming one credible third option.
defs: Slippery slope
Claiming a first step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome without showing each link.
False dilemma
Presenting two options as the only ones when others exist.
tips: Say when each is NOT a fallacy (genuine evidence for each link; genuinely exhaustive options like even/odd) — that is where marks are.
rq: Why can a valid argument still be a false dilemma?
Its form is a valid disjunctive syllogism, but the "either A or B" premise is false because other options exist.
How do you respond to a slippery slope argument?
Find the weakest link and ask for evidence, or show a clear point where a line could be drawn.

units.name: 3.1 Utilitarianism, deontology and virtue ethics
units.ov: Three ethical theories: consequences (utilitarianism), duties (deontology), character (virtue ethics), applied to punishment.
must: One-line definition of each theory.
Run all three on one example.
Scapegoat objection to utilitarianism; forward vs backward-looking punishment.

notes.t: The three ethical theories
pts: Utilitarianism (consequentialism): the right action produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number — judged by outcomes.
Deontology (Kant): some actions are right or wrong in themselves; follow duties/rules and treat people as ends, never merely as means.
Virtue ethics (Aristotle): ask what a good (virtuous) person would do; focus on character — honesty, courage, compassion.
Everyday example — friend's bad haircut: utilitarian weighs feelings; deontologist won't lie; virtue ethicist is honest but kind.
defs: Utilitarianism
The right action is the one that produces the best overall consequences (most happiness for most people).
Deontology
Morality is about duties and rules; some actions are wrong regardless of consequences.
Virtue ethics
Morality is about developing good character and acting as a virtuous person would.
tips: Use one example and run all three theories on it — the clearest way to show you understand the difference.
rq: How would each theory approach finding a lost wallet full of cash?
Utilitarian: return it if that produces most happiness overall; deontologist: return it — stealing is wrong; virtue ethics: an honest person returns it.
What is the key difference between utilitarianism and deontology?
Utilitarianism judges by consequences; deontology by whether the act follows a moral duty, regardless of consequences.

notes.t: Applied: punishment and the death penalty
pts: Utilitarian punishment is forward-looking: punish if it deters or protects society.
Classic objection: utilitarianism could justify punishing an innocent scapegoat if it produced good outcomes.
Deontology/retributivism is backward-looking: punish because it is deserved, in proportion to the crime.
Virtue ethics asks what a just and compassionate society/judge would do, and what punishment says about our character.
defs: Scapegoat objection
Utilitarianism seems to allow punishing an innocent person if it maximises overall happiness — which seems clearly wrong.
tips: Apply each theory to the serial-killer/death-penalty case: forward-looking (utility), backward-looking (desert), character-based (virtue).
rq: How would each theory decide on the death penalty for a serial killer?
Utilitarian: only if it deters/protects more than alternatives; deontology: if deserved and respects dignity (Kant arguably yes); virtue: what would a just, merciful society do.
What is the scapegoat objection to utilitarianism?
It could justify punishing an innocent person if that produced the best outcome, which conflicts with justice.

units.name: 4.1 Analysing an article: Rundell on AI in education
units.ov: Practice applying critical thinking: reconstruct the position, identify fallacies, evaluate the counterargument and analogy.
must: Offloading vs surrender.
Fallacies in the article: hasty generalisation, straw man, equivocation, appeal to emotion.
The sprinter analogy as an argument by analogy.

notes.t: Rundell's argument and how to critique it
pts: Position: AI in the classroom undermines learning. Reasons: cognitive harm, broken assessment, inequality, what education is for, wellbeing, democracy, wider harms.
Cognitive offloading = handing a task to a tool while keeping the ability; cognitive surrender = the ability itself withers and "we forget what was possible".
The goddaughter claim is anecdotal / hasty generalisation; the "efficient childhood" line is a straw man + equivocation + appeal to emotion.
Counterargument she addresses: "AI is coming, students must learn to use it". The Olympic sprinter analogy: the point of training was never the destination but the strength built.
defs: Cognitive offloading
Delegating mental work to a tool while keeping the ability to do it yourself.
Cognitive surrender
Losing the ability itself through dependence on a tool, and forgetting it was ever possible.
tips: For article questions: state the position, list reasons, then name fallacies with a quote and explain them.
rq: What is the difference between cognitive offloading and cognitive surrender?
Offloading keeps your ability (like a calculator); surrender loses it and you stop believing you could do it unaided.
What argument form is the Olympic sprinter passage?
An argument from analogy: like an athlete who runs to build strength, students write to build thinking — taking the bus/AI defeats the purpose.

units.name: K Rundell AI and education
units.ov: These notes cover Katherine Rundell's opinion article arguing that generative AI and large language models threaten young people's capacity to think, learn and resist injustice. She argues that AI undermines the process of reading and writing, creates cognitive dependence, widens inequality in schools, and ultimately endangers democracy. The pieces connect through one thread: thinking is built through effortful process, so replacing that process with AI weakens individual agency, education and collective power.
must: Central claim: AI risks becoming a barrier between young people and their capacity for thinking, experiment and discovery; this is an opinion article, so attribute claims to the author
Learning comes from the process of reading and writing, not the finished product (the Olympic athlete analogy is about process, not destination)
Writing is thinking: it turns half-built thoughts into sturdier, sharper ones and is not mere transcription
Cognitive offloading (handing tasks to a tool) differs from cognitive surrender (the author's term for forgetting what one can do unaided)

Evidence cited: people using AI-assisted learning gave up sooner; those who lost AI access performed worse and quit more; ChatGPT use was linked to the lowest brain activity and underperformance at neural, linguistic and behavioural levels

Academic integrity: students can now write essays without engaging with the source text, teachers cannot reliably detect AI work (especially edited), and stress pushes some to cheat; this does not mean all students cheat

Inequality: cheap AI teaching may be adopted under institutional pressure, with poorer schools using more LLM technology while rich schools move away from tech; good teachers teach human qualities a computer cannot
Risks of humanised, sycophantic chatbots for vulnerable children (the Sewell Setzer example illustrates this risk and is not a claim about all AI)

Democracy and justice: losing intellectual independence threatens democracy, and challenging concentrated wealth and power requires equal intellectual wealth (stamina, broad knowledge, real-time understanding)

Reading for pleasure and reading for power both matter, with power more urgent; the author also objects to AI's use of illegally taken labour and its environmental cost (data-centre electricity), and recognises benefits in medicine, disability access and Earth science, depending on who controls it
conn: Cognitive surrender and academic integrity: reliance on AI weakens the learning process, and finished work then stops indicating understanding, so detection and assessment both fail

Education inequality and power: if poorer schools get more AI and wealthier ones get human teaching, the intellectual wealth needed to challenge injustice becomes unequally distributed, linking SDG 4 (quality education) with SDG 10 (reduced inequalities)

Environmental cost and labour ethics versus AI's benefits: the sustainability trade-off between AI's uses (medicine, disaster warning, Earth science) and its data-centre energy demand and use of taken human labour
Reading, writing and democracy: books and shared reading build communal understanding, critical scrutiny and independent thought, which sustain democratic society against disinformation at scale
exq: Using Rundell's article, explain the difference between cognitive offloading and cognitive surrender, and evaluate the evidence she gives that AI-assisted learning harms performance.
'Learning comes from the process, not the product.' Discuss with reference to AI-generated essays and the problem of detecting them.
Critically assess the claim that AI in schools will widen educational inequality, referring to differences between rich and poor schools and to SDG 4.
To what extent is Rundell's argument a balanced assessment of AI, given that it is an opinion piece? Identify which claims are assertions that need attributing and which evidence supports them.
Evaluate the argument that losing intellectual independence through LLM use threatens democracy and the fight against injustice, including the roles of reading, writing and disinformation.

notes.t: Katherine Rundell on AI's threat to young people's minds and education
pts: AI could be transformative for good (medicine, disability access, law, disaster warning, Earth science), but its value depends on who controls it.
Large language models threaten to undermine the ability to think with clarity, which is needed in emergencies of justice.
Generative AI has already infiltrated young people's lives, and it has highlighted how fundamental books and reading are to shared understanding and democracy.
The author objects to AI's use of illegally taken human labour and its large environmental cost, including data-centre electricity demand.
The author's central claim is that AI risks becoming a barrier between young people and their capacity for thinking, experiment and discovery.
defs: Large language model (LLM)
An AI system trained on large amounts of text to generate and process human language, e.g. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.
Generative AI
AI that produces new content such as text, images or people-like outputs, rather than only analysing existing data.
Disinformation
Deliberately false information created and spread to mislead, which AI can produce at unprecedented scale.
tips: Distinguish the author's rhetorical position (opposed to AI use for children and young people) from a neutral summary of AI's pros and cons; the piece is an opinion article.
Note that the claims about power, data-centre demand and labour are the author's assertions and should be attributed, not presented as established fact.
rq: Why does the author argue that AI's benefits become 'completely irrelevant' in some circumstances?
If AI is controlled by crooks and despots, its potential benefits (medicine, justice access, disaster warning) are overridden by its use to oppress and mislead.
Why might reading matter more, not less, in an age of AI?
Books and reading underpin shared understanding of identity and democracy, and the ability to think independently, which AI may erode.

notes.t: AI-assisted learning, cognitive surrender and the risks of ed tech for children
pts: AI-assisted learning leads people to give up sooner; those who lost AI access performed worse and quit more often.
Using ChatGPT was linked to the lowest brain activity and underperformance at neural, linguistic and behavioural levels, a state the author calls cognitive surrender.
Children's work produced by AI can be mistaken by the young people themselves for their own mastery, undermining the work as an indicator of understanding.
Cheap AI teaching may be adopted under institutional pressure; rich schools may move away from tech while poorer schools use more LLM technology.
Good teachers teach human qualities (reading character, argument, love) that a computer cannot teach; constant interaction with humanised tech risks harming vulnerable children.
defs: Cognitive offloading
Handing mental work over to an external tool such as AI, reducing one's own cognitive effort.
Cognitive surrender
The author's term for the stronger state in which people, after relying on AI, forget what they were capable of doing unaided.
tips: Distinguish cognitive offloading (handing over tasks) from cognitive surrender (losing the sense of what one can do), as the author uses them differently.
Do not treat the Sewell Setzer example as a general claim about all AI; the author uses it to illustrate the risk of humanised, sycophantic chatbots for vulnerable adolescents.
rq: Why might a student who completes AI-assisted homework still fail to understand the material?
Because the polished AI output can be mistaken for their own mastery, so the work no longer reliably indicates understanding and the student may not realise the gap.
What would be lost if schools replaced teachers with AI on the grounds of efficiency?
Human qualities such as reading character, shaping arguments, commanding an audience and showing love, which the author argues only human teachers can pass on.

notes.t: AI, student learning and academic integrity
pts: Students can now produce essays without engaging with the source text, which is new compared with earlier cheating.
Learning comes from the process of reading and writing, not from the finished product, so AI cannot substitute for the thinking the work builds.
Teachers cannot reliably detect AI-written work from text alone, especially when it has been edited.
Student reading has declined, with smartphones already weakening engagement with complex text before LLMs arrived.
Students under extraordinary stress may give in to the temptation to use AI dishonestly.
tips: Do not confuse the author's claim that AI essays are hard to detect with a claim that all students cheat; the page says students 'many' may give in under stress.
The 'Olympic athlete' analogy is about the process of learning, not about the destination or the product.
rq: Why does the author argue that you cannot collaborate with AI in the way you cannot collaborate with a bus?
Because the value of the assignment lies in the mental strength and knowledge built through doing the work, which an outside tool cannot build for the student.
What is new about AI-generated essays compared with earlier forms of students not doing their work?
Earlier, students could write about a text without reading it, but AI can produce an essay with no human having engaged with the material at all.

notes.t: Thinking, writing and reading for power in the age of AI
pts: Writing is a form of thinking that transforms a half-built thought into something sturdier and sharper, not mere transcription.
Young people's first site of resistance to AI and injustice is knowledge and imagination, pursued through reading books and talking about them as a community.
Reading for pleasure is essential, but learning is also struggle and frustration, so reading must also build power of scrutiny and criticism.
Losing intellectual independence threatens democracy; letting a computer think for us endangers civilisation.
Fighting injustice against those with great financial wealth requires equal intellectual wealth: stamina, broad knowledge and the ability to understand events in real time.
tips: Do not confuse the author's call for reading for power with rejecting pleasure; the page argues both matter, with power more urgent.
Quote the essay's own claims (e.g. Forster's line) accurately when arguing that writing is thinking.
rq: Why does the author argue that spoken vivas and weekly exams cannot be the sole answer in the humanities?
Because the essay is a centuries-old method of thinking itself, not an arbitrary test; writing transforms thought, so it cannot be replaced by merely testing or certifying knowledge.
What would be lost if young people used AI to learn rather than reading and writing themselves?
Development of independent, sharp, tough thinking and the knowledge to resist; they would be sent into the world armed only with counterfeit knowledge.

units.name: K Rundell AI and education (clean)
units.ov: This material is an opinion piece arguing that generative AI and large language models threaten young people's capacity for independent thinking, which the author sees as essential to justice and to resisting concentrated wealth and power. It links cognitive harms (offloading, surrender), educational harms (work no longer shows mastery, inequality, loss of human skills), and the case for the essay and reading as methods of thought and resistance.
must: Core thesis: LLMs threaten the teaching and learning that build the clear, independent thinking needed in matters of justice; present this as the author's argument, not established empirical fact.

Cognitive offloading means delegating thinking to a tool so the user exerts less effort; cognitive surrender is the stronger form, where people stop reasoning and lose confidence in what they could do unaided.
Key evidence: people who lost AI access performed worse and quit more often; quote the 10-minute study and the MIT study precisely.

Student work no longer reliably indicates mastery, because it can look like understanding while reflecting AI output. The author stresses students' own vulnerability and mistaken self-assessment, not that all students cheat.
Inequality: cheap AI teaching may be pushed onto poorer schools while wealthier schools restrict it, widening the gap.
Human skills such as argument, communication and understanding character cannot be modelled by a computer. Humanised chatbots also pose emotional risks to vulnerable adolescents.
The essay's value lies in the process of reading and writing, which turns half-formed thoughts into sharper ones, not in the finished product. Detecting AI from text alone is unreliable.
Proposed responses are partial, not sole answers: spoken vivas and weekly exams in the humanities. The essay is not the only valid method.

Lack of real understanding is especially dangerous in law (justice), philosophy and English (the text is central). Children also get deeper meaning from paper than from screens, partly because the brain is connected to the body.

Reading serves pleasure and, more urgently, power. It is the young person's first site of resistance to people with vast financial wealth, and it demands intellectual wealth, stamina, broad knowledge and perception, ideally shared as community.
conn: Cognitive offloading leads to surrender, which leads to giving up sooner. This links the psychological evidence to the educational claim that process matters more than product.
Unreliable AI detection plus work that no longer shows mastery explains why the author proposes vivas and exams, and why the essay's value is defended as process.
AI-driven inequality between poor and wealthy schools connects to the framing of struggle against financial wealth, so intellectual wealth becomes a matter of justice.
Disinformation, surveillance and weakened independent thinking join the educational argument to the political stakes of reading for power.
exq: Explain the difference between cognitive offloading and cognitive surrender, and use the evidence cited (the 10-minute study and the MIT study) to assess how strongly the author's claim is supported.
Why does the author argue that student work is no longer a reliable indicator of understanding, and why is this not the same as claiming all students cheat?
Evaluate the author's view that the essay's value lies in process rather than product. How far do vivas and weekly exams answer the problem of unreliable AI detection?
Discuss how AI in education could widen inequality between poorer and wealthier schools, and what this implies for justice.
The passage says reading serves both pleasure and power. Explain why the author calls power the more urgent purpose and what qualities resistance requires.

notes.t: AI and education: the threat to young people's thinking
pts: Generative AI could be used to destabilise shared reality and spread disinformation at unprecedented scale, and could aid mass surveillance and authoritarian control.
Large language models threaten the teaching and learning that build clear, independent thinking needed in matters of justice.
AI-assisted learning leads people to give up sooner: those who lost AI access performed worse and quit more often.
Reliance on AI produces cognitive offloading and surrender, where people forget what they were capable of doing themselves.
Children take deeper meaning from text on paper than on screen, partly because the brain is connected to the body.
defs: Cognitive offloading
Delegating thinking tasks to an external tool, such as AI, so the user exerts less mental effort themselves.
Cognitive surrender
A stronger form of offloading in which a person stops exercising their own reasoning and loses confidence in what they could achieve unaided.
Large language models (LLMs)
AI systems trained on large text corpora to generate human-like language, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.
tips: Distinguish the author's claims about harm to thinking from the separate environmental and labour-rights objections; the exam may ask about one specifically.
