Quote evidence precisely (e.g. the 10-minute study and MIT study) rather than paraphrasing loosely, since the argument rests on it.
rq: Why might AI-assisted problem-solving make people give up sooner once the AI is removed?
Because they became reliant on the tool's support and lost the stamina and self-belief needed to persist through frustration unaided.
Why might reading on paper support deeper understanding than reading on screen?
Physical, tactile engagement with the page is tied to how the brain works as part of the body, which supports deeper processing of meaning.

notes.t: AI and education: risks to children's intellectual development
pts: Students can now produce work that looks like their own understanding but reflects AI output, so the work no longer reliably indicates mastery.
Cheap AI teaching may be pushed onto poorer schools while wealthier schools restrict it, widening inequality.
Good teaching develops human skills such as argument, communication and understanding character, which a computer cannot model.
Humanised chatbots can pose serious emotional risks to vulnerable adolescents.
Universities already faced declining reading and text-parsing ability, and LLMs have made it possible to produce essays without reading the source.
tips: Don't confuse the author's claim that AI-produced work is no longer an indicator of understanding with the claim that all students cheat; the author stresses students' own vulnerability and mistaken self-assessment.
The passage is an opinion piece, so the points are the author's argument, not established empirical findings; state them as claims being made.
rq: Why does the author think AI-produced student work is a problem even when it looks like good work?
Because students may mistake AI's fluent output for their own mastery, so the work no longer indicates real understanding, leaving them vulnerable to speed and anxiety about looking stupid.
What makes the current situation different from students in the past skipping assigned reading?

Previously an essay still required engaging with the text to some degree; now sentences can be produced with no human behind them, so the essay can exist without the reading or even the student's writing.
Why might cheap AI teaching deepen educational inequality rather than reduce it?
Wealthy schools may restrict AI and keep human teachers, while poorer schools, under cost pressure, rely more heavily on LLM technology, so the gap widens.

notes.t: Why students cannot outsource thinking to AI; the essay as a method of thought; reading as
pts: Students must build thinking skill through the work itself; the essay's value lies in the reading and writing process, not the finished product.
Essays are a centuries-old method of thinking: writing transforms half-formed thoughts into sturdier, sharper ones.
Detecting AI-written work from text alone is unreliable; only misuse of AI is clearly identifiable.
Lack of genuine understanding is especially dangerous in law, where it undermines justice, and in philosophy and English, where the text itself is central.
Reading for pleasure and reading to resist injustice are presented as the young person's first site of resistance, ideally shared as community rather than private activity.
tips: Do not confuse the essay's value as a learning process with the claim that AI can never be detected: the author says detection from writing alone is unreliable.
Note the author's qualification: the essay is not the only valid method, so spoken vivas and weekly exams are proposed as partial, not sole, answers in the humanities.
rq: Why does the author argue that a student's essay has value beyond the essay itself?
Because the value lies in the reading, writing and thinking the student undertakes to produce it, which builds intellectual strength, not in the product as such.
Why might spoken vivas or weekly exams not fully replace the essay in the humanities?
Because the essay is itself a method of thinking that transforms a nascent thought into something sturdier, so it is not merely an arbitrary test format.
Why does the author say learning should not be equated only with 'easy' pleasure?
Because learning is often a struggle and frustration with rare epiphanies, so pleasure in a broader sense includes difficult, discomfiting effort.

notes.t: Reading for power and the stakes of intellectual wealth
pts: The passage frames a looming struggle against people with vast financial wealth, and argues that resisting them requires matching intellectual wealth.
Effective resistance demands particular personal qualities: toughness, stamina, broad knowledge, and the ability to perceive events as they unfold.
Reading serves two purposes: pleasure and delight, and, more urgently, acquiring power.
tips: Do not confuse the author's 'reading for power' with a rejection of reading for pleasure; the passage says both are vital, with power being more urgent.
The passage is a short excerpt with no sustainable development content; avoid importing course material that is not on this page.
rq: Why does the author argue that reading for power is more urgent than reading for pleasure in the current situation?

Because the author believes dark days are ahead and that resisting those with great financial wealth requires intellectual wealth, which reading builds; pleasure is valuable but less pressing than this need.
What does the phrase 'understand in real time what is being done to us' suggest about the kind of knowledge the author values?
It suggests practical, situational awareness: knowledge that lets people recognise manipulation or harm as it happens, rather than only understanding it afterwards.

units.name: Phil 1 CT  AI seminar (Extra notes)
units.ov: These notes cover Rundell's argument that AI should not be used to make education 'efficient', because the value of learning lies in the effortful process of reading, writing and thinking rather than in the product. They link this to the essay as an ancient method of thinking and to the analysis of her rhetoric and fallacies in the critical thinking discussion questions. The thread is that process builds cognitive skill, and AI shortcuts replace that process instead of supporting it.
must: Rundell's central thesis: education's value is in the process of thinking, not the product, so using AI to make learning 'efficient' defeats its purpose
Skipping effortful reading and writing loses the cognitive skills the process builds: swiftness, resilience and suppleness of thinking
Olympic-athlete/bus analogy: taking the bus in a sprint defeats the purpose because the training was the point
Claim that you cannot 'collaborate' with AI as a student must with a text, just as you cannot collaborate with a bus; this is about replacing the learning process, NOT a claim that AI is useless
Cognitive surrender vs cognitive offloading: surrender is deeper, as people stop exercising their own thinking and forget what intellectual possibilities they had
Pressure on students to use AI, and possible penalties for honesty, which Rundell presents as a problem with the current situation

The essay is an ancient method of thinking, not merely a testing or certification tool: writing turns half-formed thoughts into sharper, sturdier ones (Forster: we discover what we think once we write it)
Thinking needs a body of facts, ideas and texts to work with (the 'climbing frame' metaphor); you cannot think from nothing
Fallacy identification: the goddaughter line is anecdote or hasty generalisation; the 'efficient childhood' rhetorical question suggests a false equivalence between efficiency and value
conn: Process-over-product links the athlete analogy, the loss of cognitive skills and the essay as a thinking tool: each shows that bypassing effort removes the benefit
Cognitive surrender builds on the bus analogy: not collaborating with AI means handing over thinking, which then erodes awareness of what one could think
The claim that thinking needs knowledge (climbing frame) supports the objection to AI shortcuts, since skipping reading leaves nothing to think with
Evaluating Rundell's rhetoric (anecdote, rhetorical questions, analogy) connects to assessing whether her argument is sound, not just persuasive
exq: Explain Rundell's claim that the value of education lies in process rather than product. How does the Olympic-athlete/bus analogy support it, and where might the analogy fail?
Distinguish cognitive offloading from cognitive surrender. Why does Rundell regard the latter as more serious?
Identify and evaluate two fallacies or weak rhetorical moves in Rundell's argument (e.g. the goddaughter anecdote, the 'efficient childhood' question). Do they undermine her conclusion?

'The essay is not just an assessment tool but a method of thinking.' Explain this claim with reference to Forster and the climbing-frame metaphor, and assess whether AI could legitimately play any role in essay writing.
Does Rundell's argument imply that AI is useless in education? Use the 'collaborating with a bus' point to defend your answer.

notes.t: Critical thinking and AI in the classroom (Rundell)
pts: Rundell opposes using AI to make learning 'efficient', arguing that the value of education lies in the process of thinking, not the product produced.
Students who skip the effortful process of reading and writing lose the cognitive skills (swiftness, resilience, suppleness of thinking) that the process builds.
Rundell uses the Olympic-athlete analogy: taking the bus defeats the purpose of the sprint, because the training was the point.
Her core claim is that AI cannot be collaborated with in the way a student must engage with a text, just as one cannot collaborate with a bus.
Students feel pressure to use AI and may be penalised for honesty, which Rundell presents as a problem with the current situation.
defs: Cognitive surrender
Rundell's term for a deeper loss than cognitive offloading: people stop exercising their own thinking and so forget what intellectual possibilities they had.
tips: Do not confuse Rundell's claim that AI can't be collaborated with in the same way as a bus with a claim that AI is useless; her point concerns replacing the learning process.

Be precise when identifying fallacies: the goddaughter line appeals to anecdote and possibly hasty generalisation, while the 'efficient childhood' line is a rhetorical question suggesting a false equivalence between efficiency and value.
rq: Why does Rundell think the process of writing matters more than the finished essay, even if the essay is excellent?

Because the essay's value to the student lies in the reading, thinking and writing that produced it; these build lasting intellectual capacities and knowledge of the text that a product alone cannot provide.
Does the Olympic-athlete analogy show that AI is always harmful, or only that it is harmful when it replaces the training itself?
Only when it replaces the training: the analogy targets using AI to skip the effortful cognitive work the task is meant to develop, not every use of technology.

notes.t: Essay writing as a method of thinking (Rundell, critical thinking discussion questions)
pts: Thinking requires a body of facts, ideas and texts to work with; you cannot think from nothing.
The essay is not just a testing or certification tool but an ancient method of thinking; writing transforms a half-formed thought into something sharper and sturdier.
Writing is a process that clarifies thought: we often discover what we think only once we have written it down (Forster's point).
tips: Do not treat the essay as only an assessment device; the key claim is that writing itself is the act of thinking.
Use the 'climbing frame' metaphor: knowledge and texts are the material you need in order to think, not an optional extra.
rq: Why does Rundell argue that the essay is more than a method of assessment?
Because writing is a form of thinking that transforms nascent ideas into clearer, stronger ones, rather than merely recording a finished thought.
Why might writing reveal thoughts you did not know you had?
Putting ideas into words forces precision and structure, exposing gaps and vagueness that remain hidden while the thought stays in the head.

units.name: Phil 1 lecture 2 handout
units.ov: This lecture introduces philosophy as critical inquiry, taking Socrates as the model of a questioning, self-examining thinker who uses dialectic and Socratic ignorance to pursue truth and happiness. It then defines critical thinking and the basic vocabulary of argument: propositions, premises and conclusions. It also sets out the three skills of identifying, reconstructing and evaluating arguments. The Socratic attitude motivates critical thinking, and argument analysis is the practical toolkit for it.
must: Critical thinking: reasonable, reflective thinking about what to believe or do (Ennis); active, persistent, careful consideration of a belief in light of its supporting grounds (Dewey).
Its aim is to make us better deliberators and decision makers, including knowing which questions to ask before significant decisions.
Argument: a set of propositions in which one is the conclusion and the rest are premises offered as support. Its purpose is to convince others of a point of view.
Conclusion = the view being established (the claim the person is arguing for). Premises = the statements offered in support. Never mix them up.
Several claims together do not make an argument; there must be intended support for one claim by the others.

Proposition (statement): a sentence that can in theory be judged true or false. Questions and directives are not propositions and must be reworded as declaratives before use as premises or conclusions, including rhetorical questions.
Identifying arguments: read closely to work out the claim being made. Indicator words ('therefore', 'my reasons are') help but are not guaranteed, so always check the context.
Three linked skills: identify, reconstruct, evaluate arguments. They improve both our own arguments and our assessment of others'.
Socratic ignorance: a deliberate recognition of the limits of one's own knowledge that drives inquiry. It is not general ignorance.

Dialectic: inquiry by question and answer, testing claims through argument and counter-argument. Socrates' facets (critical thinker, self-examiner, gadfly/rebel, social activist) are distinct from his ultimate aim, the search for truth and happiness, possibly overcoming alienation.
conn: Socratic questioning and dialectic are the historical model for critical thinking: testing claims by asking for reasons is the same as evaluating premises and conclusions.
Socratic ignorance (admitting you don't know) motivates the careful reading and reconstruction needed to identify arguments instead of accepting received opinion.
Propositions underpin arguments: only truth-evaluable statements can be premises or conclusions, so questions or commands (including rhetorical ones) must be converted before reconstruction.
Socrates as gadfly or social activist links to the aim of critical thinking: challenging community assumptions is a form of better deliberation about what to believe and do.
exq: Define 'argument', 'premise' and 'conclusion', and explain with an example why a list of related claims need not form an argument.
Explain Socratic ignorance and why it is not simply ignorance. How does it relate to dialectic as a method?
Given a short passage containing a rhetorical question and a command, identify the conclusion and premises, rewording any non-propositions as statements.
Discuss the claim that Socrates is best understood as a critical thinker, self-examiner and gadfly, and whether these facets serve a deeper aim of truth and happiness.
Compare Ennis's and Dewey's definitions of critical thinking, and explain why indicator words like 'therefore' are helpful but unreliable for finding conclusions.

notes.t: Socrates and the Spirit of Philosophy: Critical Thinking
pts: Socrates valued independence of thought and a questioning attitude, seeking first-hand knowledge rather than accepting received opinion.
Socratic ignorance: recognising the limits of one's own knowledge is the starting point for genuine inquiry.
Socrates acted as a social activist, challenging the assumptions of his community through questioning.
Dialectic is the method of inquiry by question and answer, testing claims through argument and counter-argument.
The philosopher appears as critical thinker, self-examiner, and rebel/gadfly, and ultimately as a seeker of truth and happiness, possibly trying to overcome alienation.
defs: Socratic ignorance
The recognition that one does not really know what one claims to know, which motivates the search for knowledge through questioning.
Dialectic
A method of philosophical inquiry proceeding through dialogue, question and answer, in which claims are tested and refined.
Critical thinking
The disciplined practice of defining concepts, identifying arguments, and evaluating reasons for and against a claim.
tips: Do not confuse 'Socratic ignorance' with general ignorance; it is a deliberate acknowledgement of the limits of one's knowledge that drives inquiry.
Distinguish the facets (critical thinker, self-examiner, gadfly) from the ultimate aim (seeker of truth and happiness) when answering questions about Socrates' character.
rq: Why might admitting ignorance be a better starting point for inquiry than claiming knowledge?
Admitting ignorance removes false certainty, opening the question to genuine examination and first-hand investigation rather than reliance on unexamined opinion.
How does the 'gadfly' role connect Socrates' critical thinking to his social activism?
By persistently questioning accepted beliefs, the gadfly stings society into examining its assumptions, so critical thinking becomes a public challenge to the community.

notes.t: Critical thinking and arguments
pts: Critical thinking is active, persistent and careful consideration of beliefs in light of the grounds that support them (Dewey).
The aim of critical thinking is to make us better deliberators and decision makers, including identifying the right questions to ask before significant decisions.
An argument is a set of propositions in which one is the conclusion and the rest are premises offered in support of it.
The point of offering an argument is to convince someone else of your point of view.
The point of view forms the conclusion; the statements offered in support are the premises.
defs: Critical thinking
Reasonable, reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do (Ennis); active, persistent and careful consideration of a belief in light of the grounds supporting it (Dewey).
Argument
A set of propositions of which one is a conclusion and the remainder are premises, intended as support for the conclusion.
Premise
A statement offered in support of the conclusion of an argument.
Conclusion
The point of view an argument seeks to establish, supported by its premises.
tips: Do not confuse premises with conclusion: the conclusion is the view being supported, premises are the supporting statements.
Mere presence of several claims does not make an argument; there must be intended support for one claim by others.
rq: Why does Dewey's definition stress 'persistent' and 'careful' consideration rather than just thinking?
Because critical thinking requires sustained, disciplined scrutiny of grounds, not casual or first-impression belief.
If a passage contains claims but no claim is offered as support for another, is it an argument? Why or why not?
No; an argument requires at least one statement (premise) intended to support a conclusion, so mere assertions are not arguments.

notes.t: Arguments: identification, reconstruction and evaluation
pts: Critical thinking in this course covers three linked skills: identifying arguments, reconstructing them, and evaluating them.
Learning argument skills improves both our ability to generate strong arguments and to assess arguments made by others.
To identify a conclusion, work out the claim the person is making; this requires close, accurate reading.
Premise and conclusion indicator words (e.g. 'therefore', 'my reasons for this are') are an alternative way to locate premises and conclusions.
defs: Argument
A set of claims in which one or more premises are offered as reasons supporting a conclusion.
Conclusion
The claim that a person is trying to establish, supported by the premises.
tips: Do not confuse a claim that is merely mentioned with the conclusion; the conclusion is the claim the person is arguing for.
Indicator words such as 'therefore' do not guarantee a conclusion; always check the surrounding text.
rq: Why might a close, accurate reading be more reliable than simply scanning for words like 'therefore' when identifying a conclusion?
Indicator words are not always present or used consistently, so the conclusion must be identified from the claim the author is actually making, which requires careful reading of the text.
How does learning to reconstruct an argument help you evaluate it?
Reconstructing it makes premises and conclusion explicit, so you can check whether the premises actually support the conclusion and whether each premise is plausible.

notes.t: Propositions in arguments
pts: Premises and conclusions must be propositions (statements) that can be judged true or false.
Most everyday sentences we say are propositions, including claims of fact, opinion and belief.
Questions and directives are not propositions and must be reworded before they can appear as premises or conclusions.
Turning a question into a statement lets it be assessed as a premise or conclusion in an argument.
defs: Proposition
A sentence that makes a claim about something and can, in theory, be judged to be true or false; also called a statement.
Question
A non-propositional sentence that asks something rather than claiming it is true or false; must be reworded to be used in an argument.
Directive
A non-propositional sentence that issues a command or instruction rather than asserting a claim.
tips: Do not include questions or commands directly as premises or conclusions; reword them as declarative statements.
Rhetorical questions in essays still count as non-propositions and need converting into claims.
rq: Why can't a question such as 'where's my drink?' serve as a premise in an argument?
Because it makes no claim that can be judged true or false, so it is not a proposition.
How does rewording 'Wouldn't Scotland and England continue to grow further apart?' into a statement help the argument?
It turns the rhetorical question into an assertion (P2) that can be evaluated as true or false and used as a premise.

units.name: Philosophy 1 fallacies seminar 2026
units.ov: This material is a seminar-preparation pack on informal logic. It covers how to identify and explain common argument forms and fallacies (ad hominem, no true Scotsman, correlation/cause, generalization errors, authority, popularity, equivocation, false dilemma, cherry picking, slippery slope). It also stresses a key distinction: some forms are always fallacious, while others are only sometimes weak and must be assessed with critical questions. Many fallacies are easily confused neighbours, so precise naming and distinguishing are central.
must: Distinguish forms that are always fallacious from forms that vary in strength; the latter are assessed with critical questions
Critical questions: the criteria used to judge the strength or weakness of a not-always-fallacious form (e.g. authority, correlation to cause, slippery slope)
Ad hominem attacks the arguer rather than the argument; name the variant: abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque, guilt by association
Hasty generalization (too few or unrepresentative cases) differs from sweeping generalization/secundum quid (general rule misapplied to exceptions)
Correlation vs cause, and post hoc ergo propter hoc ('after this, therefore because of this'): co-occurrence or sequence does not establish causation
No true Scotsman (ad hoc rescue): redefining a category to exclude a counterexample; do not confuse with ad hominem
Appeal to authority (ad verecundiam): fallacious when the authority lacks relevant expertise or their say-so is treated as conclusive; ad populum: popularity is not evidence of truth
Cherry picking (suppressed evidence): presenting only supporting evidence; false dilemma (false dichotomy): only two options offered when more exist
Equivocation: a term shifts meaning between premises and conclusion
Use the required readings (Tindale, Walton, Hanscomb, IEP) and give a clear own-words definition plus two examples, one of your own invention
conn: Hasty generalization, sweeping generalization and cherry picking all misuse evidence, yet they err differently: sample size, rule application, and selective omission
Correlation/cause and post hoc connect with slippery slope, since all involve unjustified causal claims that critical questions can test
Ad hominem, ad populum and appeal to authority all shift attention from the argument's content to people (the arguer, the crowd, the expert), and authority is a form needing critical questions
No true Scotsman and false dilemma both manipulate categories or options to protect a claim; equivocation does so by shifting meaning
exq: Explain the difference between hasty and sweeping generalization, giving one original example of each and stating which error is made in each.
Name and define the four variants of ad hominem, and show with an example how tu quoque differs from guilt by association.
A study finds that cities with more ice cream sales have more drownings. Identify the fallacy, explain why the inference fails, and suggest critical questions to test a causal claim.
Which argument forms are always fallacious and which depend on critical questions? Use appeal to authority to show how critical questions assess strength.
Construct an example of no true Scotsman on a topic you care about, explain how it protects the claim from refutation, and say why it is not ad hominem.

notes.t: Argument forms and fallacies seminar preparation
pts: Students must research their assigned argument form or fallacy and describe it in their own words.
Each student must provide two examples, one of which is their own invention, ideally on a topic they care about.
Some argument forms are always fallacious, while most vary in strength or weakness.
For non-always-fallacious forms, critical questions are used to assess strength or weakness.
Required reading should be used rather than poor-quality internet sources.
defs: Critical questions
Criteria used to determine the strength or weakness of an argument form that is not always fallacious.
tips: Do not rely on poor-quality internet sources; use the assigned required reading instead.
Distinguish clearly between forms that are always fallacious and those that are only sometimes weak.
rq: Why might some argument forms be always fallacious while others are only sometimes weak?
Some forms have a structure that guarantees invalidity or unreliability regardless of content, whereas others depend on the specific premises and context, so their strength varies.

notes.t: Common argument forms and fallacies (seminar research task)
pts: The seminar task is to research the fallacies listed beside one number (e.g. 1a and 1b), so each student covers a matched pair.
Ad hominem attacks the person making an argument rather than the argument itself; variants include abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque and guilt by association.
No true Scotsman is an ad hoc rescue that redefines a category to exclude a counterexample, protecting a claim from refutation.
Confusing correlation with cause assumes that because two things occur together, one causes the other; post hoc ergo propter hoc assumes causation from temporal sequence.
Hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too few cases, while sweeping generalization applies a general rule to cases where exceptions apply; these are different errors.
defs: Ad hominem
A fallacy in which an argument is rejected by attacking the character, motives or circumstances of the person advancing it rather than addressing its content.
Post hoc ergo propter hoc
Latin for 'after this, therefore because of this': the fallacy of inferring causation merely from one event preceding another.
Ad populum
Appeal to popular opinion: arguing that a claim is true because many people believe or accept it.
Secundum quid
The fallacy of applying a general rule without accounting for relevant special circumstances (sweeping generalization).
False dilemma
Presenting only two options as if they were the only possibilities when further alternatives exist.
Cherry picking
Selectively presenting only the evidence that supports a position while suppressing contrary evidence.
tips: Do not confuse hasty generalization (too few samples) with sweeping generalization (rule misapplied to exceptions); they are distinct fallacies.
Name the specific variant of ad hominem (abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque, guilt by association) rather than just 'ad hominem'.
rq: Why is ad hominem a fallacy even when the person attacked really is biased?
Because a speaker's character or motives do not logically bear on whether the premises support the conclusion; the argument must be assessed on its content.
How does a no true Scotsman move differ from simply revising a definition for good reason?
It adjusts the definition only to exclude a counterexample, without independent justification, making the claim unfalsifiable.
What might make a slippery slope argument fail?
It asserts a chain of consequences without evidence that each step will actually follow, or that the chain cannot be halted.

notes.t: Required reading for fallacies seminar (ad hominem, no true Scotsman, correlation/cause, p
pts: The page is a reading list: each fallacy is paired with named chapters or sections in Tindale, Walton, Hanscomb, and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
Ad hominem arguments are covered in Tindale's Fallacies & Argument Appraisal, Ch.5, and the IEP entry.
The 'No true Scotsman' fallacy is also called 'ad hoc rescue' and is covered in Hanscomb, Ch.8, p.209.
Confusing correlation with cause is covered in Tindale's section on 'Argument from correlation to Cause' and in Walton, Fundamentals of Critical Argumentation, Ch.9.
Slippery slope arguments are covered in Tindale, Ch.9, pp.185-188, Hanscomb, Ch.8, pp.210-18, and the IEP.
defs: False dilemma
Also called false dichotomy, false choice or 'black or white': presenting only two options when more exist.
tips: Know which textbook chapter covers each fallacy, since the reading list pairs them differently across sources.
Do not confuse 'ad hoc rescue' with the ad hominem fallacy; they are separate entries on this list.
rq: Why might a 'no true Scotsman' move be called an ad hoc rescue?
It redefines the group criteria after a counterexample appears, protecting the generalisation without independent justification.

notes.t: Fallacies: references and reading list (page 4)
pts: The page is a reading list pointing to textbook chapters and online encyclopedia entries for several informal fallacies.
Each fallacy is linked to a specific chapter and page range in Hanscomb's Critical Thinking: The Basics (2nd Ed.), with IEP entries as supplementary sources.
Arguments from authority (ad verecundiam) are covered in Tindale's Fallacies & Argument Appraisal, Ch.7.
Hasty and sweeping generalization (secundum quid, 'fallacy of accident') are both covered in Hanscomb Ch.8, pp.203-6.
Cherry picking is also called 'suppressed evidence' and is covered in Hanscomb Ch.8, pp.204-5.
defs: Argument from authority (ad verecundiam)
Fallacy of appealing to an authority who is not a genuine expert on the relevant matter, or treating their say-so as conclusive.
Appeal to popular opinion (ad populum)
Fallacy of arguing that a claim is true or good simply because many people believe or accept it.
Equivocation
Fallacy of using a word or phrase with two or more different meanings within one argument, so the premises and conclusion shift in sense.
Cherry picking (suppressed evidence)
Fallacy of selecting only the evidence that supports a conclusion while omitting relevant counter-evidence.
Hasty generalization
Fallacy of drawing a general conclusion from an insufficient or unrepresentative sample.
Sweeping generalization (secundum quid)
Fallacy of applying a general rule to a particular case where exceptions or special circumstances make the rule inapplicable.
tips: Do not confuse hasty generalization (too small a sample) with sweeping generalization (rule misapplied to an exception).
Popular opinion is not evidence of truth; an appeal to popularity is fallacious even if the belief is widespread.
rq: Why might an appeal to authority be fallacious even when the authority is well known?
Because fame or status does not guarantee expertise on the specific question; the authority must be relevant and reliable in that field.
How does cherry picking differ from hasty generalization?
Cherry picking selects favourable evidence while hiding contrary evidence; hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too few cases.

units.name: Philosophy 1 fallacies seminar handout
units.ov: This material introduces rhetoric, in neutral and negative senses, and contrasts it with philosophy, which aims at truth rather than mere persuasion. It sets out Aristotle's three means of persuasion (logos, pathos, ethos) and a catalogue of common informal fallacies that exploit persuasion at the expense of rational argument. The link is that fallacies are the working tools of negative rhetoric, and spotting them is how critical thinking resists it.
must: Distinguish the neutral sense of rhetoric (skilful persuasive language) from the negative sense (underhand, misleading language that undermines critical thinking), which Socrates and Plato criticised.
Aristotle's three means of persuasion: logos (content, argument forms, examples), pathos (audience emotions), ethos (speaker's character); these are Aristotle's categories, not Socrates' or Plato's.

Philosophy aims at truth through self-examination, open-mindedness and willingness to be corrected (the socially progressive gadfly); rhetoric aims at persuasion, producing belief or conviction rather than knowledge.

Plato (Gorgias) held that rhetoric produces false confidence rather than real education, and is often driven by wealth and power; 'making the weaker argument the stronger' (Aristophanes, The Clouds) captures the negative sense.
Later Plato and Aristotle accepted legitimate uses of rhetoric, such as gaining and keeping attention, provided it serves independent intellectual engagement.
Ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument; it is fallacious only when character replaces evidence about the claim, not merely when a person is mentioned.
Causal and chain fallacies: confusing correlation with cause, and slippery slope (fallacious only when the chain of consequences is unsupported).
Fallacies of authority and popularity: appeal to authority and appeal to popular opinion accept a claim without evaluating the evidence.
Fallacies of evidence and scope: hasty/sweeping generalization, cherry picking (distinct from hasty generalization), false dilemma, perfectionist fallacy, equivocation, no true Scotsman.
Know where other fallacies are covered: straw man in the Argument Reconstruction slides; affirming the consequent and argument from analogy in the Assessing Arguments handout.
conn: Aristotle's logos, pathos and ethos map onto fallacies: ad hominem and appeals to authority relate to ethos, emotive or popular appeals to pathos, and faulty argument forms and examples to logos.
Plato's critique of rhetoric (false confidence, persuasion without knowledge) explains why fallacies matter: they generate conviction without justification.
Hasty generalization and cherry picking both misuse evidence but differ (too little evidence versus selective evidence), and can co-occur.
The qualifications (ad hominem, slippery slope, Plato's later view of rhetoric) show that the label depends on context, so exam answers should justify why an argument is fallacious.
exq: Distinguish the neutral and negative senses of rhetoric, and explain which Socrates and Plato objected to and why.
Explain Aristotle's three means of persuasion and give an example of a fallacy associated with each.
Is every argument that mentions a person's character an ad hominem? Explain, using the conditions for fallacy.
Compare hasty generalization and cherry picking, with an example from sustainable development policy where both occur.
To what extent did Plato and Aristotle accept rhetoric? Discuss how philosophy differs from rhetoric in its aims.

notes.t: Rhetoric: neutral vs negative meanings and Aristotle's three means of persuasion
pts: Socrates and Plato contrast philosophy with non-dialogical education (e.g. rote learning) and with the practice of rhetoric.
Rhetoric has a neutral sense (skilful persuasive language) and a negative sense (underhand, misleading use of language that disrupts critical thinking).
The negative sense is captured by the ability to 'make the weaker argument the stronger', a phrase from Aristophanes' The Clouds.
Rhetoric was taught by the Sophists and was highly effective in Athenian law courts and the Assembly, which created the problem Socrates and Plato responded to.
Aristotle identified three means of persuasion: logos (content, argument forms, examples), pathos (audience emotions) and ethos (speaker's character); all three can relate to fallacies.
defs: Rhetoric
The art of persuasive speaking or writing; neutrally, using language persuasively, negatively, using language in an underhand or misleading manner to persuade, undermining rationality.
Logos
Aristotle's means of persuasion concerning the content of a speech, including argument forms and the use of examples.
Pathos
Aristotle's means of persuasion appealing to the emotions created in the audience.
Ethos
Aristotle's means of persuasion based on the character of the speaker.
tips: Do not confuse the neutral and negative senses of rhetoric; the negative sense is what Socrates and Plato criticised.
Remember that logos, pathos and ethos are Aristotle's categories, not Socrates' or Plato's.
rq: Why did Socrates and Plato see rhetoric as opposed to the spirit of philosophy, given it was effective in democratic Athens?
Because rhetoric aims at persuasion through potentially misleading means that disrupt critical thinking, whereas philosophy seeks truth through dialogue and rational examination.
How could a single persuasive speech use logos, pathos and ethos to produce a fallacy?

Logos might contain an invalid argument form, pathos might exploit emotion to replace evidence (e.g. appeal to pity), and ethos might rely on the speaker's authority rather than reasons (appeal to authority).

notes.t: Philosophy vs Rhetoric and the uses of rhetoric
pts: Philosophy aims at truth and involves self-examination, open-mindedness and willingness to be corrected; the philosopher is a socially progressive gadfly.
Rhetoric aims at persuasion and generates belief or conviction rather than knowledge.
Rhetoric is often driven by seeking wealth and political power rather than self-knowledge or social benefit.
Plato (Gorgias) saw rhetoric as producing false confidence in audiences rather than genuine education.
Plato and Aristotle later accepted that rhetoric has legitimate uses, such as gaining and maintaining attention, provided it serves independent intellectual engagement.
defs: Rhetoric
The art of persuasion, aiming to generate belief or conviction in an audience rather than knowledge.
Philosophy
The pursuit of truth through self-examination, open-mindedness and willingness to be corrected.
False confidence
The illusion or feeling of being right produced in an audience by rhetoric, without genuine education.
tips: Do not confuse rhetoric's goal (persuasion) with philosophy's goal (truth); persuasion alone does not guarantee truth.
Remember that Plato's critique was not absolute: later Plato and Aristotle accepted rhetoric's uses under conditions.
rq: Why did Plato think rhetoric is dangerous even when its audience feels convinced?
Because it produces belief or conviction and a feeling of being right without knowledge, so audiences are not truly educated.
What makes rhetoric acceptable by Aristotle's standards?
When it is used as a means to independent, intellectual engagement, e.g. capturing attention to support genuine reasoning.

notes.t: Argument forms and fallacies
pts: Ad hominem attacks the person making an argument rather than the argument itself.
Confusing correlation with cause assumes that because two things occur together, one must cause the other.
Slippery slope arguments claim that a small first step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome without showing why.
Appeals to authority accept a claim merely because an authority endorses it, rather than on the strength of evidence.
Appeal to popular opinion treats a claim as true simply because many people believe it.
defs: Ad hominem

A fallacy in which an argument is rejected or discredited by attacking the character, motives or circumstances of the person presenting it, rather than addressing the argument's premises or conclusion.
Slippery slope
A fallacy in which a claim that one step will trigger a chain of unlikely, increasingly extreme consequences is presented without adequate evidence for each link in the chain.
No true Scotsman fallacy
A fallacy in which a generalisation is protected from counterexamples by redefining the category so that any counterexample is excluded, e.g. 'No true Scotsman would do that.'
tips: Do not label an argument ad hominem merely because it mentions a person; it is fallacious only when the person's character replaces evidence about the claim.
A slippery slope is only fallacious when the chain of consequences is unsupported; some causal chains are genuinely likely.
rq: Why is an ad hominem attack a flaw even if the person attacked really is dishonest?
Because the truth of a premise or conclusion is independent of the speaker's character; the argument must be evaluated on its own reasons.
How could you test whether a correlation between two variables reflects a causal link?
Check for a plausible mechanism, control for confounding variables, look for temporal order, and seek experimental or dose-response evidence.

notes.t: Fallacies seminar: remaining fallacies and where others are covered
pts: Several fallacies are listed for study on this page: perfectionist fallacy, false dilemma, hasty/sweeping generalization, cherry picking, and equivocation.
The straw man fallacy is covered in the Argument Reconstruction slides, not on this page.
Affirming the consequent and argument from analogy are covered in the handout for Assessing Arguments.
defs: Perfectionist fallacy
Rejecting a claim, policy or action because it is not flawless or does not solve every problem completely, even when it is an improvement on the alternative.
False dilemma
Presenting a situation as having only two options when further alternatives exist.
Hasty/sweeping generalization
Drawing a general conclusion about a whole group from too few or unrepresentative cases (hasty), or applying a general rule to cases it does not properly cover (sweeping).
Cherry picking fallacy
Selecting only the evidence that supports a position while ignoring relevant evidence that counts against it.
Equivocation
Using a word or phrase with two or more different meanings within one argument so that the conclusion appears to follow when it does not.
tips: Do not confuse hasty generalization (too little evidence) with cherry picking (selective evidence); they can occur together but are distinct.
Straw man, affirming the consequent and argument from analogy are not on this page; refer to the Argument Reconstruction slides and Assessing Arguments handout.
rq: Why does cherry picking undermine a generalization even when every chosen example is accurate?
Because the selection is biased; omitted counter-evidence means the sample does not represent the whole, so the conclusion is unsupported.
How could you tell a false dilemma from a genuine two-option choice?
Check whether there are realistic alternatives beyond the two offered; if further options exist, the dilemma is false.

units.name: Philosophy 1 Socrates
units.ov: These notes introduce Socrates through Plato's Euthyphro and Apology, read alongside Kidd's commentary. Socrates is tried for impiety and corrupting the youth, and the underlying conflict is between state-sanctioned religious authority and his commitment to free, rational, independent thought. The Euthyphro shows his method (questioning a self-proclaimed expert), while the Apology shows his self-understanding and defence. The notes are brief, so the details of the arguments must be supplemented from the dialogues themselves.
must: The charges: impiety (not honouring the gods accepted by the Athenian state) and corrupting the youth
The core conflict: Socrates' insistence on freedom of thought and education that encourages rational, independent thinking vs. state religious and civic authority
Impiety is not simple atheism: it means failing to honour the state-accepted gods, or worshipping other gods
Euthyphro: Socrates tests whether Euthyphro really understands piety, while Euthyphro is prosecuting his own father for murder
Apology: Socrates' defence speech at trial, explaining the nature of his wisdom in contrast to people claiming religious expertise like Euthyphro
Socratic method: persistent questioning that exposes the gaps in claimed knowledge
The dialogues are Plato's, so they illustrate Kidd's points but are Plato's portrayal of Socrates
Be able to discuss Socrates' character, teaching approach, social/political role, criticisms of him, and modern equivalents
Be able to apply Socratic ideas to contemporary issues such as generative AI and education
conn: Euthyphro and Apology: the same critique of false expertise appears in both, in a private conversation and then in a public defence
The charge of corrupting the youth links to Socrates' teaching approach and to debates on education and independent thinking, including AI use today
Impiety and Socrates' political role: religion was part of civic identity, so questioning it was seen as a threat to the state
Socratic wisdom (awareness of one's own ignorance) links to the criticism that his questioning can unsettle society and offers no positive answers
exq: Explain the two charges against Socrates and assess how far they reflect a conflict between freedom of thought and state authority.
Using the Euthyphro, how does Socrates test whether Euthyphro understands piety? What does this reveal about his method?
In the Apology, how does Socrates contrast his own wisdom with that of people claiming religious expertise?
Is impiety the same as atheism? Discuss in relation to Socrates' trial.
What might Socrates say about the use of generative AI in education? Justify using his approach to teaching and independent thinking.

notes.t: Philosophy 1: Socrates – class instructions and reading task
pts: Socrates was tried for impiety (not worshipping the state-accepted gods) and for corrupting the youth, with the core conflict being his insistence on freedom of thought and education as encouraging rational, independent thinking.
In the Euthyphro, Socrates queries Euthyphro's logic to test whether he truly understands what piety is, while Euthyphro accuses his father of murder.
In the Apology, Socrates explains the nature of his wisdom in contrast to people like Euthyphro, who claim religious expertise.
Readings are Plato's dialogues used to illustrate Kidd's points and let students experience Socrates' style first-hand.
Reflection tasks ask what Socrates stands for, his personal characteristics, teaching approach, possible views on generative AI, social/political role, criticisms, and modern equivalents.
defs: Impiety
Lack of religious devotion; in Socrates' case, worshipping gods other than those accepted by the Athenian state, and corrupting the youth by teaching a similar impiety.
tips: Do not confuse impiety with simple atheism; it means failing to honour the gods accepted by the Athenian state.
Remember the Euthyphro is about Socrates' questioning of a self-proclaimed religious expert, while the Apology records his defence speech at trial.
rq: Why does Socrates' insistence on independent thinking clash with the Athenian state's charges against him?
Encouraging rational, independent thinking challenges state-accepted religious belief and authority, so it was framed as impiety and corruption of youth.
How does Socrates test whether Euthyphro truly understands piety?
By querying the logic of Euthyphro's claim that his father's act is wrong according to the gods, exposing whether his definition holds up under questioning.

units.name: 1 Front matter and drone ubiquity
units.ov: This material introduces a journal article on the ubiquity, use and ethics of military drones (unmanned aerial systems), covering their spread since 2002, the RAF Reaper's deployment in Afghanistan from 2007, and the range of platforms from micro air vehicles to Global Hawk. The central idea is that the drone debate is polarised and confused, because objections to drones as a technology are often mixed up with objections to targeted killing policy. The notes are thin, so the key skill is defining terms precisely and separating the different ethical targets of criticism.
must: Core distinction: objections to drones per se (the technology) versus objections to US 'targeted killings' (a policy that could use helicopters or special forces)
Definition: an unmanned aerial system (UAS) or remotely piloted aircraft system (RPAS) is an aircraft with no onboard pilot, controlled remotely by a crew through communications links
Definition: ISR means intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, the gathering and processing of information about an adversary or area
Drones are widespread in military operations, and US Army numbers have risen sharply since 2002
RAF Reapers were first deployed in Afghanistan in 2007 and gained firepower (armed capability) from 2008, flown by remotely located pilots
Drones cover a huge range of platforms, from micro air vehicles to Global Hawk
Drones are suited to 'dull, dirty or dangerous' jobs, a key argument in their favour
The debate is highly polarised and often unclear about what exactly is objected to, so answers should clarify the target of the objection
Do not assume drones replace all manned systems: the article contrasts ISR drones with combat platforms
conn: Distinguishing drones from targeted killing policy links the technology's ubiquity to the ethics: a policy objection would persist even if drones were replaced by helicopters or special forces
The range of platforms (micro air vehicles to Global Hawk) and the ISR versus combat distinction show that 'drone' covers very different uses, so moral judgments differ by role
The dull, dirty, dangerous rationale connects to remote piloting (Reapers flown from afar), which links operational benefits to ethical debates about distance from the battlefield
The rise in US drone numbers since 2002 and the RAF's 2007-2008 deployment link spread of the technology to the polarised debate
exq: Explain why the drone debate is described as polarised and confused. Distinguish between objections to drones per se and objections to targeted killing.
Define UAS/RPAS and ISR, and discuss how the range of drone platforms, from micro air vehicles to Global Hawk, complicates ethical evaluation.
Outline the timeline of drone use mentioned in the article (US Army growth since 2002; RAF Reapers in Afghanistan in 2007, armed from 2008) and assess what it shows about the spread of drones.
Would the ethical objections to US targeted killings disappear if helicopters or special forces were used instead of drones? Justify your answer.
Evaluate the claim that drones suit 'dull, dirty or dangerous' tasks, and say why this does not mean they replace all manned systems.

notes.t: Killer drones: ubiquity, use and ethical debate
pts: Drones are now widespread in military operations, with US Army numbers rising sharply since 2002.
The RAF's Reapers were first deployed in Afghanistan in 2007 and gained firepower from 2008, flown by pilots located remotely.
The debate on drones is highly polarised and often confused about what is actually being objected to.
Some objections target US 'targeted killings' rather than drones themselves, since such strikes could use helicopters or special forces.
Drones cover a huge range of platforms, from micro air vehicles to Global Hawk, and suit dull, dirty or dangerous jobs.
defs: Unmanned aerial system (UAS / RPAS)
An aircraft flown without an onboard pilot, controlled remotely by a crew via communications links.
ISR
Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance: gathering and processing information about an adversary or area.
tips: Do not treat all drone criticism as one issue; separate objections to drones per se from objections to targeted killing policy.
Remember the article contrasts drones with ISR and combat platforms, so avoid assuming drones replace all manned systems.
rq: Why might objecting to 'drones' be the wrong target for some critics of targeted killing?
Because the same targeted killings could be carried out by helicopter gunships or special forces, so the concern is about the act, not the remote means.
Why are drones considered attractive for dull, dirty or dangerous jobs?
They can operate around the clock and in treacherous conditions without putting a human crew at direct risk.

units.name: 2 Autonomy and the human-in-the-loop debate
units.ov: This material covers the debate over autonomy in armed drones: the UK terminology (Remotely Piloted Air Systems) that stresses human control, and the possibility of future fully autonomous 'human-out-of-the-loop' weapons. The ideas connect through one chain: technical limits (no reliable combatant/non-combatant discrimination) justify the human-in-the-loop requirement, while AI research and political incentives threaten it, and removing the human raises accountability problems.
must: Definition of RPAS: the UK MoD term for drones, stressing that a human operator remains in control even though many functions are automated.
Definition of human-out-of-the-loop: a fully autonomous weapon that identifies and fires on targets with no human decision-making.
Drone is not the same as autonomous: most drones are human-supervised, and autonomous killing is a future risk, not current practice.
Technical core of the UK position: no current system can reliably distinguish combatants from non-combatants in a combat zone, so a human must be in the decision process.
The UK position is conditional: the human stays in the loop until systems can meet Law of Armed Conflict standards. Do not present it as an absolute or permanent ban.
Why autonomy could arrive: AI target-selection research is advancing even though such systems are not yet armed.
Political driver: leaders attracted by casualty-free conflict may arm autonomous systems if the political or military situation changes, so current restraint is contingent.
Ethical and legal problem: if an autonomous system targets inaccurately, responsibility and accountability become unclear (the accountability gap).
Terminology is not neutral: 'RPAS' is a framing choice that emphasises human control despite extensive automation.
conn: Discrimination problem and Law of Armed Conflict: the technical inability to tell combatants from non-combatants is why the human-in-the-loop condition exists, and the LOAC standard is the benchmark for removing it.
Casualty-free warfare and political incentives: lower risk to own forces makes autonomous arming more attractive, undermining the current restraint.
Automation versus autonomy: many drone functions are automated, yet a human still makes the lethal decision. Questions often test where that line lies.
Accountability and human control: removing the human from the loop leaves unclear who is responsible (operator, commander, programmer, state) for inaccurate targeting.
exq: Distinguish between a Remotely Piloted Air System and a human-out-of-the-loop weapon, and explain why treating 'drone' and 'autonomous' as synonyms is a mistake.
Explain why the UK requires a human in the decision-making process, and evaluate whether this position is permanent or conditional.
Discuss how advances in AI target selection and political attraction to casualty-free conflict might lead to armed autonomous systems despite current policy.
Who should be held accountable if a fully autonomous weapon inaccurately targets civilians? Assess the challenges for responsibility and accountability.
Critically assess whether the term 'RPAS' accurately describes how modern military drones operate, given the high level of automation.

notes.t: Autonomous killing and the human-in-the-loop debate
pts: Drones are called Remotely Piloted Air Systems to stress that a person stays in control, even though many functions are automated.
No current system can reliably tell combatants from non-combatants in a combat zone, so the UK position requires a human in the decision-making process.
Research into AI target selection is advancing even though such systems are not yet armed, so fully autonomous killing could become possible.
Politicians attracted by casualty-free conflicts may arm autonomous systems when the political or military situation changes.
Fully autonomous 'human-out-of-the-loop' systems raise serious questions of responsibility and accountability if they target inaccurately.
defs: Remotely Piloted Air System (RPAS)
The UK MoD term for drones, emphasising that a human operator remains in control of the system rather than the platform acting entirely on its own.
Human-out-of-the-loop system
A fully autonomous weapon system that can identify and fire on targets without any human decision-making in the process.
tips: Do not treat 'drone' and 'autonomous' as synonyms: most drones are supervised by a person, and autonomous killing is discussed as a future risk rather than current practice.
Be precise that the UK position is conditional: the human stays in the loop until systems can meet Law of Armed Conflict standards.
rq: Why might renaming drones as RPAS be considered more accurate than calling them UAVs?
'Unmanned' implies no human input, whereas RPAS stresses that a person remains in control and supervises the system's activity, even when many functions are automated.
What would have to change for a drone system to move from supervised use to autonomous killing, and why is that change dangerous?

It would need the ability to make the qualitative assessments required by the Law of Armed Conflict, such as distinguishing combatants from non-combatants; if deployed before that is reliable, errors could cause unlawful deaths with unclear accountability.

units.name: 3 Distance, moral disconnection and psychological effects on operators
units.ov: This material examines whether physical stand-off in remote killing (sniper, fast-jet pilot, drone operator) produces moral disconnection, and what psychological effects follow for drone operators. It argues that distance does not map neatly onto emotional or moral separation: it can ease suspension of moral concern and reduce risk, yet operators still suffer PTSD, and detachment may either improve or impair conduct. Situational awareness limits are presented as technical rather than inherent to drones.
must: Stand-off (physical distance, from close contact to operation from thousands of miles away) is distinct from emotional separation; the two do not always correspond
Moral disconnection: emotional and moral distancing from killing caused by physical separation between attacker and target
Greater stand-off does not automatically make a moral difference between a sniper, a fast-jet pilot and a drone operator
Remote killing reduces risk to own personnel, which some argue is a moral imperative
Dehumanisation ('otherness', targets seen as expendable non-entities) and military training ease the emotional barrier to killing
Distance can ease suspension of moral concerns, making terrible acts more possible
Distance does not guarantee emotional separation: drone operators can suffer PTSD
Counter-argument: remote operators may suffer less harm than ground combatants, and physical safety gives time and detachment to deliberate and double-check decisions

Situational awareness problems (bandwidth, time delay, sensor field of view) are technical, mostly sensor-choice issues and being minimised; richer awareness comes from other drones and ISR assets, though shift changes can break continuity
Evidence is mixed: detachment may aid just behaviour, but the 2006 US MHAT report links anger and combat stress to mistreatment of non-combatants
conn: Distance and risk reduction (moral imperative to protect own forces) versus distance easing moral disconnection and dehumanisation: the same stand-off cuts both ways
Moral disconnection versus PTSD evidence: the claim that distance detaches operators is challenged by operator trauma, so 'dislocation' as a source of moral distance is questioned
Detachment as aid to better decisions (time to deliberate) versus MHAT evidence that stress and anger worsen treatment of non-combatants, linking psychology to conduct and legality of targeting

Situational awareness as a technical issue (sensors, ISR, shift handover) linking to whether drones are inherently morally different from other platforms; civilian operators would lose immunity, so distance does not remove their risk
exq: Does physical stand-off create a moral difference between a sniper, a fast-jet pilot and a drone operator? Use the concepts of stand-off and moral disconnection in your answer.
Critically assess the claim that drone operators are protected from psychological harm by distance, with reference to PTSD and the contrasting argument about inhibitions against killing.
Explain how dehumanisation and military training interact with physical distance to ease killing, and evaluate whether drones add anything distinctive.
To what extent are drones' situational awareness problems inherent to the platform rather than technical? Discuss bandwidth, time delay, sensor field of view, ISR support and shift changes.
Evaluate the argument that remote killing is a moral imperative because it reduces risk to own personnel, considering the 2006 MHAT findings and the status of civilian operators.

notes.t: Physical distance, moral disconnection and killing by drone
pts: Greater physical stand-off does not automatically mean a moral difference between a sniper, a fast-jet pilot and a drone operator.
Remote killing can reduce risk to one's own personnel, which some argue is a moral imperative.
Military training and dehumanisation of an enemy ease the emotional barrier to killing.
Physical distance can ease the suspension of moral concerns, making terrible acts more possible.
Physical distance does not guarantee emotional separation; remote operators can suffer PTSD.
defs: Dehumanisation
Promoting a sense of 'otherness' in a perceived threat group so its members are seen as non-entities, expendable or undeserving, easing the act of killing.
Stand-off
The distance between a combatant and the target, ranging from close contact to remote operation from thousands of miles away.
Moral disconnection
The emotional and moral distancing from killing caused by physical separation between the attacker and the target.
tips: Do not assume physical distance removes all psychological impact; the text stresses PTSD among drone pilots.
Distinguish stand-off (physical distance) from emotional separation, which the text argues do not always correspond.
rq: Why might remote drone killing be seen as ethically preferable, and why does the author question that view?
It reduces risk to one's own personnel; but the same effect is achieved either way, and distance may erode moral restraint and emotional response.
Why might a bomber crew kill civilians from altitude yet refuse to kill with a knife?
Physical distance dulls emotional and moral response, so the act feels abstract rather than personal.

notes.t: Psychological and situational effects of drone operation at a distance
pts: Remote operators may experience less psychological harm than ground combatants, since inhibitions against killing may not need to be overcome in the same way.
Physical safety removal gives the operator time and emotional detachment to deliberate and double-check decisions, potentially improving them.
Situational awareness problems are largely technical (bandwidth, time delay, sensor field of view) and are being minimised, not inherent to drones.
Drone operators can build richer situational awareness by drawing on images from other drones and ISR assets, though switching shifts can break continuity of focus.
Evidence is mixed: detachment may aid just behaviour, while a 2006 US MHAT report links anger and combat stress to mistreatment of non-combatants.
defs: Dislocation (moral/geographic)
Physical or emotional separation between the operator and the killing they perform, which the author questions as a source of moral distance.
Situational awareness
An operator's understanding of the current state of the battle space, dependent on sensor quality, data feeds and access to other assets.
tips: Do not treat the drone's situational-awareness problems as fundamental; the author argues they are technical and mostly stem from sensor choice, not platform type.
Remember the trade-off: civilian operators would lose immunity from attack, so distance does not remove their risk of being targeted.
rq: Why might drone operators suffer less psychological damage than infantry, and what would test this claim?

Inhibitions against killing may not need to be overcome in the same way, reducing repercussions; comparing quantitative and qualitative PTSD incidence against combatants physically present in the battle space would test it.
Does physical distance automatically make decisions better?
Not automatically: distance allows calm, double-checked decisions, but situational awareness and continuity of focus can suffer, and evidence on emotional distance and behaviour is mixed.

units.name: 4 Legal status, participation in hostilities and accountability
units.ov: This material examines how remote-operated armed drones challenge the legal status of operators, the concept of direct participation in hostilities, and the allocation of accountability under the Law of Armed Conflict (LOAC). Physical distance does not remove liability: status determines protection and targetability, participation determines who may be attacked, and accountability is spread along the targeting chain according to obedience to LOAC and honesty of information.
must: Physical distance from the battlefield does not remove legal liability; LOAC obligations and participation rules still apply to remote operators.
Civilian drone operators outside the conflict country may lose combatant status and hence prisoner-of-war protection.
Civilian operators using lethal force not in self-defence may face murder charges, as they lack combatant immunity.
Direct participation in hostilities: acts directly contributing to an attack or military operation can make even a non-combatant lawfully targetable for that period.
Remote operation blurs the line of direct participation: anyone directly facilitating an attack, even a chauffeur, may be legitimately targeted.
Accountability is distributed across everyone in the targeting chain; each person must obey LOAC and may refuse unlawful orders.
Culpability depends on the honesty, not merely the accuracy, of the situational assessment behind an action or order.
Anyone who withholds pertinent information shares moral responsibility for resulting mistakes.
JTAC: a qualified person who relays the commander's engagement instructions to the delivering platform (artillery or drone), so is a link in the accountability chain.
Operators moving between combat and home life face psychological strain and potential cognitive dissonance.
conn: Status and participation: losing combatant status (no POW protection, possible murder charges) links to direct participation, which determines targetability and liability.
Targeting chain and culpability: the distributed accountability of commanders, JTACs and operators links to honesty of assessment and withholding of information.
Remote warfare and psychology: the blurring of battlefield and home affects both legal participation and the operator's moral and psychological burden.
Right to refuse unlawful orders connects individual LOAC obligations to shared responsibility within a hierarchy.
exq: Explain why a civilian drone operator based outside the conflict country may lose combatant status, and discuss the legal consequences, including POW protection and potential murder charges.

A chauffeur drives a commander to a site from which a drone strike is launched. Using the concept of direct participation in hostilities, assess whether the chauffeur is lawfully targetable and for how long.
Discuss how accountability is distributed among commander, JTAC and drone operator, and the role of the right to refuse unlawful orders.
'Culpability depends on honesty, not accuracy.' Evaluate this statement with reference to an intelligence provider who withholds pertinent information before a mistaken strike.
Critically assess whether physical distance from the battlefield reduces legal liability and what psychological effects remote operators may experience.

notes.t: Killer Drones: legal status, participation in hostilities, and accountability
pts: Civilian drone operators outside the conflict country may lose combatant status and prisoner-of-war protection, and may face murder charges if they use lethal force not in self-defence.
Remote operation blurs who counts as directly participating in hostilities; anyone directly facilitating an attack, even a chauffeur, may be legitimately targeted.
Remote operators face psychological strain from moving between combat and home life, creating potential cognitive dissonance.
Accountability is spread across everyone in the targeting chain, since each person must obey the Law of Armed Conflict and may refuse unlawful orders.
Culpability depends on honesty of the situational assessment; anyone who withholds pertinent information shares moral responsibility for resulting mistakes.
defs: Direct participation in hostilities
Acts that directly contribute to an attack or to the military operation, which can make even a non-combatant lawfully targetable for that period.
Joint terminal attack controller (JTAC)
A qualified person who passes a commander's engagement instructions to the platform (artillery or drone) that delivers the munition.
Culpability
Moral blame linked to the honesty, not merely the accuracy, of the situational assessment behind an action or order.
tips: Do not treat physical distance from the battlefield as removing legal liability; participation and obligations under the Law of Armed Conflict still apply.
Culpability concerns honesty of the assessment, not just whether the outcome was accurate.
rq: Why might a civilian drone operator outside the conflict zone be legally exposed?
Because they may not count as combatants, losing prisoner-of-war protection, and using lethal force not in self-defence may be charged as murder.
If a drone pilot refuses an unlawful strike order, what does this imply about responsibility?
Responsibility is shared; the pilot retains a duty under the Law of Armed Conflict and is not a moral automaton, so the ground commander does not bear it alone.

units.name: 5 Precision, asymmetry and legitimacy
units.ov: This material examines how precision weapons such as drones change the ethics and politics of force. Precision can reduce collateral damage, but it raises public expectations (the paradox of precision), cannot remove fog of war and friction, and may lower the threshold for using force. Drones also reverse the usual asymmetric-threat dynamic, and legitimacy depends on in bello rules and on public and international opinion in liberal democracies.
must: Paradox of precision: the more accurate the weapon, the greater the scrutiny and blame attached to any miss, even though accuracy does not remove civilian casualties
Precision can reduce collateral damage by allowing smaller, fewer weapons to achieve the same military outcome
Fog of war (uncertainty and incomplete information) and friction (uncontrollable factors that derail plans) mean precise weapons never eliminate civilian casualties
Collateral damage is foreseeable but unintended and unwanted civilian death and destruction resulting from an attack on a legitimate target
Proportionality (jus in bello) means not using more force than necessary for the required ends; it does not mean fairness or a level playing field

Asymmetric threat: weaker actors avoid matching a stronger military technologically and use other means such as guerrilla attacks or IEDs; drones reverse this, leaving the weaker side exposed to pinpoint strikes
Asymmetric warfare: each side exploits the other's weakness rather than its strength; drones push this to an extreme when the pilot is far from the weapon
Opponents may deliberately position themselves so that any response violates, or appears to violate, in bello rules (discrimination and proportionality)
Legitimacy is subjective: it depends on legality, morality and liberal political culture, and democratic governments rely on public and international opinion

Lower casualties from stand-off precision weapons sustain public support but may lower the threshold for war, making force a first rather than last resort; this worry is plausible but hard to test empirically
conn: Paradox of precision and legitimacy: higher accuracy raises public expectations, so each miss damages legitimacy in democracies that depend on opinion
Asymmetric threat and its reversal: weaker opponents exploit in bello rules by positioning themselves among civilians, which links to discrimination, proportionality and fog of war
Casualty reduction and the threshold to force: precision builds public support and may make war easier to start, which connects back to the last-resort principle
Proportionality and precision: smaller weapons help meet proportionality, but this is about necessary force, not fairness between the sides
exq: Explain the 'paradox of precision'. Why does greater accuracy not remove civilian casualties, and how do fog of war and friction contribute?
Critically assess the claim that drones reverse the traditional asymmetric-threat dynamic. How might weaker opponents respond using in bello rules?
Does proportionality require a level playing field between combatants? Define the principle and use drone warfare to illustrate your answer.
Evaluate the argument that precision stand-off weapons lower the threshold for going to war. How strong is the evidence, and what does this mean for public legitimacy in democracies?
Discuss why military legitimacy is described as subjective, and how public and international opinion shape the use of precision weapons.

notes.t: Precision, its paradox, and asymmetric legitimacy in drone warfare
pts: Drones' precision can reduce collateral damage by allowing smaller, fewer weapons to achieve the same military outcome.
Greater accuracy raises scrutiny of every miss, so public expectations of perfection become a problem for policy-makers.
Technical accuracy does not eliminate civilian casualties because of the fog of war and friction.
Opponents may deliberately position themselves so any response violates, or appears to violate, in bello rules.
Drones reverse the traditional asymmetric-threat dynamic, since the stronger side now holds the technological advantage and the weaker side is the one exposed to pinpoint strikes.
defs: Collateral damage
Foreseeable but unintended and unwanted civilian death and destruction resulting from a military attack on a legitimate target.
Paradox of precision
The more accurate the weapons employed, the greater the public attention and blame attached to any miss or mistake, even though accuracy does not remove civilian casualties.
Fog of war
Uncertainty and incomplete information in combat that cannot be controlled and can derail plans.
Friction
The factors in war that cannot be controlled and therefore have the potential to derail plans.
In bello
The law governing conduct during armed conflict, including discrimination and proportionality.
Asymmetric threat
A threat in which weaker opponents avoid matching a stronger military technologically and instead use different rules, such as guerrilla attacks or IEDs.
tips: Do not conclude that precise weapons eliminate civilian casualties; the page stresses fog of war and friction persist.
Distinguish the asymmetric threat concept (weaker side using unconventional tactics) from how drones reverse that asymmetry.
rq: Why might greater precision make public tolerance for civilian deaths lower rather than higher?
Because accurate weapons create an expectation of perfect targeting, so any civilian death is seen as a clear mistake or intent, drawing more scrutiny.
How could an opponent exploit the rules in bello using drone-era tactics?
By positioning themselves among civilians so that any strike causes substantial civilian casualties, making the response appear to violate the rules.

notes.t: Asymmetry, public legitimacy and the threshold to military force
pts: Drone warfare is inherently asymmetric: the operator exploits the opponent's weakness rather than attacking their strength, taking asymmetry to an extreme when the pilot is far from the weapon.
Proportionality means not using more force than necessary to achieve the required ends; it is not about fairness or a level playing field.
Democratic governments depend on public and international opinion, so military legitimacy is subjective and tied to legality, morality and prevailing (liberal) political culture.
Lowering casualties through precision stand-off weapons helps sustain public support for military action, but may also lower the threshold for going to war.
Drones may turn war from a 'last resort' into a first or early response to crises, which is a worry even if hard to test empirically.
defs: Asymmetric warfare
Conflict between a technologically sophisticated actor and a less sophisticated one, in which each side exploits the other's weakness rather than attacking its strength.
Jus in bello
The body of principles governing the conduct of war (e.g. proportionality), as distinct from whether a war is justified.
Proportionality
The principle that force used should not exceed what is necessary to achieve the required military ends.
tips: Do not equate proportionality with fairness or a level playing field; the page explicitly rejects this reading.
Note that the author treats the ease-of-war objection as intuitively plausible but hard to test empirically, so do not present it as proven.
rq: Why does the author argue that refusing to use drones because the opponent lacks them would be morally perverse?
Because it would cause additional, unnecessary death and destruction and expose one's own forces to avoidable harm, misreading proportionality as a demand for fair play.
Why might drones make public support for military action more durable, and what risk does this create?
