tips: Do not confuse the three virtue categories: forgiveness and humility belong to temperance, not justice.
Sub-virtues are listed under each category; name the parent category when asked to classify a trait.
rq: Why might humility be classed under temperance rather than justice?
Humility restrains excess self-regard, which fits temperance's role of protecting against excess, whereas justice concerns fairness and social responsibility.
How could humour count as a virtue of transcendence rather than a mere pleasure?
Humour can connect people to something beyond themselves and foster perspective and shared joy, linking it to transcendence rather than simple amusement.

notes.t: Examples of vices (J.S. Mill)
pts: Mill lists recognisable moral vices that together constitute a bad and odious moral character.
Vices include cruelty, envy and insincerity, plus irascibility and disproportionate resentment.
Vices of self-regard include domineering over others and seeking more than one's share of advantages.
Egotism, treating self and its concerns as more important than everything else and deciding doubtful questions in one's own favour, is a vice.
defs: Moral vice
A settled bad character trait, such as cruelty or egotism, which Mill identifies as part of a bad and odious moral character.
tips: Mill's list describes vices as character traits, so do not treat them as isolated single acts when answering.
Be precise that the quote is from On Liberty, Ch. III; the page's images are not part of Mill's argument and should not be cited as evidence.
rq: Why does Mill say that egotism is a vice rather than merely a personal preference?
Because it makes self and its concerns more important than everything else and decides doubtful questions in its own favour, distorting fair judgement toward others.
What would it show if someone had irascibility on insufficient cause but never acted cruelly?
It would still count as a vice on Mill's list, since vices are character traits (dispositions) and not only actions.

notes.t: Critical thinking virtues
pts: Virtues, not just skills, better guarantee that critical thinking skills transfer to new contexts.
Virtues internalise the value of critical thinking: being a critical thinker matters to us personally.
Certain virtues motivate critical thinking, so their presence drives people to think critically.
The practice of critical thinking in turn helps develop these virtues, creating a reinforcing relationship.
defs: Virtue (in critical thinking)
A stable, internalised disposition to value and pursue good thinking, as opposed to a learned technical skill alone; it makes critical thinking something we care about and do habitually.
tips: Do not confuse virtues with skills: skills are abilities to perform tasks, while virtues are motivational dispositions that make us want to use those abilities.
Remember the two-way implication: virtues motivate critical thinking AND critical thinking develops virtues; stating only one direction is incomplete.
rq: Why would two students with identical critical thinking skills behave differently when assessing an argument that challenges their beliefs?

The student who has the relevant virtues (e.g. intellectual honesty, open-mindedness) is motivated to apply the skills fairly, whereas one lacking them may use the skills selectively to defend their own views.
What would it imply if critical thinking were practised only as a set of skills with no internalised value?
Skills would be less likely to transfer to new situations, because nothing motivates the person to use them beyond the contexts where they are explicitly required.

notes.t: Virtues of the ideal critical thinker
pts: Asks what character virtues an 'ideal critical thinker' would be expected to have, and what the corresponding vices (opposites) are.
Virtues are framed as character traits of a person, so critical thinking is treated as a matter of character as well as skill.
tips: Do not answer only with skills (e.g. spotting fallacies); the question asks for virtues of character and their opposites.
Name each virtue together with its vice (e.g. open-mindedness vs dogmatism) rather than listing virtues alone.
rq: Why might a person with excellent reasoning skills still fail to be a good critical thinker?

Because critical thinking also requires virtues of character (e.g. open-mindedness, intellectual honesty), so skill without the right dispositions can be undermined by bias, arrogance or self-deception.

notes.t: Critical thinking virtues (Facione et al., 1995)
pts: Truth-seeking: valuing truth above personal success or convenience.
Open-mindedness: tolerance of diverse views and awareness of one's own biases.
Systematicity: an organised, focused and diligent approach to analysis, linked to identifying and reconstructing arguments.
Analyticity: valuing judgements grounded in sound reasoning, linked to evaluating arguments.
defs: Truth-seeking
A critical thinking virtue of valuing truth above personal success.
Open-mindedness
A critical thinking virtue of being tolerant of diverse views while being aware of one's own biases.
Systematicity
A critical thinking virtue involving an organised, focused and diligent approach to analysis, relating to argument identification and reconstruction.
Analyticity
A critical thinking virtue of valuing judgements based on sound reasoning, relating to argument evaluation.
tips: Do not confuse systematicity (structuring analysis) with analyticity (judging soundness of reasoning); students often swap them.
Open-mindedness is not simply agreeing with everyone; it includes awareness of one's own biases.
rq: Why might open-mindedness require awareness of one's own biases rather than just tolerance of other views?
Tolerance alone can still leave one's own assumptions unexamined; recognising personal biases lets one assess views fairly, including one's own.
How do systematicity and analyticity differ in the stages of critical thinking they support?
Systematicity supports argument identification and reconstruction (structuring the argument), while analyticity supports argument evaluation (judging whether its reasoning is sound).

notes.t: Critical thinking virtues
pts: Critical thinking rests on intellectual virtues, starting with a commitment to truth and open-mindedness.
Humility means not overestimating one's own status and abilities, and recognising implied equality between people.
Self-knowledge covers awareness of our own particular commitments and our cognitive limitations or biases.
Metacognition is self-awareness during deliberation and decision making.
Beyond the core virtues, 'dialogical dispositions' such as courage and staying focused also matter in critical thinking.
defs: Commitment to truth
A settled disposition to seek and follow what is true, rather than what is convenient or wished for.
Open-mindedness
Willingness to consider alternative views and evidence, and to revise one's beliefs when reasons require it.
Humility
A non-overestimation of one's own status and abilities, combined with recognition of implied equality between people.
Self-knowledge
Awareness of one's own particular commitments and of one's cognitive limitations and biases.
Metacognition
Self-awareness of one's own processes of deliberation and decision making.
tips: Do not confuse humility with low self-confidence; the term refers to not overestimating one's status and abilities.
Distinguish self-knowledge (of commitments and biases) from metacognition (awareness of the reasoning process itself).
rq: Why might humility be considered essential to critical thinking rather than a merely personal trait?
Because overestimating one's abilities or status leads to dismissing evidence and others' views, and recognising implied equality keeps reasoning open to challenge from anyone.
How does self-knowledge of cognitive biases help you reason better in practice?
Knowing where your biases lie lets you check your reasoning against them, so you can spot when a conclusion is driven by preference rather than evidence.

units.name: 2 What is philosophy?
units.ov: This introductory material defines philosophy as an academic discipline: reasoned analysis of fundamental questions about humans and the world that the scientific method cannot answer. It separates this from the everyday 'philosophy on life', contrasts systematic traditions with Western analytic philosophy, and maps the main branches (metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, free will, aesthetics, existential questions). The ideas connect because the definition sets the method (argument, not empirical testing alone), and the branches show the kinds of questions that method addresses.
must: Academic definition of philosophy: the application of reasoned analysis to fundamental questions about human beings and the world that cannot be answered through the scientific method
Do not define philosophy as merely 'thinking deeply' or 'having opinions'; the definition stresses reasoned analysis and questions beyond scientific method
Distinguish academic philosophy from a 'philosophy on life' (a set of basic beliefs or principles a person tries to live by)
Philosophical questions are answered by argument and analysis, not simply by citing scientific data or observation alone
Analytic philosophy: the dominant Western approach, applying careful reasoning to specific questions rather than building comprehensive systems
Systematic, holistic philosophies exist, e.g. Buddhism and Marxism, so philosophy is not only Western; the contrast is system-building versus analytic reasoning on specific questions
This course is based on Western philosophy, traced back to the Greeks, e.g. Aristotle
Three core branches with examples: metaphysics (does God exist, what is consciousness), epistemology (how do we know what is true), ethics (is it wrong to harm animals or plants)

Other key questions: free will (are decisions genuinely free), whether moral claims are objective facts or mere opinion, and whether aesthetic taste and the point of existence can be objectively grounded

A non-religious scientific/materialist worldview is an assumption that can underpin philosophical work, not a universal truth of philosophy; and 'opinion' differs from 'view': the issue is whether a subject has objective answers, not whether people disagree
conn: Definition and method: because philosophical questions lie beyond the scientific method, they are tackled by reasoned argument, which links the definition to the analytic approach
Analytic versus systematic philosophy: analytic philosophy tackles specific questions (e.g. animal ethics), whereas Buddhism and Marxism offer holistic worldviews, and both count as philosophy

Ethics and objectivity: the question of whether moral claims are objective or just opinion connects ethics to metaphysics and epistemology (what exists, how we could know it), and also to aesthetic questions
Materialist assumptions and free will/consciousness: a scientific/materialist worldview shapes how questions about mind, consciousness and free will are approached, yet remains an assumption
exq: Define philosophy as an academic discipline and explain why it is not the same as a 'philosophy on life'.
Why can philosophical questions not be answered by the scientific method alone? Illustrate with examples from metaphysics, epistemology and ethics.
Compare analytic philosophy with systematic traditions such as Buddhism and Marxism. Is it accurate to say philosophy is a Western enterprise?
Explain the difference between asking whether people disagree about morality and asking whether moral claims are objective. Why does this matter?
Discuss the status of a scientific/materialist worldview as an assumption within philosophical work.

notes.t: What is philosophy?
pts: As an academic discipline, philosophy applies reasoned analysis to fundamental questions about human beings and the world.
Philosophical questions are those that cannot be answered through the scientific method.
Thinking philosophically means thinking deeply and with a sense of perspective.
More generally, a person can have a 'philosophy on life': basic beliefs or principles they try to live by.
defs: Philosophy (academic discipline)
The application of reasoned analysis to fundamental questions about human beings and the world that cannot be answered through the scientific method.
Philosophy on life
A set of basic beliefs or principles that a person holds and tries to live by.
tips: Do not define philosophy as merely 'thinking deeply' or 'having opinions'; the academic definition specifically stresses reasoned analysis of questions beyond scientific method.
Distinguish the academic sense of 'philosophy' from the everyday sense of 'a philosophy on life'; mixing them up loses marks.
rq: Why can't philosophical questions be settled by the scientific method, and what does this imply about the kind of evidence philosophy relies on?

Philosophical questions concern fundamental matters (e.g. meaning, value, knowledge) that are not open to empirical testing or experiment, so philosophy relies on reasoned analysis, argument and conceptual clarification rather than observation and experiment.
What is the difference between philosophy as an academic discipline and having a 'philosophy on life'?

The academic discipline is a systematic, reasoned investigation of fundamental questions, whereas a 'philosophy on life' is a personal set of basic beliefs or principles one holds and tries to live by, which need not be argued for systematically.

notes.t: What is philosophy?
pts: Some philosophies are systematic, holistic bodies of thought, such as Buddhism and Marxism.
Most Western (analytic) philosophy applies reasoning to specific questions rather than building whole philosophical systems.
Certain assumptions, such as a non-religious scientific/materialist worldview, can underpin philosophical work.
This course is based on Western philosophy, traced back to the Greeks, e.g. Aristotle.
defs: Analytic philosophy
The dominant Western approach that applies careful reasoning to specific questions rather than constructing comprehensive philosophical systems.
tips: Do not treat 'philosophy' as only Western; systematic traditions like Buddhism and Marxism are also philosophies, and the contrast here is between holistic systems and analytic reasoning on specific questions.
Remember that the non-religious, scientific/materialist worldview is an assumption that can be made, not a universal truth of philosophy.
rq: Why might analytic philosophy avoid building holistic systems like Marxism or Buddhism?
It prefers to tackle specific, well-defined questions with rigorous reasoning, which is more tractable and testable than defending an entire worldview at once.
What is the difference between a holistic philosophy and a piece of analytic reasoning?
A holistic philosophy offers a complete system covering many areas of life, while analytic reasoning targets particular questions and may proceed from shared assumptions without a full system.

notes.t: What is philosophy?
pts: Philosophy asks fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, mind, value and free will that cannot be settled by simple observation alone.
Philosophical questions span metaphysics (does God exist, what is consciousness), epistemology (how do we know what is true) and ethics (is it wrong to harm animals or plants).
Ethical questions ask whether moral claims are objective facts or merely matters of opinion.
Questions about free will ask whether our decisions are genuinely made freely.
Aesthetic and existential questions probe whether artistic taste and the point of existence can be objectively grounded.
defs: Philosophy
The rigorous, reasoned investigation of fundamental questions about reality, knowledge, morality, mind and value, pursued through argument rather than empirical testing alone.
tips: Do not confuse 'opinion' with 'view': the question asks whether a subject has objective answers, not whether people disagree about it.
Philosophical questions are typically answered by argument and analysis; avoid claiming they are resolved simply by citing scientific data.
rq: Why might questions like 'Does God exist?' count as philosophical rather than purely scientific?
Because they cannot be settled by empirical observation or experiment alone; they require conceptual analysis and argument about meaning, evidence and reasoning.
What would it mean for morality to be 'just a matter of opinion', and how would that differ from it being objective?
If morality is merely opinion, moral claims express personal or cultural attitudes with no truth independent of them; if objective, some moral claims are true regardless of what anyone thinks.

units.name: 3 Course overview, aims and learning outcomes
units.ov: These notes outline a first-year Philosophy 1 course (despite the Global Sustainable Development label) that introduces philosophy through four core branches: metaphysics, epistemology, logic, and values (ethics and aesthetics). These are studied through set texts and themes (Plato's Last Days of Socrates, basic symbolic logic, free will, the ethics of war). The learning outcomes progress from understanding, to explaining, to critically evaluating, to applying critical thinking beyond philosophy. The notes contain no numerical content and the detailed course content is in a separate handout.
must: Define metaphysics (ontology): the fundamental nature of reality, what exists and the basic categories of being
Define epistemology: the nature, sources and limits of knowledge and justified belief
Define logic: the study of valid reasoning, distinguishing correct from incorrect inference
Define values: ethics (good and right, moral philosophy) and aesthetics (art and beauty)
Do not confuse metaphysics (what exists) with epistemology (what and how we can know)
Know the four learning outcomes: understand the branches, explain key concepts, critically engage, apply to other areas
Distinguish explaining a text's concepts (outcome 2) from critically evaluating them (outcome 3); exams test both separately
Know the example texts and themes and which branch each illustrates: Plato's Last Days of Socrates, symbolic logic, free will, the ethics of war
Critical and reflective thinking is a transferable skill valued beyond philosophy and university
Check the course handout for detailed content, as these notes only give an overview
conn: Free will links metaphysics (is the world determined?) with ethics (moral responsibility) and epistemology (what can we know about our own choices?)

Plato's Last Days of Socrates combines epistemology (knowledge versus belief, Socratic questioning), ethics (justice, obeying the law and death) and metaphysics (the soul and what happens after death)
Logic underpins critical engagement with every topic: assessing argument validity in the ethics of war or in metaphysical and epistemological assumptions
Explaining a concept and evaluating it are paired skills: a top answer states the view accurately and then tests its assumptions and the validity of its arguments
exq: Distinguish metaphysics from epistemology, using one example from the course for each.
Explain the key concepts in one set text or topic (such as Plato's Last Days of Socrates), then critically evaluate one of its central arguments.
Using basic symbolic logic, show whether a given argument is valid, and explain why validity differs from truth.
Discuss how the free will debate draws on both metaphysical and ethical questions.
How can philosophical methods such as critical thinking be applied to another academic subject or to life beyond university? Give a worked example.

notes.t: Course Overview: Philosophy 1
pts: The course introduces students to philosophy as a discipline, beginning with its core subject matter.
Core areas covered are metaphysics (ontology), epistemology, logic, and values (ethics and aesthetics).
Topics are studied through selected texts and themes, such as Plato's Last Days of Socrates, free will, and the ethics of war.
A key learning goal is the value of critical and reflective thinking, applied beyond philosophy to other subjects and life after university.
defs: Metaphysics (ontology)
The branch of philosophy concerned with the fundamental nature of reality, including what exists and the basic categories of being.
Epistemology
The branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, sources, and limits of knowledge and justified belief.
Logic
The study of valid reasoning and the principles that distinguish correct inference from incorrect inference.
Values (ethics and aesthetics)
The branch of philosophy concerned with what is good, right, and beautiful, covering moral philosophy (ethics) and the philosophy of art and beauty (aesthetics).
tips: Do not confuse metaphysics with epistemology: metaphysics asks what exists, while epistemology asks what and how we can know.
rq: Why does the course begin by explaining the four core areas before looking at specific texts?
Students need a map of the discipline's fundamental subject matter so that individual topics and texts can be placed within the broader areas they represent.
How might critical and reflective thinking from philosophy help in a subject like Global Sustainable Development?
It encourages questioning assumptions, evaluating arguments and evidence, and examining value judgements, which are central to sustainability debates.

notes.t: Learning Outcomes
pts: Course aims students to understand the nature and value of the fundamental branches of philosophy: metaphysics, epistemology, logic, and values (ethics and aesthetics).
Students should explain key concepts and questions from texts and topics such as Plato's Last Days of Socrates, basic symbolic logic, the ethics of war, and free will.
Students should critically engage with texts using philosophical analysis, such as questioning metaphysical and epistemological assumptions and argument validity.
Students should apply philosophical ideas and methods, such as critical thinking, to other academic areas and to contexts beyond formal education.
tips: Do not confuse explaining a text's key concepts (outcome 2) with critically evaluating them (outcome 3); exams will test both skills separately.
rq: Why does the course pair abstract branches like metaphysics with concrete topics like the ethics of war?
Concrete topics show how the branches of philosophy apply to real questions, making the abstract branches understandable and useful.
What would it mean to critically engage with an argument rather than just explain it?
It means testing whether the argument is valid and questioning its underlying metaphysical and epistemological assumptions.

units.name: 4 Assessments, penalties and extenuating circumstances
units.ov: This material sets out how the module is assessed: a 15% in-class short answer test, a 50% 1500-word essay, and a 35% exam. It also covers the rules around them: plagiarism, compulsory oral feedback, late penalties, and the DAP and EC routes for extensions on medical or compassionate grounds. The ideas connect because each deadline and requirement carries a consequence, and the formal processes are the only way to avoid those consequences.
must: Weightings: short test 15%, essay 50%, exam 35%, totalling \(15+50+35=100\%\)
The essay is the largest component: 1500 words, 50%, due Wednesday 25th November at 5PM, uploaded to Moodle (which also sends it to Turnitin)
Short answer test: 15%, taken in class under exam conditions on Monday 26th October, 10-11 AM (1 hour)
Attendance at the oral feedback session is compulsory to receive the essay mark; missing it means losing the mark even if the essay was submitted on time
Exam: 35%, usually held in Week 12 or Week 13
Plagiarism is passing off others' work as your own and carries severe penalties; Turnitin screens submissions
Late submission incurs penalties by default; do not assume an extension exists without approval
A Delayed Assessment Permit (DAP) is an approved extension to a deadline on medical or compassionate grounds
Extenuating Circumstances (EC) are medical or compassionate circumstances formally declared to allow an extension or other adjustment
The procedure is in the Student Information Hub under the Student Absence Policy; check it for exact steps and deadlines instead of relying on memory
conn: Weighting and risk: the essay is worth 50%, so a late penalty or a missed oral feedback session costs far more there than on the 15% test
Plagiarism and submission: uploading through Moodle triggers the Turnitin check, so the submission route is also the integrity check
DAP vs EC: both rest on medical or compassionate grounds, but a DAP is the approved extension itself, whereas EC is the declared circumstance that may lead to an extension or adjustment
Timeline planning: the test (26 Oct), the essay deadline (25 Nov) and the exam (Week 12 or 13) are close together, so a problem in one may require an EC application affecting several
exq: State the weighting of each assessment component and show that they total 100%. Which component carries the most marks?
A student submits their 1500-word essay on time on 25th November but does not attend the oral feedback session. What happens to their essay mark, and why?
Define plagiarism and explain how the submission process for the essay helps detect it.
Distinguish between a Delayed Assessment Permit and Extenuating Circumstances, and explain what happens if a student submits late without either.
A student is ill the week before the 26th October short answer test. Outline the steps they should take and where they should find the official procedure.

notes.t: Assessments
pts: Short answer test is worth 15% and is taken in class under exam conditions on Monday 26th October, 10-11 AM.
The essay is 1500 words, worth 50%, uploaded to Moodle (which also sends it to Turnitin) and due Wednesday 25th November, 5PM.
Attending the oral feedback session is compulsory to receive the essay mark.
The exam is worth 35% and is usually held in Week 12 or Week 13.
Plagiarism, passing off others' work as your own, carries severe penalties.
defs: Plagiarism
Passing off the work of others as your own; it carries severe penalties.
tips: Missing the oral feedback session means losing the essay mark entirely, even if the essay is submitted on time.
Note the exact weightings: short test 15%, essay 50%, exam 35%; these add to 100%.
rq: Why must you attend the oral feedback session even though the written feedback is already provided?
Because attendance at the oral feedback session is a condition for receiving the mark for the essay; written feedback alone does not award the mark.
How does the Moodle submission relate to plagiarism checking?
Uploading to Moodle automatically uploads the essay to Turnitin plagiarism software, so the submission is checked for plagiarism.

notes.t: Penalties and Extenuating Circumstances
pts: Assessments submitted after the deadline incur late penalties.
Extensions may be requested on medical or compassionate grounds through Delayed Assessment Permits (DAPs) and Extenuating Circumstances (EC) applications.
Full details of the process are given in the Student Information Hub under the Student Absence Policy.
defs: Delayed Assessment Permit (DAP)
An approved extension to an assessment deadline granted on medical or compassionate grounds.
Extenuating Circumstances (EC)
Medical or compassionate circumstances that may be formally declared to allow an extension or other adjustment to assessment.
tips: Do not assume an extension exists without an approved DAP or EC; late penalties apply by default.
Check the Student Information Hub for the exact application procedure and deadlines rather than relying on memory.
rq: Why might a student with a genuine medical problem still be penalised if they only tell staff after the deadline?
Extensions are granted through formal DAP or EC applications, so the claim must be submitted through the official process; informal reporting alone does not automatically remove the late penalty.
What is the difference between a late penalty and an extension via a DAP or EC?

A late penalty is applied automatically to work submitted after the deadline, whereas a DAP or EC approved on medical or compassionate grounds can allow the deadline to be extended so the penalty need not apply.

units.name: 5 Workload, reading and course administration
units.ov: This material covers course administration for a 20-credit Global Sustainable Development module: the expected workload, how to prepare for seminars through reading, and the rules on email and electronic devices. The ideas connect because roughly 170 of the 200 study hours are independent, so preparation and staying informed by email determine how well the limited class time works, and the no-device policy protects that class time.
must: A 20-credit course is recommended to need about \(200\) hours of total study time.
Only about \(30\) of those \(200\) hours are scheduled class time, so about \(170\) hours (\(85\%\)) are independent study.
Plan around the full 200 hours, not the 30 contact hours.
Read the assigned seminar readings and/or attempt the tasks before each seminar, rather than arriving unprepared.
The Moodle reading list is not the full set of readings: the course also supplies readings directly.
Note unclear concepts, vocabulary or instructions while reading, and raise questions with the instructor.
Check your university student email regularly, because attending lectures alone will not keep you informed of course communications.
Take notes by hand with pen and paper; devices are not allowed in class.
The rationale for the device ban has two parts: devices distract the user, and they disrupt other students' learning.
The device ban has exceptions: a learning disability or a similar reason can permit device use. It is not an unconditional ban, and you should check the exact policy for each course.
conn: Workload and reading: the 170 independent hours are where seminar preparation happens, so reading beforehand is the main use of that time.
Reading and questions: noting unclear concepts while preparing gives you specific questions to raise with the instructor, which makes seminars more productive.
Email and workload: course communications arrive by official email, so checking it is part of managing independent study (instructions, readings and changes can be missed otherwise).
Device policy and learning: handwritten notes and the ban on devices protect both individual focus and the shared learning environment, with exceptions that support accessibility.
exq: A 20-credit course recommends 200 hours of study and about 30 hours of scheduled class time. Calculate the independent study hours and the percentage of the total they represent, and explain why planning around 30 hours would be a mistake.
Describe how a student should prepare for a seminar, including what to do about unclear concepts, vocabulary or instructions.
Explain why the Moodle reading list alone may not give you all the required reading.
Give the two reasons for the no-electronic-devices policy, and state the exception to it. Why should the policy not be described as an absolute ban?
Why is it risky to rely on attending lectures as your only source of course information, and what should you do instead?

notes.t: Workload expectations for a 20-credit course
pts: A 20-credit course is recommended to require about 200 hours of total study time.
Only around 30 of the 200 hours are spent in scheduled class time, so most study is independent.
tips: Do not confuse the 200 total hours with the roughly 30 contact hours; the figure to plan around is the full 200 hours of study.
rq: Why does a 20-credit course involve far more study time than the hours spent in class, and what should a student do with the remaining time?
Roughly 170 of the 200 hours are independent study (reading, coursework, revision), so students must plan self-directed work outside timetabled sessions.

notes.t: Reading for seminars
pts: Use the Moodle reading list, though the course will also supply readings directly.
Prepare for each seminar by reading the assigned seminar readings beforehand.
Attempt the readings and/or tasks before attending, rather than arriving unprepared.
Note any concepts, vocabulary or instructions that are unclear so they can be addressed.
Raise questions with the instructor whenever you are unsure about anything.
tips: Do not assume the Moodle reading list is the full set of readings; the course also provides readings separately.
rq: Why is it useful to note down concepts or vocabulary you do not understand before a seminar, rather than simply skimming the reading?
Identifying gaps in understanding in advance lets you ask targeted questions, so they can be resolved before the seminar where the material is discussed.

notes.t: Course administration: email and electronic devices
pts: Students are expected to check their university student email regularly for course communications.
Rules governing the use of electronic devices during class are also set out for students.
tips: Do not assume that attending lectures alone keeps you informed; regularly check official university email.
Check the exact device policy for your course, as rules on phones, laptops and tablets may differ between classes.
rq: Why might missing an email from the course team harm your performance even if you attend every lecture?
Important announcements, deadlines, changes to timetable or assessment, and feedback are often sent by email, so missing them can cause missed deadlines or misunderstood requirements.
Why might a university restrict electronic devices in lectures, and what does that imply about how you should take notes?
Devices can distract you and others and may be used off-task; restrictions imply you should follow the stated device policy and take notes by hand or on permitted devices.

notes.t: No Electronic Devices in Class
pts: Students should take notes by hand using pen and paper rather than devices.
Electronic devices are a source of distraction for the student using them.
Devices also disrupt the learning of other students in the room.
The ban has an exception where a learning disability or similar reason requires device use.
tips: The rule is not absolute: exceptions for learning disability or similar reasons are explicitly allowed, so do not state it as an unconditional ban.
Note the difference between the distraction to the user and the distraction to other learners; both are reasons given, and both should be cited when explaining the policy's rationale.
rq: Why might a rule banning devices exist even if a student says they can multitask well?
Distraction also affects other learners, so individual multitasking ability does not remove the classroom-wide cost.
How should a student with a learning disability proceed if they need a device?
They should raise it with the teaching staff, since the notes state the staff are willing to discuss exceptions.

units.name: 6 This week's seminar
units.ov: The notes supplied for this section are minimal: they only state that the week's seminar is driven by a reading and instructions provided in a separate handout and on Moodle. No substantive content (topics, data, theories, case studies) is included, so this report cannot say what the seminar covers. It gives a revision framework and flags what to check in the handout.

Identify the reading's central argument or thesis in one sentence, since seminar-based questions usually start from it.
Note the key terms and definitions the reading uses (e.g. any sustainable development concepts, frameworks or indicators) and be able to define each precisely.

Complete the seminar tasks in the handout and keep your own notes or group conclusions, as these show the intended applications of the reading.

Reading evidence and SDG trade-offs: a case study may illustrate how progress on one goal affects another, and questions ask you to evaluate this.
Critique and policy implications: assessing the reading's strengths and limitations often leads into what it implies for policy or practice.
exq: Summarise the main argument of this week's seminar reading and evaluate how well the evidence supports it, using at least two specific examples.
Using the reading as a case study, discuss one synergy and one trade-off between SDGs that it reveals.

notes.t: This week's seminar
pts: The seminar this week is driven by a reading and instructions, which are provided in a separate handout and on Moodle.

units.name: 1 Seminar overview and exercise answers intro
units.ov: The notes are only slide titles from a seminar on argument identification and reconstruction, with an answers-to-exercises section, and they contain no substantive content. The material appears to belong to a Philosophy seminar rather than Global Sustainable Development, so this report relies on standard knowledge of the topic and not on the notes. The central idea is that you identify arguments in text, separate premises from conclusions, and reconstruct them in standard form so their validity and soundness can be assessed.
must: Argument = set of premises offered to support a conclusion; distinguish it from mere assertion, explanation, or description
Identify the conclusion first, using indicator words (therefore, thus, hence) and the question 'what is the author trying to convince me of?'
Premise indicators (because, since, given that, for) and how they differ from conclusion indicators
Standard form reconstruction: number premises P1, P2... then conclusion C, written in clear, neutral, complete sentences
Deductive validity: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true; soundness = validity + all premises actually true
Inductive/abductive strength: the premises make the conclusion probable, not certain; assessed as strong or weak, not valid or invalid
Spotting and supplying implicit (suppressed) premises using charity, so the argument is the strongest reasonable version
Distinguishing validity from truth: a valid argument can have false premises, and a true conclusion does not make an argument valid
Principle of charity and avoiding straw-manning when reconstructing others' arguments
Check your reconstruction by testing: does C follow from the premises, and have I added or lost anything the author said?
conn: Argument reconstruction feeds evaluation: a clear standard form lets you test validity first, then premise truth (soundness)
Implicit premises link to charity: choosing what to add is a trade-off between making the argument valid and staying faithful to the author
Indicator words help find structure but can mislead, for example 'since' used temporally or explanations that look like arguments
Reconstruction applies to sustainability debates too, where policy arguments often rely on hidden value premises, such as 'we ought to protect future generations'
exq: Reconstruct the following passage in standard form (numbered premises and conclusion), and identify any suppressed premise you add and why.
Is the following argument valid? Is it sound? Explain the difference, using a counterexample with true premises and a false conclusion if it is invalid.
Explain why distinguishing an argument from an explanation matters, and give an example of a passage that could be read either way.
Identify the conclusion and premises in a short passage containing misleading indicator words, and justify your reading.
Discuss how the principle of charity constrains the addition of implicit premises when reconstructing an argument.

units.name: 2 Deductive vs inductive: turtle/shrimp and spy ring head
units.ov: This seminar material teaches how to analyse arguments: identify premises and conclusion, then decide whether the reasoning is deductive (judged by validity) or inductive (judged by strength). It applies this to a turtle/shrimp net argument (hedged, inductive) and two spy ring head arguments (practical conclusions that depend on a hidden premise about the missing fingertip). The link throughout is that evaluation starts with structure, then checks the truth of the premises and any unstated assumptions.
must: Definitions: an argument is a set of premises offered as reasons for a conclusion; a premise is a statement given as evidence; a conclusion is what the argument tries to establish
First step in evaluating any argument: identify the premises and the conclusion, then ask whether the premises give good reason to accept the conclusion
Deductive arguments are judged by validity (premises guarantee the conclusion); inductive arguments are judged by strength (premises make the conclusion probable)
Hedge words like 'probably' signal an inductive inference, so do not treat the conclusion as a deductive proof
Turtle/shrimp argument: two premises plus a hedged conclusion; P1 evidence supports the net explanation only if the generalisation in P2 about turtle feeding is true
Always check the truth of generalised premises (e.g. P2), because inductive strength depends on them
Spy ring head argument: P1 (dangerous, clever, skilled at disguise) and P2 (missing fingertip cannot be disguised) lead to a practical conclusion to be cautious of anyone missing a fingertip
Hidden (unstated) premise: the conclusion needs 'a missing fingertip identifies the spy head', which is not stated, so it does not follow deductively as given
In the alternative version, C1 (master of disguise) is an intermediate conclusion and does not establish C2 directly; C2 needs the extra premise that the fingertip is a reliable identifier
Distinguish a claim of fact (he is dangerous) from a recommendation (be careful); the conclusion is the practical recommendation
conn: Hedged conclusions and inductive strength: the turtle/shrimp argument contrasts with the spy arguments, where you must decide whether the reasoning is meant to be deductive or inductive/abductive before judging it
Hidden premises and validity: making the implicit identification premise explicit can turn an apparently invalid spy argument into a valid one, but then its truth must be assessed
Intermediate versus final conclusions: C1 serves as a premise for C2, so the argument's structure (chain of inference) affects evaluation
Premise truth and argument quality: both the turtle generalisation and the fingertip identifier show that good logical form is not enough without true or plausible premises
exq: Identify the premises and conclusion in the turtle/shrimp argument, state whether it is deductive or inductive, and justify using the word 'probably'.
Explain why the turtle/shrimp argument is assessed by strength rather than validity, and say what would make P2 weak or false.
Reconstruct the spy ring head argument (P1, P2, C), identify the hidden premise, and state whether the argument is deductively valid without it.
In the alternative spy argument, map out C1 and C2 and explain why C1 does not by itself establish C2.
Distinguish between a claim that someone is dangerous and a recommendation to be careful, and explain why this matters for identifying the conclusion of an argument.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Deductive/inductive argument analysis (turtle and shrimp)
pts: The argument has two premises and a conclusion; the conclusion is hedged with 'probably', so it is an inductive (probabilistic) inference rather than a deductive proof.
P2 is a strong generalisation about turtle feeding; if it is true, the evidence in P1 supports the net explanation.
Identifying the premises and conclusion is the first step in evaluating whether the argument is good, i.e. whether the premises give good reason to accept the conclusion.
defs: Argument
A set of premises offered as reasons in support of a conclusion.
Premise
A statement given as a reason or evidence for the conclusion of an argument.
Conclusion
The statement an argument is trying to establish, drawn from the premises.
tips: Do not confuse a conclusion that is only 'probably' true with a deductively valid conclusion; judge inductive arguments by strength, not validity.
Check whether a generalised premise such as P2 is actually true, since the argument's strength depends on it.
rq: Why does the word 'probably' in the conclusion matter for how we judge this argument?
It signals an inductive argument: the premises make the conclusion likely, not certain, so it is judged by strength and plausibility rather than validity.
What would have to be true of P2 for the conclusion to follow with high probability, and what if turtles could catch shrimp by other means?
P2 must be a reliable generalisation; if other methods of catching shrimp existed, the net inference would be weakened.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Deductive argument about the spy ring head
pts: The argument is a short deductive argument: two premises (P1 and P2) lead to a conclusion (C) about how to act.
P1 claims the spy ring head is dangerous, clever and skilled at disguise; P2 says his missing fingertip cannot be disguised; the conclusion infers caution toward anyone missing a little fingertip.
The conclusion is a practical recommendation, and it relies on an assumed identification link (missing fingertip implies the spy head) that the premises do not state outright.
tips: Do not treat the conclusion as following deductively: check whether the premises actually guarantee the conclusion or whether a hidden premise (the missing fingertip identifies the spy head) is needed.
Distinguish between a claim that a person is dangerous and a recommendation to be careful; the argument's conclusion is the recommendation.
rq: Is the argument valid, i.e. would the conclusion follow necessarily if both premises were true?

Not strictly: the conclusion needs an extra premise that anyone with a missing fingertip is the spy head, which is not given, so the inference is at best inductive or practical rather than deductively valid.
What would make the conclusion more reasonable?
Adding premises such as that the spy head is the only person with a missing fingertip, or that his missing fingertip is the sole distinguishing mark he cannot hide.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Alternative argument on the spy ring head
pts: The argument moves from the spy ring head being clever with many disguises to the conclusion that he is a master of disguise (C1).
P2 introduces a limitation: despite his skill, he cannot disguise a missing little finger tip, which becomes a identifying feature.
Combining P2 with P3 (he is very dangerous) yields a practical conclusion: a man missing a fingertip should prompt caution.
C2 is a practical or advisory conclusion, so its validity depends on whether the premises establish that the missing fingertip reliably identifies the head.
tips: Do not treat C1 as establishing C2 directly; C2 needs the extra premise that the fingertip is a reliable identifier, which is not stated.
Check whether the argument is deductive or inductive/abductive before judging it valid.
rq: Why does the argument's conclusion C2 not follow strictly from the premises?

Because a missing fingertip only shows a person might be the head; many people lack fingertips, so the inference to a dangerous spy is not deductively guaranteed and is at best a probabilistic or heuristic warning.
What role does P2 play in the argument structure?
It is a premise that identifies a weakness in the head's disguise skill, providing a concrete, observable marker that links the abstract description to a practical warning.

units.name: 3 Fake degrees argument and validity
units.ov: This material teaches how to reconstruct and evaluate deductive arguments, separating validity (does the conclusion follow?) from soundness (are the premises true?). It applies these tools to two cases: the fake-degree argument, which fails because of a gap between premises and conclusion, and the American colonists' right-to-rebel argument, which is valid and whose soundness depends on its empirical premise P3.
must: Deductive argument: the conclusion is claimed to follow necessarily from the premises, so if the premises are true the conclusion must be true.
Validity concerns logical form only; soundness = valid form + all premises actually true. Always assess the two separately.
Identify the structure first: the 'Therefore' marks the conclusion, and the rest are premises. Do not confuse the two.
Non sequitur (incorrect argument): the conclusion does not follow even if the premises are true. Do not judge an argument by the truth of its premises alone.

Fake-degree case (seminar 2): P1 says a fake degree is easy to make and P2 says buying one is a waste of money. Both concern ease and cost, but the conclusion claims 'just as good', which is a claim about quality. This topic shift makes it a non sequitur.
The bridging premise (p7 version): 'a self-made fake is just as good as a purchased one' is needed to link the options. If it is false, the waste-of-money conclusion is not established.

Colonists' argument: P1 (equal people with unalienable rights; governments exist to protect them), P2 (when a government violates those rights, people may rebel and form a new one), P3 (the king has repeatedly violated colonists' rights), C (the colonists may rebel). The form is a valid syllogism.

P3 is the empirical premise, so evaluating soundness means checking the evidence that the king violated rights. Distinguish normative premises (P1, P2: what governments should do) from factual ones (P3).
Define unalienable rights (cannot be given or taken away, held by virtue of being human) and the right to rebel (justified overthrow of a government that systematically violates natural rights).
Watch for shifts in topic between premises and conclusion, and check for missing or hidden premises.
conn: Validity vs soundness links both cases: the colonists' argument is valid, with soundness resting on P3, while the fake-degree argument fails at the validity stage, so soundness never arises.

Hidden or bridging premises connect the two p7 and p8 readings of the fake-degree argument. Adding 'self-made is just as good' would make the argument closer to valid, but then its truth must be assessed.
General premises plus a particular premise (P1, P2 + P3) give the syllogism structure. Normative principles are applied to empirical facts, so critique can target the principles or the facts.
Natural rights theory (P1) underpins the conditional right to rebel (P2), linking logic to political and sustainable-development ideas about legitimate government.
exq: Reconstruct the fake-degree argument in standard form (premises P1, P2, conclusion C). Explain why it is a non sequitur, identifying the topic shift from ease and cost to quality.
What premise would need to be added to make the fake-degree argument valid? Is the resulting argument sound? Justify your answer.
Set out the colonists' right-to-rebel argument as P1, P2, P3 and C. Is it valid? What evidence would you need to decide whether it is sound?
Distinguish validity from soundness, using one example in which an argument has true premises but is invalid and one in which it is valid but unsound.
Classify each premise of the colonists' argument as normative or empirical, and explain why this matters for how you would challenge the argument.

notes.t: Evaluating a deductive argument about buying fake degrees
pts: The argument is a deductive argument with two premises and a conclusion, where the conclusion is that buying a fake degree online is a waste of money.
P1 says a fake degree is easy to make yourself, which supports P2 by suggesting self-made fakes are an available alternative.
P2 claims a self-made fake degree is just as good as a purchased one, which is the key bridging premise linking the two options.
The conclusion only follows if P2 is true; if self-made fakes were worse, the argument would not establish the waste-of-money conclusion.
defs: Deductive argument
An argument in which the conclusion is claimed to follow necessarily from the premises, so that if the premises are true the conclusion must be true (valid if the form guarantees this).
tips: Do not confuse the conclusion with a premise; the 'Therefore' signals the conclusion.
Evaluate validity and soundness separately: the form may be valid, but soundness depends on whether P2 is actually true.
rq: Why does the conclusion depend on P2 rather than P1 alone?
P1 only says self-making is easy; P2 is needed to say a self-made fake is equivalent in value to a bought one, so buying offers no advantage and is therefore wasteful.
What if P2 were false because self-made fakes are easily detected?
Then the conclusion would not follow, since buying might still be worthwhile if purchased fakes are better quality.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Identifying an incorrect argument (fake college degrees)
pts: The argument is labelled incorrect: its conclusion does not follow from the premises, since neither premise compares the quality of a self-made fake degree with a bought one.
P1 says a fake degree is easy to make at home; P2 says buying one online is a waste of money. Both concern ease and cost, not whether the two degrees are equally good.
The conclusion equates the two degrees in value ("just as good"), a claim the premises never establish, so it is a non sequitur.
defs: Incorrect argument (non sequitur)
An argument whose conclusion does not logically follow from its premises, even if the premises are true; the truth of the premises does not guarantee the conclusion.
tips: Do not judge an argument by whether its premises are true; check whether the conclusion actually follows from them.
Watch for a shift in topic: P1 and P2 discuss ease and cost, but the conclusion makes a claim about quality.
rq: Why does the conclusion fail even if both premises are true?

Because the premises only say the degree is easy to make and buying is wasteful; they say nothing about the quality or value of a self-made degree compared with a bought one, so "just as good" is unsupported.
What premise would be needed to make the argument valid?
A premise linking the two degrees' quality or value directly, e.g. "Two fake degrees that are equally easy to obtain are equally good."

notes.t: Seminar 2: Argument structure of the American colonists' right to rebel
pts: The argument is a valid deductive syllogism-style argument with two general premises (P1, P2), one particular premise (P3), and a conclusion (C) drawn from them.
P1 grounds government in natural rights: people are equal and have unalienable rights, and governments exist to protect them.
P2 gives the conditional right of revolution: when government violates those rights, people may rebel and create a new government.
P3 is the empirical premise applying the general principles to the case: the king of GB has repeatedly violated colonists' rights.
The validity of the conclusion depends on all premises being true; to evaluate it, one must assess whether P3 is actually supported by evidence.
defs: Unalienable rights
Rights that cannot be given away or taken away by others, held by people simply by virtue of being human (natural rights).
Right to rebel
The justified permission of a people to overthrow a government that systematically violates their natural rights and replace it with a new one.
tips: Distinguish the logical form (valid vs. sound): the argument is only sound if all premises are true, so do not treat the conclusion as proven just because it follows logically.
Do not confuse a premise about what governments should do (P1) with a factual claim about what the king has done (P3).
rq: Why does the argument need P1 and P2 as well as P3? What would follow if only P3 were given?

P3 alone only reports a fact about the king's conduct; P1 and P2 supply the general principle that such violations justify rebellion, so without them the conclusion about a right to rebel does not follow.
What would happen to the argument's force if P1 were dropped and governments were not understood as existing to protect rights?
The link between violation and legitimacy would be lost, since P2 depends on governments having a purpose of protecting rights; without P1, a violation would not clearly make rebellion a right.

units.name: 4 Charter schools and public-school bureaucracy
units.ov: This material is a seminar exercise in argument analysis, using the claim that charter schools associated with the public-school bureaucracy outperform independent ones. It breaks the argument into premises (P1 support, P2 concession that obstruction is outweighed) and conclusions (C1 comparative performance, C2 a further conclusion built on C1). The skills are separating premises from conclusions, exposing hidden premises, and testing whether the evidence supports the claim.
must: Structure: P1 (bureaucracy gives associated charter schools invaluable support) and P2 (it can obstruct, but support outweighs this) lead to C1, and C1 leads to C2
C1 is the comparative conclusion that associated charter schools outperform independent ones; it is inferred from P1 and P2 together, not from P1 alone
P2 contains a hidden premise: support outweighs obstruction. It is a weighing judgement, so state it explicitly and evaluate it
C2 is a chained conclusion drawn from C1, not directly from the premises; it is only as strong as C1 is established
'Unsurprising' (an expectation claim) is not the same as 'true' (an evidential claim); the argument supports the former more directly
Correlation vs causation: association with the bureaucracy may not cause better performance, so consider confounders and selection effects (e.g. which schools choose to associate)
P1 is asserted, not evidenced: 'invaluable' is vague and needs evidence of what support is given and how it affects outcomes
A concession in P2 strengthens credibility but also adds a vulnerability, because the whole argument then depends on the weighing
Method for a top answer: identify the conclusions, map the inference chain, list the hidden premises, then assess each step's strength
conn: Hidden premises and weighing judgements: P2's concession only protects the conclusion if the 'outweighs' premise is stated and defended
Chained inference: the strength of C2 depends on C1, which depends on P1 and P2, so weakness upstream propagates downstream
Correlation vs causation links to evaluating evidence for sustainable development policy, where institutional support and outcomes are often confounded
Distinguishing expectation from truth connects to separating a plausible argument from a well-evidenced one
exq: Reconstruct the argument that associated charter schools outperform independent ones, labelling P1, P2, C1 and C2 and identifying the hidden premise in P2.
Explain why C1 does not follow from P1 alone, and what extra claim is needed for the inference to work.
Evaluate whether the argument shows that associated charter schools are better, or only that this is unsurprising. Distinguish the two claims.
How might correlation and causation be confused in this argument? Suggest two confounders and say what evidence would address them.
Assess how far C2 depends on C1, and whether C2 could be true even if C1 were false.

notes.t: Seminar 2, Argument 9: Charter schools and public-school bureaucracy
pts: The argument claims public-school bureaucracy gives charter schools associated with it invaluable support and services.
P2 concedes the bureaucracy can obstruct progress but argues this is outweighed by its support, so the conclusion rests on a weighing judgement.
The conclusion is that associated charter schools outperform independent ones, presented as unsurprising given P1 and P2.
tips: Do not treat the conclusion as following from P1 alone; check that the hidden premise in P2 (support outweighs obstruction) is stated and evaluated.
Distinguish 'unsurprising' (a claim about expectation) from 'true' (a claim about evidence); the argument supports the former more directly.
rq: Why does the conclusion depend on the weighing claim in P2 rather than on P1 alone?
Because P1 only establishes support; P2 is needed to dismiss the costs of bureaucracy, so the conclusion follows only if the support outweighs the obstruction.
What would weaken this argument most?
Evidence that the bureaucracy's obstruction is large enough to outweigh its support, or that performance differences have causes other than association (e.g. selection of students).

notes.t: Seminar 2: Argument analysis – public-school bureaucracy and charter schools
pts: The argument is a two-premise argument whose conclusions are drawn from the premises about bureaucratic support.
P1 claims the public-school bureaucracy provides invaluable support to associated charter schools, which is the key supporting premise for C1.
P2 concedes the bureaucracy can make things hard, but argues this does not outweigh the support it gives.
C1 is an inference from the premises to a comparative claim about charter schools' performance; C2 is a further conclusion built on C1.
C2 is a conclusion drawn from C1 (the normative/attitudinal claim), so its strength depends on whether C1 is established.
tips: Distinguish the premises that support C1 from C2, which is drawn from C1 rather than directly from the premises.
Check whether the argument assumes correlation (association with the bureaucracy) implies causation (support causes better performance).
rq: Why does C1 follow from P1 and P2 rather than just from P1?
P2 establishes that the bureaucracy's drawbacks do not outweigh its benefits, so the net effect of support is positive, supporting the comparative claim that associated charter schools do better.
What would weaken the inference from the premises to C1?
Evidence that the bureaucracy's difficulties are more costly than its support, or that charter schools' performance differences come from other factors such as selection effects.

units.name: 5 Motive arguments: disjunctive syllogism and evidence
units.ov: This material uses a murder-motive example to show how a disjunctive syllogism ('political or private; not political; so private') is built from evidence. Footprints support an intermediate conclusion about how long the murderer stayed. A generalisation about political assassins then rules out the political motive. The evaluation skill throughout is separating validity from soundness and spotting weak premises, namely the defeasible generalisation and the assumed exhaustive disjunction.
must: Disjunctive syllogism: from 'P or Q' and 'not P', infer 'Q'. The form is deductively valid.
Validity is not soundness: a sound argument needs a valid form and all premises true. A dubious premise makes a valid argument unsound or only weakly convincing.
The argument's structure: evidence (footprints throughout the room) → C1 (the murderer stayed a long time) → P3 (political assassins act quickly and flee) → 'not political' → C2 (private motive).
P3 is an inductive generalisation. It is defeasible and only probabilistic, so the elimination of 'political' is not guaranteed and C2 is only as strong as P3.

Exhaustiveness of the disjunction: 'political or private' must cover all motives. An unstated third option (e.g. robbery, mistaken identity, a mixed motive) breaks the inference, so state this assumption explicitly.
The inference from footprints to a long stay (C1) is itself an inference from evidence. Ask whether other explanations exist, such as a frantic search or a quick but wide-ranging movement.
Check whether C1 is actually used: identify which premises the final conclusion depends on and which steps are intermediate or redundant.

Evaluation method: (1) identify premises and conclusions, (2) check whether the conclusion follows (validity), (3) check whether the premises are true or acceptable, (4) consider objections and unstated assumptions.
Distinguish deductive certainty (the form of the syllogism) from the inductive support behind its premises. A valid form can carry an uncertain conclusion.
conn: Validity vs soundness links to premise assessment: a valid disjunctive syllogism is only as good as its weakest premise, usually the generalisation P3.
Inductive generalisation (P3) feeds the deductive step (elimination). Exam answers should show how probabilistic premises weaken a deductively valid conclusion.
Evidence-to-conclusion reasoning (footprints → duration) connects to the exhaustiveness check: both rely on unstated assumptions and alternative explanations.
Argument reconstruction (labelling P1, P2, C1, C2) underpins evaluation, since you must see the structure before you can say which step fails.
exq: Reconstruct the footprint/motive argument in standard form, labelling premises, the intermediate conclusion C1 and the final conclusion C2. Identify the disjunctive syllogism within it.
Is the argument valid? Is it sound? Explain the difference, using the generalisation about political assassins as your example.
Give two alternative motives or explanations that would undermine the exhaustiveness of 'political or private'. How does each affect the conclusion?
Evaluate the strength of the inference from footprints throughout the room to a long stay. Suggest evidence that would strengthen or weaken it.
Explain why a generalisation like 'political assassins act quickly and flee' supports a conclusion only probabilistically. How could the argument be reworded to reflect this?

notes.t: Seminar 2: Argument analysis (disjunctive syllogism with a dubious premise)
pts: The argument has the form of a disjunctive syllogism: either political or private motive; not political; therefore private.
Premise 2 is used to rule out the political option by inferring a long stay in the room, which is then linked to the non-political (private) motive via premise 3.
Premise 3 is a generalisation about political assassins; it is only a defeasible claim, so the conclusion is not guaranteed.
Evaluate the argument by checking whether premises are true and whether the conclusion follows; a valid form can still yield an unsound argument if a premise is false or merely probable.
defs: Disjunctive syllogism
A valid argument form: from 'P or Q' and 'not P', infer 'Q'.
tips: Do not confuse validity with soundness: the form may be valid while a premise (especially the generalisation in P3) is doubtful.
Check that the disjunction is exhaustive; an unstated third motive breaks the inference.
rq: Why does the conclusion only follow if premise 1 is exhaustive?
Because the inference to 'private' requires that political and private are the only possible motives; if another motive exists, ruling out 'political' does not establish 'private'.
What if political assassins sometimes linger at the scene?
Then premise 3 is false or weaker, so the link from long presence to 'not political' fails and the conclusion is undermined.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Reasoning from evidence to motive (alternative argument 10)
pts: The argument moves from evidence (footprints throughout the room) to a conclusion about duration spent in the room.
The first conclusion (C1) is an inference about how long the murderer stayed, drawn from the extent of footprints.
P2 sets up a disjunction: the motive was either political or private.
P3 is a generalisation that political assassins act quickly and flee, which is used to rule out the political option.
C2 follows by eliminating the political option (modus tollens style with the disjunction), concluding the crime was private.
defs: Disjunctive syllogism
An inference of the form 'P or Q; not P; therefore Q', used here by ruling out one motive to conclude the other.
Inductive generalisation
A claim drawn from observed cases ('political assassins move quickly') that is applied to a particular case; it supports conclusions probabilistically rather than with certainty.
tips: Check whether C1 is actually used in the argument; a conclusion can be drawn without relying on the preceding one.
A disjunctive premise only works if the two options are exhaustive; state this assumption explicitly.
rq: Why does C2 only follow if P2 is taken as exhaustive?
Because the disjunction 'political or private' must cover every possibility; if another motive existed, ruling out political would not force a private motive.
What if some political assassins linger in the room?
Then P3 is false or weaker, so the step from 'not quick, not fleeing' to 'not political' is undermined and C2 loses its support.
Does C1 actually support the conclusion about motive?
No; C1 concerns duration in the room and is not used in deriving C2, so the argument's structure is weaker than its presentation suggests.

units.name: 6 High school size and implicit premises
units.ov: This seminar material trains argument reconstruction using a case: smaller high schools are claimed to be better because of higher graduation and college-going rates, leading to a policy of breaking up large schools in NY. It shows how to separate premises from conclusions, expose implicit premises, and evaluate inferences, especially the gap between correlation and causation and between evidence and policy action. Three versions of the argument show how different implicit premises change what the argument needs.
must: Reconstruct arguments in standard form: label stated premises (P1, P2), intermediate conclusion (C1), and final conclusion (C2), keeping them distinct.
Implicit premise: an unstated assumption the argument needs for its conclusion to follow; make it explicit and label it [implicit].
P1 (higher graduation rates) and P2 (higher college-going proportions) are empirical claims about outcomes; C1 ('smaller schools are better') is evaluative.
Missing premise for P1,P2 → C1: that graduation and college-going rates capture overall school quality; the premises do not prove 'better' in every respect.
C2 (policy: break up large schools) does not follow from C1 alone; it needs P3 'NY wants better high schools' plus the assumption that breaking up schools makes them smaller and better.
Correlation vs causation: 'shown to have higher rates' does not establish that size causes the outcomes; check for confounders (e.g. student intake, funding, selection effects, location).
Moving from 'smaller schools do better' to 'making schools smaller improves them' is a further causal and policy leap.
Alternative version: appeals to NY's policy as evidence, needing the implicit premise that NY makes sound educational decisions (an appeal to authority, weak if unjustified).
Argument strength depends on the plausibility of the implicit premises, not just the stated statistics.
conn: Implicit premises and causation: the assumption that breaking up schools makes them better is exactly a causal claim needing support beyond correlational data.
Evaluative conclusions and measures: choosing graduation and college rates as proxies for 'better' links empirical premises to value judgements via a hidden premise.
Policy conclusions: descriptive claim (C1) → normative/policy claim (C2) requires a bridging premise about goals (NY wants better schools) and means.
Comparing reconstructions: different implicit premises (policy goals vs NY's soundness) yield different arguments, and evaluation depends on which is chosen.
exq: Reconstruct the smaller-school argument in standard form with P1, P2, C1, and C2, and identify and label all implicit premises.
Explain why C2 ('NY should break up large high schools') does not follow from C1 alone. What additional premises are required?
Using the school-size example, distinguish correlation from causation and give two plausible confounders that could explain higher graduation rates in small schools.
Evaluate the alternative argument that relies on NY's policy. What implicit premise does it need, and how plausible is it?
To what extent do graduation and college-going rates support the claim that smaller schools are 'better' overall? State the missing premise and assess it.

notes.t: Seminar 2 – Argument on smaller vs larger high schools
pts: The argument is an inference from two premises (graduation rates and college-going proportions) to a conclusion that smaller high schools are better overall.
Both premises are empirical claims about outcomes; the conclusion evaluates 'better' in a broader sense that the premises only partly support.
tips: Do not treat the two premises as proving 'better' in every respect; note the missing premise that these measures capture overall quality.
Check whether the premises show correlation or causation; 'shown to have higher' does not establish that size causes the difference.
rq: Does the conclusion follow deductively from P1 and P2, or only inductively/defeasibly?
Only defeasibly: the premises support 'smaller schools do better on these two measures', but 'better' overall needs further premises about other outcomes, so the inference is not deductively valid.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Argument analysis – smaller high schools and an implicit premise
pts: The argument moves from evidence about graduation and college rates (P1, P2) to a general evaluative claim that smaller schools are better (C1).
C2 does not follow from C1 alone; it needs the implicit premise P3 that NY wants better high schools, plus the assumption that breaking up schools is how to make them smaller and better.
The argument is an inference to a conclusion about a policy action, so its strength depends on whether the statistics show causation rather than correlation.
defs: Implicit premise
An unstated assumption that an argument needs for its conclusion to follow; it must be identified and made explicit when reconstructing an argument.
Conclusion
The claim an argument is trying to establish, supported by premises.
tips: Do not treat the conclusion as following from the statistics alone: check for a missing link between the evidence and the policy action in C2.
Watch for correlation versus causation: higher rates in small schools do not prove that making schools smaller improves them.
rq: Why can't C2 be derived from P1, P2 and C1 alone?

Because C2 is a factual claim about what NY has done, while C1 is only evaluative and says nothing about NY's actions; the step needs P3 and a policy link (NY wants better schools, and splitting schools is a means to that).
What would make P1 and P2 weak support for C1?
If the correlation is due to confounding factors (e.g. wealthier or more selective schools being smaller), so size is not the cause of higher graduation and college rates.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Further alternative argument on high school size
pts: The argument infers that smaller high schools are better because they show higher graduation rates and college-going proportions, supported by NY's policy of breaking up large schools.
The conclusion depends on an implicit premise that NY makes sound educational decisions, which is needed to justify the policy evidence.
The argument moves from correlational outcome data to a general claim that smaller schools are better, so the link between size and outcomes must be examined for confounding factors.
defs: Implicit premise
An unstated assumption that an argument needs in order for its conclusion to follow from its stated premises.
tips: Do not treat the implicit premise as a stated premise; label it clearly as [implicit] when reconstructing the argument.
Distinguish correlation between school size and outcomes from causation when evaluating whether smaller schools are genuinely better.
rq: Why does the argument need P4, even though it is not stated?
Because the evidence that NY broke up large schools only supports the conclusion if NY's decisions were sound; without P4 the policy fact alone does not show smaller schools are better.
What would weaken the inference from P1 and P2 to the conclusion?
Evidence that other factors, such as school funding, socioeconomic background or selection of students, explain the outcome differences rather than school size.

units.name: 7 Cautious driving and human nature arguments
units.ov: This material uses short worked arguments from Seminar 2 to train argument analysis: the cautious-driving reductio shows that a valid argument can have an absurd conclusion, and the human-nature/goodness arguments show how to test validity, scope and premise truth. The common thread is separating logical form (validity) from truth of premises (soundness) and spotting hidden assumptions or scope shifts. The notes are partly inconsistent about whether the human-nature argument is valid, so treat that point carefully.
must: Validity: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true; it concerns form only, not whether the premises or conclusion are actually true
Soundness = validity + all premises actually true; always evaluate the premises after checking form

Cautious driving argument (P1: goal of encouraging cautious driving; P2: people drive carefully when life is at risk; C: put a spear at the driver's chest) is valid but absurd, so the fault lies in the premises

Cautious driving weakness: the means-end inference (most effective means = what we ought to do) ignores other values such as the driver's wellbeing and others' safety, plus side effects; challenge P1's 'everything' and the unstated assumption that the goal outweighs other values
Human nature argument: P1 'human nature cannot be learned', P2 'goodness must be learned', so C: goodness is not part of human nature (not inherently good)
The alternative version adds an intermediate step C1 (nothing learned/learnable is part of human nature), derived from P1, then applies it to goodness; this step is logical, not empirical evidence
Slide 20 marks a version as 'Incorrect': the conclusion C1 does not follow, and P2 and P3 are flagged; check for scope shifts and for conflating 'must be learned' with 'cannot be innate'
Critique method: first test whether the conclusion follows (validity), then identify the specific premise to challenge, and do not judge an argument by whether its premises seem plausible
Reductio-style reasoning: show a premise set is faulty by deriving an absurd conclusion from it
conn: Validity vs soundness links the driving and human nature examples: both are valid-looking, and the question is always which premise fails
Means-end reasoning (driving) and scope/quantifier problems (human nature) are both hidden assumptions that make an apparently valid step illegitimate

Human nature claims about goodness feed into sustainable development debates: whether people are inherently cooperative or must be incentivised mirrors the debate over policies that force behaviour change at a cost to other values
The reductio technique can be applied to the human nature argument: if the same reasoning yields absurd results elsewhere, the form or premises are faulty
exq: Define validity and soundness. Show with the cautious driving argument that one can be satisfied without the other, and identify which premise you would reject and why.
Reconstruct the human nature argument in standard form (P1, P2, C). Is it valid? Explain whether 'goodness must be learned' really entails 'goodness is not part of human nature'.
Explain why the slide marks the C1 argument as 'Incorrect'. Identify the scope shift and rewrite the premises so that the conclusion would follow.
Evaluate the means-end inference in the cautious driving argument: what values does it ignore, and how would you add a premise to block the absurd conclusion?
Using one of the Seminar 2 arguments, explain the steps you would take to critique an argument in an exam answer, and why checking truth of premises before form is a mistake.

notes.t: Seminar 2: Argument from cautious driving (reductio-style example)
