The SRC provides training, and the role is recognised on your academic transcript.
The Traitors UK is used as a source of good examples of poor reasoning, as applied critical thinking.
The new series starts on Thursday (1/10), and students can watch it before the seminar.
The module theme is critical thinking and the 'Spirit of Philosophy': question assumptions and evaluate arguments.
The Thursday seminar is where these ideas are discussed, so prepare examples beforehand.
conn: The Traitors as a case study links to critical thinking: spotting fallacies in accusations, group persuasion and evidence use in the show.
Student representation links to the feedback loop of SSLC, then actions, then reports back to classmates. This is a reasoned, evidence-based process for improving teaching.
The seminar links to the TV examples, since the show gives concrete cases to apply philosophical reasoning to.
Critical thinking skills carry over to sustainable development debates, where claims and evidence must be assessed.
exq: Describe the role of a student representative, including how often they attend the SSLC and what they do afterwards.
Using an example from The Traitors UK, identify a piece of poor reasoning and explain why it is flawed.
Explain what is meant by critical thinking and the 'Spirit of Philosophy' in the context of this module.
Evaluate how the SSLC process can improve teaching, facilities and student support. What are its limits?
What training and recognition do student reps receive, and why might this benefit the student as well as the university?

notes.t: Becoming a Student Representative
pts: Student reps voice students' views on all learning and teaching matters.
Reps attend the Staff Student Liaison Committee once per semester.
Reps relay issues and actions back to their classmates.
The role aims to improve teaching, facilities and student support.
Training is provided by the SRC and the role is recognised on your academic transcript.

notes.t: New series of The Traitors UK
pts: The TV series The Traitors UK can be used as a source of good examples of poor reasoning.
The new series starts on Thursday (1/10), so students can watch it in the meantime.
rq: Why might a reality game show like The Traitors be a useful source of examples of poor reasoning rather than good reasoning?
Contestants often make decisions based on emotion, weak evidence, hasty generalisations, or social pressure, which provide clear, memorable instances of fallacies and reasoning errors to analyse.

units.name: 2 Socrates as philosopher and critical thinker
units.ov: This material presents Socrates as a philosopher whose core commitments are independent thinking, a questioning attitude and first-hand knowledge over received opinion. His facets (critical thinker, self-examiner, gadfly/agitator, seeker of truth and happiness) are unified by one aim, the search for truth, pursued through Socratic ignorance and dialectics. That search is held to yield eudaimonia, a flourishing life.
must: Socrates prizes independent thinking, questioning and first-hand knowledge over accepting received opinion.
Socratic ignorance: recognising the limits of one's own knowledge is the starting point of inquiry. It is not claiming to know nothing.
Dialectics: systematic question and answer that tests claims and beliefs in order to reach truth; this is his main method.
Four facets: critical thinker, self-examiner, rebel/agitator (gadfly), seeker of truth and happiness. They are connected, with the seeker as the underlying aim.
Self-examination turns critical scrutiny inward on one's own beliefs and life, and Socrates regards it as essential to a worthwhile life.
Gadfly: Socrates' image of himself as an irritant sent by the god to rouse complacent Athens into examining its beliefs. It shows his role as a public social activist.
Eudaimonia means flourishing or well-being achieved through the pursuit of truth and virtue, not mere pleasure or everyday happiness.
The goal is truth, and a life devoted to seeking it is judged more fulfilling than other kinds of life.
Alienation (estrangement from self, others or society) is offered only as a possible reading of his questioning. Present it as tentative ('maybe'), not as fact.
conn: Socratic ignorance leads to dialectics: admitting ignorance motivates questioning, and questioning tests claims in pursuit of truth.
Self-examination and the gadfly role are the inward and outward faces of the same critical attitude, applied to oneself and to society.
Truth-seeking leads to eudaimonia: the examined life is argued to be the fulfilling one, which links the method to the ethical goal.
The alienation reading links the four facets: questioning as an attempt to overcome estrangement fits the seeker of happiness, but it remains an interpretation.
exq: Explain Socratic ignorance and discuss why it is not the same as knowing nothing. How does it function as a starting point for inquiry?
Describe the four facets of Socrates as a philosopher. To what extent does the 'seeker of truth and happiness' unify the others?
Evaluate the claim that Socrates acted as a social activist, with reference to the gadfly image and public dialectical conversation.
What does eudaimonia mean for Socrates, and why does he judge a life devoted to the pursuit of truth more fulfilling than other lives?
Critically assess the suggestion that Socrates' questioning was an attempt to overcome alienation. How strong is the evidence for this reading?

notes.t: Socrates: Summary
pts: Socrates values independent thinking, a questioning attitude, and first-hand knowledge rather than accepting received opinion.
Socratic ignorance means recognising the limits of one's own knowledge as the starting point for inquiry.
Socrates is portrayed as a social activist who challenged others' assumptions in public conversation.
Dialectics, a method of question and answer aimed at testing claims, is his main tool of inquiry.
The overall goal is truth, and a life devoted to its search is judged more fulfilling than other kinds of life.
defs: Eudaimonia
Greek term for flourishing or well-being; for Socrates, a good life achieved through the pursuit of truth and virtue.
Socratic ignorance
The recognition that one does not really know what one claims to know, which motivates the search for knowledge.
Dialectics
A method of inquiry through systematic question and answer, used to examine and test beliefs in order to reach truth.
tips: Do not confuse Socratic ignorance with simply knowing nothing; it is a claimed awareness of the limits of one's knowledge.
Eudaimonia means flourishing or well-being, not merely pleasure or happiness in the everyday sense.
rq: Why might admitting ignorance be a necessary first step in the pursuit of truth?
Admitting ignorance removes false certainty, opening the mind to questioning and genuine inquiry rather than repeating unexamined opinions.
How does the claim that a truth-seeking life contributes to eudaimonia link knowledge to living well?
For Socrates, understanding what is good and examining one's life makes a person better and more fulfilled, so knowledge and flourishing are connected.

notes.t: Socrates: facets of the philosopher
pts: Socrates is first presented as a critical thinker who questions received opinions.
He is also a self-examiner, turning critical scrutiny inward on his own beliefs and life.
He acts as a rebel or agitator, a 'gadfly' stinging the complacent Athenians into thought.
Ultimately he is a seeker of truth and of happiness, possibly attempting to overcome alienation.
defs: Gadfly
Socrates' self-image as a stinging irritant sent by the god to rouse the Athenian state from complacency, forcing citizens to examine their beliefs.
Self-examination
The practice of critically testing one's own beliefs and way of life, which Socrates regards as essential to a worthwhile human life.
Alienation
A sense of estrangement from oneself, others or society; the lecture suggests Socrates' questioning may be an attempt to overcome it.
tips: Do not present the four facets as separate, unrelated roles; the lecture frames the seeker as the ultimate underlying aim.
'Overcome alienation' is offered as a 'maybe' interpretation, so present it as a possible reading rather than established fact.
rq: Why might a critical thinker who questions everyone end up appearing as a rebel to the city?
Because questioning received opinions exposes ignorance and challenges authority and social norms, which unsettles those invested in them and makes the questioner seem disruptive.
How can the self-examiner and the seeker of happiness be the same figure?
Examining one's beliefs and life is presented as the route to understanding what is good, so self-examination serves the pursuit of truth and a happy, well-lived life.

units.name: 3 Philosophy vs rote learning and rhetoric (Socrates, Plato, Kierkegaard)
units.ov: This material defines philosophy, for Socrates and Plato, by contrast with rival practices: non-dialogical education such as rote learning, and rhetoric (developed later in the course). Socrates treats knowledge as a personal achievement reached through dialogue and self-criticism. Kierkegaard extends the worry: he predicts handbook-style education (1846) and counters it with indirect communication and pseudonyms that push readers to think for themselves.
must: Socratic-Platonic claim: philosophy is defined against rivals, namely non-dialogical education (rote learning) and rhetoric
Non-dialogical education transmits information without question-and-answer, so learners never examine or justify their beliefs
For Socrates knowledge is not second-hand opinion that can be bought or handed over; it is a personal achievement
Socratic self-criticism: continually examining one's own beliefs to expose inconsistency and ignorance; this is how learning is stimulated, through dialogue not passive transmission
Dialogue is the method; rote learning is the contrasted example, so do not conflate method and example
Kierkegaard (1846) predicts education reduced to memorising compendiums from handbooks, success being skilled retrieval like a typesetter picking letters, not understanding
Inauthentic education: accumulating and retrieving second-hand information without personal engagement; this evaluative verdict is the course's, while the prediction is Kierkegaard's

Indirect communication: Kierkegaard uses devices such as pseudonyms (e.g. Johannes de Silentio, Fear and Trembling) to distance himself from the ideas, prompting readers to reach their own conclusions
Rote learning (non-dialogical memorisation) and rhetoric (persuasive speech) are distinct; detailed rhetoric is deferred to later (Week 4)
conn: Socrates' dialogue and self-criticism vs Kierkegaard's indirect communication: different methods (face-to-face questioning vs literary distance) with the same aim of making learners think independently
Rote learning (Socrates/Plato) and handbook learning (Kierkegaard) as the same problem: knowledge treated as transferable second-hand information, which is inauthentic
Knowledge as personal achievement links to self-criticism: because knowledge cannot be handed over, it must be reached by examining one's own beliefs
Rote learning and rhetoric as two separate rivals to philosophy, to be distinguished carefully when the rhetoric material arrives
exq: Explain why Socrates and Plato define philosophy by contrast with non-dialogical education such as rote learning. Why can knowledge not simply be handed over?
What does Socrates mean by self-criticism, and how does dialogue stimulate it?
Outline Kierkegaard's 1846 prediction about handbook education, including the typesetter image, and assess why it is called inauthentic.
What is indirect communication, and how do pseudonyms such as Johannes de Silentio encourage readers to think for themselves?
Compare Socratic dialogue and Kierkegaard's indirect communication as responses to passive, second-hand learning.

notes.t: The anti-philosopher: philosophy contrasted with non-dialogical education and rhetoric
pts: For Socrates and Plato, philosophy is defined against rival practices rather than in isolation.
The first contrast is forms of non-dialogical education, such as rote learning, which transmit information without questioning or dialogue.
The second contrast is the practice of rhetoric, which is treated as a rival to philosophy and is discussed later in the course.
defs: Non-dialogical education

Forms of teaching, such as rote learning, that transmit knowledge without question-and-answer exchange, so the learner is not led to examine and justify beliefs; Socrates and Plato contrast this with philosophy, which proceeds through dialogue.
tips: Do not treat rote learning and rhetoric as the same thing: rote learning is non-dialogical memorisation, while rhetoric is persuasive speech.
The page only sets up the contrast; the full discussion of rhetoric is deferred to the end of the session or Week 4, so do not present detailed rhetoric arguments as drawn from this page.
rq: Why might Socrates and Plato define philosophy by contrast with rote learning rather than by listing its positive features?
Because philosophy is understood as an active, dialogical process of questioning and testing beliefs, so it is most clearly identified by what it is not: passive memorisation of received content.
What might make rhetoric a useful rival to define philosophy against?
Rhetoric aims at persuasion and winning audiences, whereas philosophy aims at truth through dialogue, so comparing them highlights the difference between persuading and knowing.

notes.t: Education: Socratic-Platonic contrast between dialogue and rote learning
pts: For Socrates and Plato, philosophy is contrasted with non-dialogical education such as rote learning.
For Socrates, knowledge is not second-hand opinion that can be bought and handed over, but a personal achievement.
Learning, understood as self-criticism, is stimulated through dialogue rather than passive transmission of information.
defs: Non-dialogical education
Forms of teaching, such as rote learning, in which knowledge is passively received without questioning or exchange, contrasted by Socrates and Plato with philosophical dialogue.
Self-criticism (Socratic)
The continual examination of one's own beliefs and claims to expose inconsistency and ignorance; for Socrates, the route by which genuine knowledge is achieved.
tips: Do not describe Socratic knowledge as the accumulation of information; the key point is that it is personally achieved through self-criticism, not handed over.
Be precise that dialogue is the method, and rote learning is the contrasted example of non-dialogical education.
rq: Why would Socrates consider an encyclopaedia-style transfer of information to be a poor model of knowledge?

Because knowledge for Socrates must be personally achieved through self-criticism; information that is merely accepted and stored does not involve the examination of one's own beliefs, so it is second-hand opinion rather than knowledge.
What might a rote-learning student miss that a Socratic dialogue partner gains?
The student who memorises misses the testing and revision of their own beliefs prompted by questioning, so they never discover their ignorance or refine their understanding.

notes.t: Kierkegaard on education and handbook learning
pts: Kierkegaard predicts education will reduce to memorising compendiums of observations taken from handbooks.
Success becomes a matter of skill in retrieving the right item from stored information, like a typesetter picking letters, rather than understanding.
The lecturer's verdict is that this model of education is inauthentic and should not be how education works.
defs: Inauthentic education
Learning that consists of accumulating and retrieving second-hand information from handbooks without personal engagement or genuine understanding, which the page rejects as a model for education.
tips: Do not present Kierkegaard's prediction as the lecturer's own view; the page itself labels the handbook model inauthentic, which is the evaluative claim to attribute to the course.
Note the date (1846) and work title when citing, as the page gives them explicitly.
rq: Why does Kierkegaard compare the student to a typesetter, and what does this comparison reveal about the kind of knowing he is criticising?

A typesetter selects existing letters without composing meaning; the comparison reveals that the student merely retrieves pre-packaged items rather than understanding, thinking, or making knowledge their own.
What would an 'authentic' education need to include that the handbook model lacks?
Personal engagement, reflective understanding and the ability to form and examine one's own judgements, rather than only recalling stored observations.

notes.t: Kierkegaard's indirect communication and pseudonyms
pts: Kierkegaard used stylistic devices such as pseudonyms to create distance between himself and the ideas he wrote about.
The purpose of this distance is to encourage readers to think for themselves rather than accept ideas passively.
This method of writing is called indirect communication.
defs: Indirect communication

Kierkegaard's literary method of conveying ideas through devices such as pseudonyms, so that the author stands at a distance from the views expressed and readers are prompted to reach their own conclusions.
Pseudonym
A fictitious author name under which a writer publishes, used by Kierkegaard to separate himself from the ideas in a text.
tips: Do not confuse indirect communication with simply hiding the author; the key point is that the distance is purposeful and aims at encouraging independent thought.
Be precise that the pseudonym is a fictitious author name (here Johannes de Silentio for Fear and Trembling), not merely a stylistic flourish.
rq: Why might an author deliberately distance himself from the ideas he writes about, and what does this suggest about how philosophical truth should be received?

Distance prevents readers from simply adopting the author's views on authority; it forces readers to engage actively and reason for themselves, suggesting that genuine understanding must be personally appropriated rather than passively received.
How would Fear and Trembling be read differently if the reader believed Johannes de Silentio was Kierkegaard himself?

The reader might treat its claims as Kierkegaard's settled doctrine; knowing it is pseudonymous invites the reader to evaluate the pseudonym's arguments critically, including noticing where the pseudonym's views may fall short.

units.name: 4 Criticisms and limitations of Socratic dialectic
units.ov: This material evaluates the Socratic dialectic (elenchus), the method of questioning to examine beliefs and expose ignorance, by setting out four main criticisms. These cover its epistemic limits, its presupposed view of the good life, the unequal or non-collaborative character of the questioning, and the personal cost and role-model question raised by Socrates' obsessiveness. The criticisms connect because each asks whether dialectic alone is sufficient: for knowledge, for living well, for dialogue and for social responsibilities.
must: Epistemic criticism: dialectic alone may not yield positive knowledge and can end in aporia, 'knowing that we know nothing'
Correct framing of that criticism: dialectic is insufficient on its own, not useless; other sources (scientific methods, practical experience) must complement it
'The unexamined life is not worth living' presupposes a particular, contestable conception of the good life (a life of philosophical self-examination)
Dialogue criticism: Socratic questioning can be un-collaborative or unequal, with Socrates controlling the questions and the other person on the defensive
Kidd's stingray image: Socrates 'numbs' his interlocutors, as a stingray does its victims, which illustrates the one-sidedness and disempowerment of the method
There is more than one kind of dialogue, so Socratic questioning is one model and not the model of good conversation
Personal-cost criticism: Socrates' obsession with questioning may have led him to neglect his family, which raises the question of whether other role models exist
Exam skill: distinguish the specific complaint that Socrates' questioning is one-sided from the broader point that dialogue takes several forms
Exam skill: state each criticism, give its textual or example support, and weigh whether it undermines the method or only limits its scope
conn: Epistemic limits and the good-life claim: if dialectic only shows ignorance, why should the examined life be uniquely valuable? Both questions concern whether dialectic can justify itself
Stingray/unequal dialogue and the 'more than one kind of dialogue' point: use alternative, collaborative models of dialogue as a response to the one-sidedness charge
Neglect of family and the role-model question: link the critique of the examined life to wider conceptions of the good life, including care, relationships and practical responsibilities
Insufficiency of dialectic and the need for scientific methods and practical experience: relevant to sustainable development, where questioning values must be combined with evidence and action
exq: Outline and assess the criticism that the Socratic dialectic can only lead to 'knowing that we know nothing'. How might a defender of Socrates respond?
'The unexamined life is not worth living.' Does this claim presuppose a particular conception of the good life? Discuss with reference to at least one alternative.
Using Kidd's stingray image, evaluate whether Socratic questioning is a genuinely collaborative form of dialogue. What other kinds of dialogue are there?
Does Socrates' neglect of family undermine his status as a role model? Consider what other role models might offer.
Which one of the four criticisms of Socratic dialectic is most damaging to the method, and why? Justify your answer by distinguishing criticisms of insufficiency from criticisms of uselessness.

notes.t: Possible criticisms/limitations of Socratic dialectic
pts: The dialectical method alone may not yield knowledge; it can end in only knowing that we know nothing, so other sources of knowledge (scientific methods, practical experience) need attention.
The claim 'the unexamined life is not worth living' seems to presuppose a very particular conception of the good life.
Socratic questioning may be giving yet un-collaborative or unequal, as Kidd's image of numbing victims like a stingray suggests; there is more than one kind of dialogue.
Socrates' obsessiveness with questioning may come at the cost of neglecting family, raising the question of whether other role models exist.
tips: Do not treat 'knowing that we know nothing' as the end of the method; the criticism is that dialectic alone is insufficient, not that it is useless.
Distinguish the criticism that Socrates's questioning is one-sided from the broader point that there is more than one kind of dialogue.
rq: Why might a purely dialectical method leave us in an unsatisfying position, and what other sources of knowledge could complement it?
Because elenchus can expose ignorance without producing positive knowledge, so scientific methods and practical experience are needed to supplement it.
What would have to be true about the good life for 'the unexamined life is not worth living' to be a universal claim, and why might that be contested?
It would require that reflective self-examination is the essential component of a good life; this is contested because it assumes one particular conception of value that others may reject.

units.name: 5 Defining critical thinking and its discipline
units.ov: This material defines critical thinking through Dewey's (1910) and Ennis's (1996) definitions, then presents it as a discipline (informal logic) that improves deliberation and decision making. It distinguishes an expansive version (Hanscomb, 2019), which adds psychology, dispositions and dialogue, from narrower approaches. All versions share one core: the analysis of arguments.
must: Dewey (1910, p.6): critical (reflective) thinking is active, persistent and careful consideration of a belief in light of the grounds which support it.
Ennis (1996, p.166): critical thinking is reasonable, reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do.
Dewey centres on grounds (evidence for beliefs); Ennis broadens the aim to action as well as belief. This contrast is the key comparison.
Both definitions stress reflection: deliberate, self-aware thinking, not automatic acceptance.
Critical thinking (informal logic) is a discipline of knowledge, methods and a frame of mind that improves deliberation and decision making.
Its aims: identify the questions to ask before significant decisions; construct, assess and improve arguments; learn the pitfalls of reasoning.
The three pitfall categories: weak arguments and their psychological biases, unconstructive dialogues, and dispositions that make us prone to poor reasoning.
Expansive version (Hanscomb, 2019) covers psychology, dispositions and dialogue alongside argument analysis; narrower approaches omit some of these.
All approaches to CT share a focus on arguments: structured premises offered in support of a conclusion.
'Critical' is a technical term meaning careful, evidence-based evaluation, not fault-finding or simply disagreeing. Cite source and year accurately.
conn: Dewey's focus on grounds links to argument analysis: grounds are the premises supporting a conclusion, so evaluating beliefs means evaluating arguments.
Ennis's belief-or-action aim links to the discipline's purpose of better decision making, for example in sustainable development policy choices.
The expansive version links the pitfalls list (biases, unconstructive dialogue, dispositions) to the psychology, dialogue and dispositions elements that narrower approaches omit.
The 'not mere disagreement' point links the definitions to the method: CT constructs and improves arguments, including your own, rather than just attacking others'.
exq: Compare Dewey's (1910) and Ennis's (1996) definitions of critical thinking. What does each emphasise, and what do they share?
Explain what is meant by the 'expansive version' of critical thinking (Hanscomb, 2019). Which elements might a narrower approach omit, and what do all approaches share?
Outline the three categories of reasoning pitfall that critical thinking as a discipline addresses, with an example of each.
Why is critical thinking not the same as disagreeing or finding fault? Answer with reference to the aims of informal logic.
Discuss how critical thinking could improve a significant decision, such as a sustainable development policy choice, using the discipline's stated aims.

notes.t: Defining critical thinking
pts: Dewey defines critical (reflective) thinking as active, persistent, careful consideration of a belief in light of the grounds supporting it.
Ennis defines critical thinking as reasonable, reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do.
Both definitions stress reflection: thinking is deliberate and self-aware rather than automatic acceptance.
Dewey's definition centres on grounds: beliefs must be evaluated against the evidence that supports them.
Ennis broadens the aim: critical thinking guides action as well as belief.
defs: Critical (reflective) thinking (Dewey, 1910)
Active, persistent and careful consideration of a belief in light of the grounds which support it.
Critical thinking (Ennis, 1996)
Reasonable, reflective thinking that is focused on deciding what to believe or do.
tips: Do not confuse 'critical' in the everyday sense of finding fault with the technical sense of careful, evidence-based evaluation of beliefs.
Quote the source and year when citing Dewey (1910, p.6) or Ennis (1996, p.166) to earn credit for accurate attribution.
rq: Why does Dewey insist that belief be considered 'in light of the grounds which support it' rather than simply held firmly?
Because firmness of belief does not make it true or justified; critical thinking requires checking the evidence and reasons behind it, so beliefs are only accepted when well supported.
What is the practical difference between Dewey's and Ennis's definitions?
Dewey focuses on evaluating beliefs against their grounds, while Ennis adds that the purpose is deciding what to believe or do, extending critical thinking to action and decision-making.

notes.t: The discipline of critical thinking (informal logic)
pts: Critical thinking aims to make us better deliberators and decision makers through knowledge, methods and a frame of mind.
It helps us identify the questions we should ask before making significant decisions.
It helps us construct, assess and improve our own arguments.
It teaches the pitfalls of reasoning: weak arguments and their associated psychological biases.
It also covers features of unconstructive dialogues and dispositions that make us prone to poor reasoning.
defs: Critical thinking (informal logic)

The discipline of knowledge, methods and a frame of mind that improves deliberation and decision making by helping us ask the right questions, build and assess arguments, and recognise reasoning pitfalls.
tips: Do not confuse critical thinking with simply disagreeing; it is a method for constructing, assessing and improving arguments.
Remember the three pitfall categories: weak arguments and biases, unconstructive dialogues, and dispositions.
rq: Why does critical thinking include psychological biases alongside weak arguments?
Because biases are often the psychological source of weak reasoning, so recognising them helps us avoid flawed arguments and poor decisions.
How might unconstructive dialogue undermine good decision making in a group?
It can shut down exchange of reasons, so arguments are not properly tested or improved, leading to poorer collective decisions.

notes.t: The discipline of critical thinking (CT)
pts: CT can be understood in an expansive version that includes psychology, dispositions and dialogue, not just logic.
Many approaches to CT are narrower, omitting psychology, dispositions and/or dialogue.
Despite differences, all approaches to CT share a focus on arguments.
defs: Expansive version of critical thinking
Hanscomb's (2019) term for a broad conception of CT that covers psychology, dispositions and dialogue alongside argument analysis.
Arguments (in CT)
The central object of study in critical thinking: structured sets of premises offered in support of a conclusion, which all CT approaches focus on.
tips: Do not confuse the 'expansive' view with a view that drops argument analysis; the expansive view adds psychology, dispositions and dialogue to arguments.
Be ready to name which elements (psychology, dispositions, dialogue) a narrower approach omits.
rq: Why might a narrow approach to CT that ignores dispositions be less effective than an expansive one?
Because good reasoning also depends on attitudes such as open-mindedness and willingness to test one's beliefs; without dispositions, a person may know argument techniques yet fail to use them.
What is gained by including dialogue in the study of CT?
Dialogue shows that arguments are often exchanged with others, so CT includes questioning, responding to objections and collaborative reasoning, not just solitary evaluation.

units.name: 6 What is an argument? Premises and conclusion
units.ov: This material introduces the academic sense of 'argument' in critical thinking: a set of statements in which premises are offered as reasons for a conclusion. It shows how to identify and separate premises from conclusion (using indicator words and worked examples on capital punishment and Newton), and how this structure leads into evaluating arguments through validity and soundness.
must: Definition: an argument is a set of statements in which premises are intended to support a conclusion. It is not a quarrel or dispute.
Conclusion = the claim being established. Premises = the reasons or evidence offered for it. Identify the conclusion first, then the premises.
Intended support is what makes something an argument, so a bad argument is still an argument.
Non-arguments: a bare assertion (e.g. 'capital punishment is wrong'), a list of claims, an explanation, or a disagreement. Each lacks premises explicitly linked to a conclusion.
Indicator words such as 'therefore', 'so' and 'thus' usually signal the conclusion.

Standard form: list premises P1, P2... then the conclusion C. For example: P1 anything that intensifies racial discrimination should be outlawed; P2 capital punishment intensifies it; C capital punishment should be outlawed.
Validity: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. It concerns logical structure, not whether the premises are actually true.
Soundness = valid form + true premises. A valid argument can be unsound if a premise is false, as with the Newton and alchemy argument.
Evaluation: challenge sweeping universal premises (e.g. 'anyone who believes in alchemy cannot be a true natural scientist').
Persuasion is not validity: an argument aims to convince, but a good argument needs premises that really support the conclusion.
conn: Identifying structure comes before evaluation: you must separate premises from conclusion before you can judge validity or soundness.
Validity versus soundness: the same example (Newton) can be valid in form yet unsound because of a contestable generalisation in P2.
Argument versus explanation or assertion: indicator words help, but you must check that reasons are intended to support a claim.

Factual versus normative statements: the capital punishment example uses a general principle and a factual premise to reach a normative conclusion, which links to how different kinds of premise are assessed.
exq: Define 'argument' in the critical thinking sense and explain how it differs from a quarrel, a list of claims and an explanation.

Set out in standard form (P1, P2, C) the argument that capital punishment should be outlawed because it intensifies racial discrimination. Identify the general premise, the factual premise and the normative conclusion.
Using the Newton and alchemy argument, explain the difference between validity and soundness. Which premise would you challenge, and why?
'A bad argument is not an argument.' Discuss with reference to the role of intended support.
Identify the conclusion and premises in a short passage containing indicator words, and explain how you decided which statement is the conclusion.

notes.t: Identifying arguments
pts: Critical thinking (CT) centrally involves using and analysing arguments.
In the academic sense, an argument is not a dispute or quarrel; it is a set of statements in which some (premises) are offered as support for another (conclusion).
defs: Argument (academic sense)
A set of statements, consisting of premises and a conclusion, where the premises are offered as reasons supporting the conclusion. Not a quarrel or dispute.
tips: Do not confuse an academic argument with a dispute or quarrel; an argument needs premises supporting a conclusion.
Listing several claims is not an argument unless some are offered as reasons for another.
rq: Why does the academic sense of 'argument' differ from everyday usage, and why does this matter for critical thinking?

Everyday 'argument' means a quarrel; academically it means premises offered in support of a conclusion. Confusing the two leads to treating disagreement as reasoning, so analysis focuses on reasons, not emotional conflict.
What would you look for to decide whether a passage is an argument rather than just a series of statements?
Whether some statements are offered as reasons supporting another statement (a conclusion), i.e. an inferential structure linking premises to conclusion.

notes.t: What is an argument?
pts: An argument is a set of propositions in which one proposition is the conclusion and the others are premises offered in support of it.
The premises are intended to support the conclusion; this intention is what makes a set of statements an argument.
Tindale characterises arguments structurally: one or more statements (premises) are given in support of a conclusion.
defs: Argument
A set of propositions, one of which is the conclusion and the remainder the premises, where the premises are intended to support the conclusion.
Premise
A statement offered as reason or evidence in support of a conclusion.
Conclusion
The statement that the premises are intended to support; the claim the argument is trying to establish.
tips: Do not confuse an argument with a mere explanation, list of claims or disagreement: an argument needs a conclusion supported by premises.
Remember that the definition concerns intended support, so an argument can be bad (premises fail to support) and still be an argument.
rq: Why does the definition require that the premises are intended to support the conclusion, rather than simply that they are related to it?

Because a set of statements may be related (e.g. both about the weather) without forming an argument; it is the intention to give support that makes the set an argument, so mere co-relevance or a list of facts does not count.
What would be the difference between a set of true statements and an argument?
A set of true statements may have no conclusion and no intended inferential link; an argument has a designated conclusion that the other statements are offered to support.

notes.t: What is an argument?
pts: An argument aims to convince someone else of your point of view.
The point of view being defended is the conclusion of the argument.
Statements offered in support of the conclusion are called premises.
defs: Argument
A set of statements in which premises are offered in support of a conclusion, with the aim of convincing someone of that conclusion.
Conclusion
The point of view that an argument seeks to establish; the claim supported by the premises.
Premises
The statements (information) offered in support of the conclusion of an argument.
tips: Do not confuse the conclusion (what is being argued for) with the premises (the reasons given for it); identify the conclusion first.
Persuasion is not the same as argument validity: the aim is to convince, but a good argument needs premises that actually support the conclusion.
rq: Why is it useful to separate the conclusion from the premises when reading someone's argument?
Identifying the conclusion shows what is being claimed, and the premises show the reasons offered for it, so you can evaluate whether those reasons really support the claim.
Can a statement that merely states a personal opinion, with no supporting reasons, count as an argument?
No. Under this definition an argument needs a conclusion supported by premises; a bare opinion with no statements offered in support is not an argument.

notes.t: What is an argument?
pts: An argument is a set of statements in which some statements (premises) are offered as reasons to support another statement (conclusion).
In the example, the conclusion is that capital punishment should be outlawed, supported by a general principle and a factual claim.
defs: Argument
A set of statements consisting of premises, which are offered as reasons, and a conclusion, which is the claim those reasons are intended to support.
tips: Do not confuse an argument with a mere assertion or a disagreement; an argument must give reasons linked to a conclusion.
Identify the conclusion by looking for indicator words such as 'therefore', 'so', or 'thus'.
rq: Why does the example count as an argument rather than just a list of opinions?

Because its statements are linked: the premises (anything that intensifies racial discrimination should be outlawed; capital punishment intensifies it) are offered as reasons supporting the conclusion that capital punishment should be outlawed.
Which statement is the conclusion in the example, and how can you tell?
'Capital punishment should be outlawed' is the conclusion, signalled by the word 'Therefore' and being what the other statements are meant to support.

notes.t: What is an argument? (Premises and conclusion)
pts: An argument is a set of premises offered in support of a conclusion; formally it lays out the reasons (premises) that lead to the claim being defended (conclusion).
In a valid-form argument, the conclusion follows from the premises: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

The example argument has a general premise (anything that intensifies racial discrimination should be outlawed), a factual premise (capital punishment intensifies racial discrimination), and a normative conclusion (capital punishment should be outlawed).
defs: Argument
A set of statements (premises) offered as reasons to support another statement (the conclusion); it is not merely a disagreement or a set of opinions.
Premise
A statement in an argument that provides reasons or evidence for the conclusion.
Conclusion
The statement an argument is trying to establish, supported by the premises; usually signalled by words such as 'therefore'.
tips: Do not confuse a conclusion with a premise: the conclusion is the claim being supported, not the claim doing the supporting.
Stating a view with no reasons given (e.g., 'capital punishment is wrong') is not an argument; reasons must be explicitly linked to the conclusion.
rq: Why does the word 'therefore' matter when identifying an argument?
It marks the conclusion, showing which statement the other statements are offered to support; identifying the conclusion is the first step in reconstructing an argument.
What would happen to the argument if Premise 2 were false?
The conclusion would no longer be supported by the reasoning, since a premise that is false removes the justification for the conclusion, even if the logical form remains intact.

notes.t: What is an argument?
pts: An argument is a set of statements in which some statements (premises) are offered as reasons to support another statement (the conclusion).

The example argument concludes that Newton was not a true natural scientist, supported by two premises: anyone who believes in alchemy cannot be a true natural scientist, and Newton believed in alchemy.
The example is an argument because it gives reasons (premises) in support of a claim (conclusion), rather than merely asserting the claim.
defs: Argument
A set of statements consisting of one or more premises offered as reasons in support of a conclusion.
Premise
A statement in an argument offered as a reason or evidence for the conclusion.
Conclusion
The statement in an argument that the premises are offered to support.
tips: Do not confuse an argument with a mere assertion or an explanation; an argument must give reasons intended to support a conclusion.
Identify the conclusion first (often the claim being supported), then the premises, before evaluating the argument.
rq: Why does the word 'because' in the example signal that an argument is present rather than a simple assertion?
Because it introduces premises given as reasons supporting the conclusion, showing the claim is being justified.
What would be needed to evaluate whether this argument is good, given that its premises are offered in support of its conclusion?
Checking whether the premises are true and whether they actually support the conclusion (validity and soundness).

notes.t: What is an argument? (premises and conclusion)
pts: An argument is a set of premises offered to support a conclusion; here it is set out formally as two premises followed by a conclusion.
The argument is deductive in form: if both premises are true, the conclusion must follow, so validity depends on the logical structure rather than on the truth of the claims themselves.
Soundness requires both valid form and true premises; the example's second premise is a contestable generalisation, so the argument's soundness is open to challenge.
defs: Argument
A set of premises (reasons) offered in support of a conclusion; in formal presentation the premises are listed first and the conclusion follows as the final line.
Premise
A statement assumed or offered as a reason for accepting the conclusion of an argument (here P1 and P2).
Conclusion
The statement the argument aims to establish, drawn from the premises (here C).
tips: Do not confuse validity with truth: an argument can be valid (the conclusion follows) yet unsound if a premise is false.
Check whether P2 is a justified generalisation before accepting the conclusion; sweeping universal claims are a common target in evaluation.
rq: Why is it useful to set an argument out as numbered premises and a conclusion rather than as a paragraph?
It makes the reasoning explicit so each assumption can be checked for truth and the inference checked for validity.
If the conclusion were false but P1 were true, which premise must be at fault and why?
P2, because a valid argument with a true premise cannot have a false conclusion unless the argument is invalid or a premise is false; the premises must be re-examined.

units.name: 7 Course learning aims and why study arguments
units.ov: This introductory material sets out the course's learning aims and teaching approach, then justifies studying arguments: learning to reason builds our own strong arguments and lets us judge others'. The skills are used by philosophers and by everyone in daily life, and they transfer to self-knowledge, other disciplines and the workplace. The notes for pages 26 and 27 (what you will learn, how you will learn it) contain no detail, so the specifics of the aims and methods must come from the course handbook or lecture slides.
must: Two core purposes of argument skills: improving our own reasoning and argument-building, and judging how strong others' arguments are
Assessing an argument means judging the strength of its reasoning, NOT simply disagreeing with its conclusion
Argument skills are used by philosophers and by everyone in daily life, not only in academic philosophy
Benefits transfer beyond philosophy: self-knowledge, other academic disciplines and the workplace
Be able to give a concrete example of each benefit (e.g. evaluating a policy claim in sustainable development, justifying a workplace decision)
Distinguish the quality of reasoning (is the conclusion well supported?) from the truth or popularity of the conclusion
Check the course handbook or slides for the exact learning aims and the teaching and assessment methods, since the notes for pp. 26-27 are blank
conn: Judging others' arguments and building your own are two sides of one skill: spotting weak reasoning helps you avoid it in your own writing
Separating argument strength from agreement with the conclusion links to critical thinking in Global Sustainable Development, where you must evaluate competing policy claims fairly
Transferable benefits link the course aims to assessment: essays and exams reward clear, well-supported reasoning, which is also what employers value
exq: Explain why studying arguments is useful beyond philosophy, giving at least two specific contexts (e.g. other disciplines, workplace, self-knowledge).
A classmate says 'I disagree with the conclusion, so the argument is bad.' Explain what is wrong with this approach to assessing arguments and describe a better one.
Discuss two ways learning argument skills benefits you as a producer of arguments and one way it benefits you as an evaluator of others' arguments.
Using an example from sustainable development, show how everyday reasoning can be assessed for strength independently of whether you agree with its conclusion.

notes.t: Why learn to reason and assess arguments
pts: Learning argument skills improves our ability to reason and build strong arguments.
Learning argument skills also lets us judge how strong arguments made by others are.
Argument skills are used by philosophers and, indeed, by everyone in daily life.
Benefits extend beyond philosophy to self-knowledge, other academic disciplines and the workplace.
tips: Do not confuse 'assessing an argument' with simply disagreeing with its conclusion; judge the strength of the reasoning itself.
rq: Why might the ability to assess others' arguments matter even for someone who never studies philosophy again?
Everyone encounters arguments in politics, media, advertising and work, so judging their strength helps avoid being misled and supports better decisions.
How could building strong arguments help you in a non-philosophy discipline?
Constructing clear, valid reasoning with explicit premises and conclusions transfers to subjects like science, economics or policy analysis where justifying claims is central.

units.name: 8 Identifying premises and conclusions
units.ov: This material teaches how to analyse an argument by finding its conclusion (the claim being defended) and its premises (the reasons offered for it). It covers conclusion and premise indicator words, their limits, and a worked example on US gun control after Sandy Hook, which is then set out in standard form. The ideas connect because the conclusion is found first, the premises are then identified by their support relationship, and validity is judged separately from truth.
must: Conclusion = the claim being argued for; premises = the reasons offered in support. Identify the conclusion first, then ask which statements support it.
Close, accurate reading of the text is essential; misreading leads to attributing the wrong claim to the author.
Conclusion indicators: therefore, thus, so, hence, accordingly, in which case. They signal that the statement following is drawn from the premises.
Indicators are unreliable: not every 'so' or 'thus' marks an inference, and an indicator at the very start of a passage cannot be a conclusion indicator because no premises precede it.
Premise indicators ('my reason is', 'this is so because', 'my evidence for this is') only often signal premises, and many premises have no indicator. Rely on the logical support relationship.

Worked example: the conclusion is that changing US gun control laws is pointless. P1: changing the laws would not stop people obtaining guns. P2: if people can get guns, shootings and massacres remain possible.
Context and source details (Sandy Hook, December 2012; Radio 4 Today) frame the argument but are neither premises nor conclusions.
A conditional premise ('if X then Y') is not the conclusion. Watch for hidden or implicit premises, such as the assumption that a law change would not reduce access to guns.
Standard form: list numbered premises, then the conclusion. Validity (does the conclusion follow?) is assessed separately from the truth of the premises.

Dialogue prompts: 'So what you're telling me is…' elicits the conclusion and 'The reason you think this is…' elicits the premises. Pragma-Dialectics treats argument as critical discussion aimed at resolving a difference of opinion.
conn: Indicator words and logical support: indicators are clues, but the final decision rests on what supports what, so questions combine indicator spotting with a check on whether the inference is real.

Identifying premises and conclusions leads to evaluation: once the argument is in standard form, you can test validity and premise truth separately, and expose implicit premises such as 'a law change would not reduce access'.

Argument in dialogue and Pragma-Dialectics: the 'So what you're telling me is…' and 'the reason you think this is…' questions are practical tools for extracting the conclusion and premises from a speaker, supporting constructive discussion.
Context versus content: separating framing details (event, date, source) from the claims is part of accurate close reading.
exq: Read this passage and identify its conclusion and premises, then set it out in standard form. State which words, if any, were indicators and which parts you identified without them.
Explain why a conclusion indicator such as 'therefore' or 'so' may not mark a conclusion. Give one example of a misleading case, including an indicator at the start of a passage.
Analyse the Sandy Hook gun-control argument. State the conclusion and the two premises, identify the conditional premise, and discuss one implicit assumption.
Distinguish between validity and the truth of premises, using the gun-control argument. Could the argument be valid but unsound?
How do the questions 'So what you're telling me is…' and 'The reason you think this is…' help in analysing arguments in dialogue, and how does Pragma-Dialectics use this approach?

notes.t: Identifying premises and conclusions
pts: To identify a conclusion, work out the claim that the person is making.
Identifying a conclusion requires a close, accurate reading of the text in question.
Close, accurate reading of the text is a vital skill for analysing arguments.
tips: Do not confuse the conclusion with the premises: the conclusion is the claim being argued for, not the reasons offered in support of it.
Accuracy matters: misreading the text can lead you to attribute the wrong claim to the author.
rq: Why must you work out the claim being made before you can identify a conclusion?
A conclusion is the claim the author is trying to establish, so you must first determine what the person is asserting before you can label any statement as the conclusion.
What might go wrong if you skim a text rather than reading it closely when analysing an argument?
You may misidentify the main claim, confuse premises with conclusions, or miss supporting reasons, leading to an inaccurate reconstruction of the argument.

notes.t: Identifying premises and conclusions: conclusion indicators
pts: Conclusions in an argument can often be spotted by conclusion indicator words that signal the claim being drawn from the premises.
Common conclusion indicators include therefore, thus, so, hence, accordingly and in which case.
A conclusion indicator is not a reliable signal when it appears at the very beginning of a passage, since there are no premises before it to support.
defs: Conclusion indicator
A word or phrase (e.g. therefore, thus, so, hence, accordingly, in which case) that signals the statement immediately following it is the conclusion of an argument, drawn from the premises.
tips: Do not assume every occurrence of 'so' or 'thus' marks a conclusion; check whether the sentence actually draws an inference from earlier statements.
Remember the exception: a conclusion indicator at the very start of a passage is not a reliable sign of the conclusion.
rq: Why does a conclusion indicator at the start of a passage fail to signal a conclusion?
Because a conclusion must follow from premises; if the word opens the passage there are no earlier statements for it to be drawn from, so it cannot function as a conclusion marker.
What if the word 'so' appears mid-passage but is used to mean 'in such a way' rather than 'therefore'?
Then it is not functioning as a conclusion indicator; indicator words must be checked in context, since the same word can have non-inferential uses.

notes.t: Identifying premises and conclusions
pts: Once the conclusion is identified, the next step is to find the separate statements given in support of it, which are the premises.
Premise indicators are phrases that often (but not always) signal a premise, so they are useful clues rather than foolproof markers.
Common premise indicators include phrases introducing a reason, evidence, or justification for a claim.
Phrases such as 'my evidence for this is' and 'this is so because' also signal that a premise follows.
A premise can be signalled by conditional framing that asks the reader to accept claims before drawing a conclusion.
defs: Premise
A statement given in support of a conclusion, offered as a reason to believe that conclusion.
Premise indicator
A word or phrase (e.g. 'my reason is', 'this is so because') that often, but not always, signals that a premise is being stated.
tips: Do not assume every premise has an indicator word; indicators are only sometimes present, so rely on the logical support relationship.
Do not confuse the conclusion with the premises: identify the conclusion first, then look for the statements that support it.
rq: Why can't premise indicators alone be relied on to identify premises?
Because they only sometimes appear; an argument may state premises without any indicator, so the reader must judge from the content and structure of the passage.
How would you find the premises once you have identified the conclusion?
Ask which separate statements are offered as reasons or support for that conclusion; these are the premises.

notes.t: Identifying premises and conclusions
pts: The conclusion of an argument is the claim being defended; here it is that changing US gun control laws is pointless.
The premises support the conclusion: changing laws won't stop people getting guns, and access to guns makes shootings possible.
The argument has a conditional premise linking access to guns with the possibility of massacres.
Context (Sandy Hook, December 2012) frames the argument but is not itself a premise or conclusion.
defs: Conclusion
The statement an argument aims to establish, supported by one or more premises.
Premise
A statement offered as reason or evidence to support the conclusion of an argument.
tips: Do not confuse the context sentence or source (Today, Radio 4) with a premise or conclusion; look for the claim being defended.
Indicator words such as 'therefore' are absent here, so identify the conclusion by asking what the other statements are used to support.
rq: Why is the 'then' clause in the passage a premise rather than the conclusion?
It gives a reason ('if people can get hold of guns, then shootings... will be a possibility') used to support the main claim that policy change is pointless, so it is a supporting statement.
What would the argument need in order to show that changing the laws is pointless, not just less effective?
It would need the premise that changing the laws would not reduce access to guns, which the argument asserts with 'people will still be able to get hold of guns'.

notes.t: Identifying premises and conclusions
pts: The argument's conclusion is that changing US gun control laws is pointless.
The first premise: changing the laws would not stop people obtaining guns.
The second premise: if people can get guns, shootings and massacres remain possible, so the reasoning links access to harm.
Indicator words such as 'if...then' and 'even if' signal premises and conditionals, while the bolded claim is the conclusion.
defs: Premise
A statement offered as a reason or evidence supporting a conclusion.
Conclusion
The statement an argument is intended to establish, supported by its premises.
tips: Do not confuse a conditional premise ('if X then Y') with a conclusion; look for the claim the author is actually defending.
Check whether a premise is hidden or implicit, such as the assumption that a law change would not reduce access to guns.
rq: Why is the claim 'there's no point in changing the laws' the conclusion rather than a premise?
Because it is the claim the passage is trying to establish; the other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
What would happen to the argument if the second premise were false, i.e. shootings were impossible even when guns were accessible?
The chain from access to massacres would break, so the conclusion would no longer follow from the premises.

notes.t: Identifying premises and conclusions
pts: An argument is set out formally by separating its premises (reasons offered) from its conclusion (the claim being supported).
Premise 1 claims that changing gun control laws would not stop people obtaining guns.
Premise 2 links access to guns with the possibility of shootings and massacres.
The conclusion is that changing US gun control laws serves no purpose, which follows from the two premises taken together.
defs: Premise
A statement offered as a reason or evidence to support another statement in an argument.
Conclusion
The statement an argument is trying to establish, supported by its premises.
tips: Do not confuse a premise with the conclusion: identify the claim being argued for first, then find the reasons given for it.
Check whether the argument is valid (conclusion follows from premises) separately from whether the premises are actually true.
rq: Why is it useful to set out an argument formally before evaluating it?
Separating premises from the conclusion makes the structure explicit, so you can see exactly what is claimed to support what and assess each step.
What would happen to the conclusion if Premise 2 were false, even with Premise 1 true?
The argument would no longer support the conclusion, since access to guns would not necessarily lead to shootings and massacres.

notes.t: Identifying premises and conclusions
pts: Argument analysis centres on exchanges where a speaker states a conclusion and then gives reasons for it.
The question 'So what you're telling me is …' asks the speaker to state the conclusion being claimed.
The question 'And the reason you think this is …' asks for the premise(s) supporting that conclusion.
Branches of critical thinking and informal logic, such as Pragma-Dialectics, study arguments within dialogue.
The aim of these branches is to understand and teach people to engage in constructive dialogue.
defs: Premise
A statement offered as a reason or evidence supporting the conclusion of an argument.
Conclusion
The statement an arguer is claiming to be true on the basis of the premises.
Pragma-Dialectics
An approach in informal logic that analyses argumentation as a critical discussion aimed at resolving a difference of opinion.
tips: Do not confuse premises with conclusions: the conclusion is what is being claimed, the premises are the reasons given for it.
Identify the conclusion first; reasons are only premises relative to a specific claim they support.
rq: Why is it useful to ask 'So what you're telling me is …?' before evaluating an argument?
It forces the speaker to state the conclusion explicitly, so you know exactly what claim the argument is trying to establish before assessing its reasons.
What might go wrong if you evaluate the reasons without first confirming the conclusion?
You may assess reasons against a claim the speaker does not actually hold, or misread which statement is the conclusion and which is the support.

units.name: 9 Propositions and recasting questions as statements
units.ov: This material covers propositions: declarative sentences that can in theory be judged true or false, and which alone can serve as premises or conclusions. It explains how questions (including rhetorical ones) and directives must be recast as statements without losing their point. Once recast, the argument's structure, premise chain and conclusion are explicit, so each step can be assessed for validity and truth.
must: Definition: a proposition (statement) is a declarative sentence that makes a claim that can, in theory, be true or false
Only propositions can be premises or conclusions; questions, commands/directives and exclamations cannot
Controversial, unproven, emotive or opinion-based claims are still propositions, because they are the kind of claim that could be true or false
Questions and directives must be re-worded as declarative sentences before being used in an argument, e.g. 'Where's my drink?' or 'Go and get me another one!'
Re-wording must preserve the point being made, not merely change the sentence form
A rhetorical question can be recast as a premise, making the hidden argument structure explicit
Premises can be written as conditionals (if…then) that chain claims together towards the conclusion, which is flagged with 'Therefore'
Definitions: a premise is a proposition offered as support; a conclusion is the proposition the argument aims to establish
Making premises explicit lets you assess each step separately for validity and truth

Check that loaded wording (e.g. 'disastrous policy') is not treated as established fact, and that the conclusion does not exceed what the premises license (e.g. long-term claims need long-term premises)
conn: Propositions and argument structure: only once questions and commands are recast as statements can you identify premises and conclusion and then evaluate validity and soundness
Rhetorical questions and conditionals: recasting a rhetorical question often yields an if…then chain, linking this topic to logical form and chain reasoning
Emotive language and evaluation: loaded wording kept in the conclusion must be tested against the premises, linking to bias, persuasion and critical assessment of truth
Scope of conclusion and premises: a mismatch (e.g. short-term premises, long-term conclusion) is a weakness found after recasting, linking to argument evaluation
exq: Define a proposition and explain why questions, commands and exclamations cannot be premises or conclusions. Give one example of each.
Recast the rhetorical question 'Who would want to live in a city with no green space?' as a proposition, explaining how you preserved its point.
Rewrite a short passage built on rhetorical questions as numbered premises (using if…then) and a 'Therefore' conclusion, then assess whether the conclusion goes beyond the premises.
True or false: a controversial opinion cannot be a proposition. Justify your answer with examples.
A policy is called 'disastrous' in an argument's conclusion. Explain how you would check whether the premises support this evaluative wording.

notes.t: Propositions
pts: Premises and conclusions of an argument must be propositions (statements), not questions, commands or exclamations.
A proposition is a sentence that makes a claim that can, in theory, be judged true or false.
Most everyday things we say are propositions, including personal feelings, contested opinions and scientific facts.
defs: Proposition (statement)
A sentence that makes a claim about something and can, in theory, be judged to be true or false. Premises and conclusions of arguments must be propositions.
tips: Do not confuse a proposition with a sentence in general: questions, commands and exclamations are not propositions and cannot serve as premises or conclusions.
Being controversial or unproven does not stop a sentence being a proposition; it only needs to be the kind of claim that could be true or false.
rq: Why must premises and conclusions be propositions rather than questions or commands?
Only propositions can be true or false, so only they can be assessed for whether they support a conclusion and whether the premises are correct; a question or command has no truth value to evaluate.
Is 'drinking your own urine has health benefits' a proposition even though it is false?
Yes. A proposition only needs to be capable, in theory, of being judged true or false; whether it actually is true is irrelevant.

notes.t: Propositions
pts: Propositions are contrasted with other kinds of sentence, most commonly questions and directives.
A question (e.g. "where's my drink?") is not a proposition and cannot be true or false.
A directive (e.g. "Go and get me another one then!") is a command or request, not a proposition.
A point expressed as a question or directive must be re-worded as a proposition before it can be included in an argument.
defs: Proposition
A declarative sentence that expresses something that is either true or false; the kind of sentence used as a premise or conclusion in arguments.
tips: Do not treat a question or command as a premise or conclusion; re-word it into a declarative sentence first.
Re-wording must preserve the point being made, not just change the sentence form.
rq: Why must a question or directive be re-worded before it can figure in an argument?

Because arguments are built from propositions, which have truth values; questions and directives do not state anything that can be true or false, so they cannot serve as premises or conclusions as they stand.
How would you re-word "Go and get me another one then!" as a proposition?
For example: "I want you to go and get me another drink" or "You ought to get me another drink" (a declarative statement about wants or obligations).

notes.t: Propositions: turning questions into statements (argument structure)
pts: A rhetorical question can be recast as a premise, so that the argument's logical structure becomes explicit.
Each premise is a conditional (if…then) that links one claim to the next, building a chain toward the conclusion.
The conclusion is the claim the argument is trying to establish, stated with 'Therefore' and tied to the premises.
Making premises explicit allows each step to be assessed separately for validity and truth.
Original emotive or loaded wording (e.g. 'disastrous policy') is preserved in the conclusion, so its evaluative strength should be checked.
defs: Proposition
A declarative statement that is either true or false; in an argument, a premise or conclusion expressed as a statement rather than a question.
Premise
A proposition offered as a reason or support for the conclusion of an argument.
Conclusion
The proposition an argument aims to establish, supported by the premises.
tips: Do not treat loaded or emotive wording in a premise or conclusion as established fact; check whether the premises actually support it.
Check that the conclusion does not go beyond what the premises license, e.g. a conclusion about the long term needs premises that address the long term.
rq: Why does rewriting a rhetorical question as a statement help when evaluating an argument?
It makes the claim explicit and assessable as true or false, so the premises and conclusion can be checked for validity and soundness.
What does the conditional structure of P1 and P2 imply about how the conclusion depends on them?
If the premises are true and the inference is valid, the conclusion follows; if any conditional link is weak, the chain of reasoning breaks.

units.name: 10 Summary of critical thinking and arguments
units.ov: This material introduces critical thinking as both a practice (evaluating claims by their reasons, evidence and logic) and a discipline (studied systematically). It sets out the building blocks of an argument: propositions, which are truth-apt statements, serve as premises that support a conclusion. Everything else in argument analysis rests on identifying these parts and the roles they play.
must: Argument = a set of statements in which some (premises) are offered as reasons supporting another (the conclusion)
Conclusion = the claim the argument aims to establish; it is defined by what is supported, not by position (not simply the last sentence)
Premise = a statement offered as a reason or evidence for the conclusion
Proposition (statement) = the meaning of a declarative sentence that is either true or false; the basic unit of premises and conclusions
Critical thinking = disciplined evaluation of claims and arguments by assessing reasons, evidence and logic
Critical thinking is both a practice (doing it) and a discipline (studied systematically in its own right)
A statement's role (premise, conclusion, or neither) depends on what it supports, not merely on appearing in the passage
Only truth-apt sentences can be premises or conclusions; this is why propositions are the basic units
Standard procedure: find the conclusion first, then identify which statements are offered as support
conn: Propositions link to premises and conclusions: arguments are built from truth-apt statements, so questions, commands and exclamations cannot function as premises or conclusions
The role of a statement depends on the support relation: the same proposition can be a premise in one argument and the conclusion in another
Critical thinking as practice applies the argument structure: evaluating reasons, evidence and logic requires first identifying premises and conclusion
Precise definitions (premise, conclusion) prevent common errors such as treating the final sentence as the conclusion or any statement in a passage as a premise
exq: Define argument, premise and conclusion, and explain how the three terms depend on one another.
Why is a conclusion not simply the last sentence of a passage? Illustrate with an example in which the conclusion appears first or in the middle.
Explain what a proposition is and why it is the basic unit of premises and conclusions. Give one example of a sentence that is not a proposition.
In what sense is critical thinking both a practice and a discipline? Use a sustainable development claim to show how you would evaluate its reasons, evidence and logic.
Given a short passage on a sustainability issue, identify the premises and conclusion and justify how you decided which statement is the conclusion.

notes.t: Summary: Key ideas of critical thinking and arguments
pts: Critical thinking can be understood both as a practice and as a discipline.
An argument is built from premises that support a conclusion.
A conclusion is the claim an argument aims to establish.
Premises are the statements offered as reasons for the conclusion.
Propositions (statements) are the basic truth-apt units that premises and conclusions are made of.
defs: Critical thinking
The disciplined practice of evaluating claims and arguments by assessing their reasons, evidence and logic, studied systematically as a discipline in its own right.
Argument
A set of statements in which some (premises) are offered as reasons supporting another (the conclusion).
Conclusion
The statement in an argument that the premises are intended to support or establish.
Premise
A statement in an argument offered as a reason or evidence for the conclusion.
Proposition (statement)
A declarative sentence's meaning that is either true or false; the basic unit of premises and conclusions.
tips: Do not confuse a statement that merely appears in an argument with a premise or conclusion; its role depends on what it is supporting.
Be precise: a conclusion is what is supported, not simply the last sentence written.
rq: Why must an argument distinguish premises from its conclusion before it can be evaluated?
Because evaluation asks whether the premises give good reason to accept the conclusion; without identifying which is which, you cannot test that support.
What would be lost if we treated critical thinking only as a practice and never as a discipline?
We would lack systematic theory and shared standards (e.g. validity, fallacies) for judging arguments, relying only on unexamined habits of reasoning.

units.name: 1 Introduction and history of the ad hominem
units.ov: This material introduces the ad hominem ('argument against the person') as a strategy of attacking an opponent's character, circumstances or associations, and traces its history from Aristotle to Locke. It separates the ethotic strategy from the fallacy proper, and shows that older textbooks treated all such attacks as fallacious while modern accounts judge them by relevance and appropriateness. The history links the two main versions: shifting from argument to person, and exposing inconsistency.
must: Definition: argumentum ad hominem is 'argument against the person', a fallacy only when the attack on character, circumstances or associations is irrelevant or problematic and displaces the merits of the argument
Strategy vs fallacy: attacking the person is a common strategy in public controversy, and the fallacy must be separately established; not every personal attack is fallacious
Ethotic arguments: arguments concerning the speaker's character; the broader category that includes ad hominem, with Aristotle as the source of the category

Aristotle's insight: a speaker's character often aids acceptance of an argument, so character is legitimately persuasive; his ad hominem concern was a response aimed at the questioner rather than the argument, close to the modern sense
Locke's contribution: ad hominem as one of four types of argument used to persuade or silence opposition, pressing a person with consequences drawn from their own principles or concessions
Locke's version is about self-consistency; he does not explicitly call it a fallacy, but it is fallacious only if the charge is inappropriate
Two fallacious versions: (1) a shift from the person's argument to the person; (2) showing the person to be inconsistent in some way
Textbook tradition vs modern treatment: older texts treated all ad hominem as fallacious; recent work recognises that drawing attention to character or circumstances is often appropriate
Assessment test: ask whether the attack is relevant to the merits of the argument; if so it is probably not the fallacy
conn: Ethotic arguments and ad hominem: Aristotle's view that character aids persuasion explains why character attacks are both effective and sometimes legitimate
Aristotle and Locke: Aristotle's focus on shifting attention to the questioner and Locke's focus on consistency correspond to the two later versions of the fallacy
Historical change and evaluation: the move from 'all ad hominem is fallacious' to 'fallacious only when problematic' ties together the strategy/fallacy distinction and the relevance criterion
Public controversy and sustainability debates: attacks on a speaker's circumstances or associations (e.g. funding, affiliations) can be legitimate or fallacious depending on relevance to the argument
exq: Distinguish between ethotic arguments, the ad hominem strategy and the fallacy of argumentum ad hominem, with an example of each
Explain how Locke's account of the ad hominem differs from Aristotle's, and why Locke's version is not necessarily fallacious
Describe the two versions of the fallacious ad hominem and give an example illustrating each
'All personal attacks in argument are fallacious.' Critically evaluate this claim with reference to the textbook tradition and modern treatments
Using a public controversy example (e.g. a debate over climate policy), assess when drawing attention to a speaker's circumstances or associations is appropriate and when it commits the fallacy

notes.t: Ad hominem arguments: introduction
pts: Attacking an opponent's character, circumstances, or associations is a prevalent strategy in public controversy and falls under ethotic arguments about the speaker's character.
Ethotic arguments concern some feature of the speaker's character; Aristotle is the source of this general category, noting the speaker's character often aids acceptance of an argument.
An attack becomes the fallacy argumentum ad hominem only when it is problematic in particular ways; the fallacy is what must be assessed, not the strategy itself.
Textbook tradition treated all such arguments as fallacious, but more recent treatments recognise that drawing attention to a person's character or circumstances is often appropriate.
defs: Argumentum ad hominem

Literally 'argument against the person': the fallacy of attacking an opponent's character, circumstances or associations when such an attack is irrelevant or problematic, rather than addressing the merits of their argument.
Ethotic argument
An argument dealing with some feature of the character of the speaker; the broader category under which ad hominem attacks fall.
tips: Do not treat every personal attack as the fallacy; the fallacy applies only when the attack is problematic (irrelevant to the merits of the argument).
Distinguish the strategy (attacking the person) from the fallacy (argumentum ad hominem); the question is whether the fallacy is committed.
rq: Why might it be appropriate, rather than fallacious, to draw attention to a speaker's character or circumstances?
