Because a speaker's character, interests or associations can legitimately bear on how much credibility their argument deserves, so raising them can be relevant to evaluating the argument.
What distinguishes a fallacious ad hominem from a legitimate ethotic appeal?
Whether the attack is problematic in particular ways, i.e. whether the personal feature is irrelevant to the argument's merits and is used to dismiss the argument instead of assessing it.

notes.t: Ad hominem arguments: history from Aristotle to Locke
pts: Aristotle's early treatment of the ad hominem identifies the problem as directing a response at the questioner rather than the argument, closer to the modern sense.

Locke introduced the ad hominem as one of four types of argument used to persuade or silence opposition, framing it as pressing a person with consequences drawn from their own principles or concessions.
For Locke the ad hominem is essentially a matter of self-consistency; he does not explicitly call it a fallacy but implies it may be fallacious depending on whether the charge is appropriate.
Two versions of a fallacious argumentum ad hominem exist: a shift from the person's argument to the person, and showing the person to be inconsistent in some way.
defs: Argumentum ad hominem

An argument that targets the person making a claim (or their inconsistency) rather than the claim or argument itself; fallacious when it shifts attention from the argument to the person or when the charge is inappropriate.
tips: Do not treat every ad hominem as fallacious; Locke's version is fallacious only when the charge is inappropriate.
Distinguish the two versions: shifting from argument to person versus showing inconsistency.
rq: Why does the author say Aristotle's account is closer to the modern sense than Locke's?
Aristotle clearly identifies the problem as a shift from the person's argument to the person, whereas Locke frames it mainly as a matter of self-consistency.
Why might a Lockean ad hominem not be fallacious?
If the charge of inconsistency is appropriate and relevant to the person's claims, pressing them with their own principles is a legitimate argument, not a fallacy.

units.name: 2 Case studies: Lomborg and character defence
units.ov: This material uses two case studies, the critique of Bjørn Lomborg in Scientific American and the defence of Charles against an accuser (Peat's argument), to examine ad hominem and ethotic argument. It asks when attacks on a person's character, expertise or circumstances are fallacious and when they are legitimate. It also treats ad hominem as the counterpart of ad verecundiam (appeal to authority).
must: Definition of ad hominem: attacking the arguer's character, expertise or circumstances as a reason to reject their argument, instead of engaging the argument itself
Definition of ethotic argument: appealing to or attacking the ethos (character, credentials, reputation) of the arguer, which can support or undermine a claim

Ad hominem is not automatically fallacious: it is acceptable when the circumstance attacked bears on the reliability of the claim, and fallacious when it substitutes for appraising the argument or evidence
Lomborg case: the critic stresses his lack of environmental expertise, his youth and status, and his absence from earlier debates, all of which target the person rather than his claims
The critic's first reason against Lomborg is ethotic (his absence from prior debates), not about the content of his claims

Rhetorical framing: the introduction sets how readers see the author before any substantive reasons are given, and the book's size and endnote count suggest scholarship without showing the claims are wrong
Such a pre-argument attack is a warning sign but plays only a contributory role in the overall case once the arguments are reviewed
Charles/Peat case: the defence combines a positive ethotic appeal to Charles's good character with an attack on the accuser's character, and these are two distinct parts

In the Charles case there is no preliminary focusing of the audience, so the attack goes straight at the accuser; the argument runs 'the accuser is unreliable, so dismiss the allegations without appraisal', the modern basic form of ad hominem that echoes Aristotle
Ad verecundiam (appeal to authority) is the counterpart of ad hominem: one draws on expertise to support a claim, the other attacks expertise to undermine it
conn: Ad hominem and ad verecundiam are mirror images: both are ethotic and both turn on whether the credentials are relevant to the reliability of the claim

The Lomborg case (an attack on the author, with a preliminary framing of the audience) contrasts with the Charles case (a direct attack on the accuser with no framing), so compare when and how the attack is delivered
Positive ethotic appeal (Charles's good character) and negative ethotic attack (the accuser's character) can be combined in one defence, so analyse each separately
Rhetorical framing and impression-building (book size, endnotes) connect to the question of whether substantive reasons are ever supplied
exq: Using the Lomborg critique, explain how an attack on an author's credentials can be ethotic without being fallacious, and identify at least two moves in the text that do target the person rather than the argument.
Distinguish the fallacious from the legitimate use of expertise or credentials in argument, illustrating with the Scientific American critique.
Analyse Peat's defence of Charles: separate the appeal to Charles's character from the attack on the accuser, and assess whether the attack is fallacious.
Compare the Lomborg and Charles cases: how does the presence or absence of a preliminary focusing of the audience change the way the ad hominem works?
Explain ad verecundiam as the counterpart of ad hominem, and discuss why neither should be labelled fallacious automatically.

notes.t: Ad hominem: attacking the arguer's credibility (Lomborg case)
pts: The critique uses Lomborg's lack of environmental expertise and youth/status to undermine his credibility rather than engaging his arguments.
The Scientific American critic's first reason against Lomborg is ethotic: his absence from prior debates, not the content of his claims.
Describing the book's size and endnote count creates an impression of scholarship without showing that the claims are wrong.
Rhetorical framing (introduction) sets how the reader should view the author before any substantive reasons are given.
defs: Ad hominem (general)
A fallacy in which an arguer's character, expertise, or circumstances are attacked as a reason to reject their argument, rather than the argument itself.
Ethotic argument
An argument that appeals to or attacks the character, credentials or reputation of the arguer rather than the merits of the claim.
tips: Do not label every mention of credentials as ad hominem; credentials are relevant when they bear on the reliability of the claim, and the fallacy lies in using them as a substitute for assessing the argument.
Distinguish the fallacious use (dismissing conclusions because of the person) from the legitimate use (noting the author's expertise as a reason to weigh evidence more carefully).
rq: Why is attacking Lomborg's credentials not by itself a refutation of his conclusions?
Because a claim's truth depends on its evidence and reasoning; a person's credentials bear at most indirectly on whether the claim is true, so the argument must be evaluated on its merits.
What makes the critic's opening remarks function as more than background?
They set the reader's prior judgement of Lomborg before the substantive examples, shaping how the subsequent reasons are received.

notes.t: Ad Hominem Arguments: relevance of circumstances
pts: An ad hominem attack targets a person's character or circumstances to weaken credibility before their arguments are considered; it is the counterpart to ad verecundiam (appeal to authority).
Attacking expertise rather than drawing on it is the defining feature of the ad hominem move in this example.
The attack is not automatically fallacious when the circumstance attacked is relevant to the arguer's claim to scientific importance.
Such an attack plays only a contributory role when the arguments are themselves reviewed later.
defs: Ad hominem argument
A fallacious (unless relevant) attack directed at the person presenting an argument, rather than at the argument itself, aimed at undermining credibility.
Ad verecundiam (Appeal to Authority)
Reasoning that draws on the expertise of an authority to support a claim; the counterpart of ad hominem.
tips: Do not label every personal attack as fallacious; check whether the attacked circumstance is relevant to the arguer's claims.
Remember that an attack made before the arguments are reviewed is a warning sign, but it is only contributory to the overall case.
rq: Why might an ad hominem attack be defensible in Lomborg's case?
Because his lack of previous standing and contributions to the field is relevant to whether his research can be presented as scientifically important.
What distinguishes a fallacious ad hominem from an acceptable one?
Whether the circumstance attacked is relevant to the arguments the person presents.

notes.t: The General Ad Hominem: attacking the accuser's character
pts: The defence against Charles's accuser combines an appeal to Charles's good character with an attack on the accuser's character.
Peat's argument has the form of an ad hominem: the accuser is unreliable, so the allegations should be dismissed without appraisal.
Unlike the previous example, there is no preliminary focusing of the audience before the allegations are appraised, so the attack goes straight at the person.
This fits the modern basic form of argumentum ad hominem and echoes Aristotle's observation that the response is directed against the person, not the argument.
defs: Argumentum ad hominem

A fallacious or dismissive response that targets the person making an argument or allegation, rather than the argument or evidence itself, implying the claim should be rejected because of the speaker's unreliability.
Ethotic reasoning
Reasoning that relies on the character (ethos) of a speaker or of an opponent to support or undermine a claim.
tips: Do not treat every attack on a person as fallacious; the key is whether the attack is used to avoid appraising the argument or evidence itself.
Distinguish the ethotic appeal to Charles's own good character from the attack on the accuser's character, since the passage treats them as two parts of the defence.
rq: Why does the passage say that an appeal to Charles's good character alone would not be enough to defend him?

Because the good-character premise would not dismiss the allegations unless the concerns about the accuser were also introduced; the attack on the accuser's reliability is what makes the dismissal work.
How does this case differ from the previous example in terms of how the audience is prepared?
In this case there is no preliminary focusing of the audience before the allegations are appraised, so the audience is directly steered toward discounting the accuser rather than the allegations.

units.name: 3 Theoretical treatments and relevance
units.ov: This material covers theoretical treatments of ad hominem arguments (attacks on the person rather than the claim) and when they are relevant. It contrasts fallacious uses, which deny a claim solely because of who advocates it, with nonfallacious uses, which give relevant information about the speaker's credibility. It then sets the stricter pragma-dialectical view, which treats ad hominem as a rule violation in dispute resolution, against modern treatments that allow legitimate uses. The ideas connect through one theme: relevance decides whether attention to the person is acceptable.
must: Fallacious ad hominem: denying a claim solely because of who advocates it, without showing the claim itself is false
Nonfallacious ad hominem: uses relevant information about the person to influence attitudes toward their advocacy of a claim
Valid conclusion from a good ad hominem is restricted: the advocacy is not a good reason to believe the claim (Y cannot be believed on X's say-so), NOT that the claim is false
Relevance is the test: personal information must bear on the person's advocacy or credibility (irrelevant example: a lawyer's family problems do not undermine their legal expertise)
Brinton's three elements that can be confused: the person, the person's advocacy of a claim, and the claim itself
Attacking character does not bear directly on the claim's truth; it bears only on how far to trust the speaker

Pragma-dialectical view: fallacies are violations of rules for resolving disagreement, and ad hominem tries to block a view by denigrating the person, questioning impartiality, or alleging inconsistency
Pragma-dialecticians treat any ad hominem as fallacious (the traditional, stricter position), whereas other treatments allow legitimate uses under the right conditions
A speaker can attack credibility and engage with the argument in the same case, so the two must be distinguished
Attending to the speaker is legitimate when it aids understanding; mentioning character is fallacious only when it replaces assessment of the claim
conn: Brinton's person/advocacy/claim distinction explains why the restricted conclusion holds: a good ad hominem undermines advocacy, not the claim
Relevance links the fallacious/nonfallacious divide to the pragma-dialectical view: irrelevant attacks violate dispute-resolution rules, while relevant ones can be legitimate in modern accounts
Credibility, impartiality and consistency attacks (pragma-dialectics) correspond to the kinds of relevant personal information in nonfallacious cases, so assess relevance case by case
Evaluating a source's trustworthiness (appeal to authority or expertise) overlaps with nonfallacious ad hominem, which affects how to judge expert advocacy in sustainability debates
exq: Distinguish fallacious from nonfallacious ad hominem arguments using Brinton's three elements, with an example of each.
A speaker's policy proposal is rejected because they have a history of unrelated family problems. Explain why this is fallacious and state precisely what conclusion, if any, could validly be drawn.
Compare the pragma-dialectical position that all ad hominem arguments are fallacious with modern treatments that allow legitimate uses. Which is more persuasive, and why?
Explain why a good ad hominem shows only that advocacy is not a good reason for belief rather than that the claim is false.
Critically discuss the role of relevance in deciding whether an attack on a person's credibility, impartiality or consistency is acceptable.

notes.t: Treatments of Ad Hominem Arguments
pts: Ad hominem arguments exploit our natural tendency to connect what is said with who says it, but attending to the speaker is legitimate when it aids understanding.
Theorists distinguish simple character attacks from questioning a person's argument or advocacy because of a characteristic or circumstance of that person.
Brinton identifies three elements that might be confused: the person, the person's advocacy of a claim, and the claim itself.
A nonfallacious ad hominem argument introduces relevant information about the person to influence attitudes toward the person's advocacy of the claim.
A fallacious ad hominem denies a claim solely because of who advocates it; a good ad hominem only shows the advocacy is not a good reason for belief, not that the claim is false.
defs: Fallacious ad hominem
Denying a claim or proposition solely on the basis of the person who advocates it, without showing the claim itself is false.
Nonfallacious ad hominem
An argument that uses relevant information about the person to influence an audience's attitude toward that person's advocacy of a claim.
tips: Do not treat every mention of a speaker's character as fallacious; it is fallacious only when it replaces assessment of the claim itself.
A good ad hominem shows that advocacy is not a good reason for belief, not that the claim is false.
rq: Why does showing that a speaker is unreliable not establish that their claim is false?
Unreliability only undermines the advocacy as a reason to believe the claim; the claim's truth depends on its own evidence and support.
What distinguishes a nonfallacious ad hominem from a simple character attack?
The nonfallacious version bears directly on the person's advocacy of the claim and gives grounds for doubting that advocacy, rather than attacking character generally.

notes.t: Relevance in ad hominem arguments
pts: Attacking a person's character does not directly bear on the truth of the claim they advance; it only bears on how much we should trust their say-so.
An ad hominem is fallacious when what is alleged about the person has no bearing on that person's advocacy of the claim.
Irrelevant personal history (e.g. family problems) does not undermine a lawyer's legal expertise in a case.
Pragma-dialecticians treat fallacies as violations of rules for resolving disputes, so ad hominem arises as a problem in dialogues aimed at resolving disagreement.
The correct conclusion in such cases is restricted: Y cannot be believed on the basis of X's advocacy, not that Y is false.
defs: Argumentum ad hominem
A fallacious argument that targets the person making a claim (character, history, circumstances) rather than the claim or its support, where the personal attack is irrelevant to the claim's advocacy.
tips: Do not conclude that the claim is false from an ad hominem; the valid conclusion is only that it cannot be believed on the basis of the speaker's advocacy.
Distinguish a relevant reason to distrust a source (legitimate) from an irrelevant personal attack on the arguer (fallacious).
rq: Why does X's history of unjustified claims fail to show that Y is false?
Because it bears only on the reliability of X as a source (our reasons for trusting X's say-so), not on the truth of Y itself.
What makes the lawyer example a fallacious ad hominem rather than a legitimate objection?
The second premise (family history) is irrelevant to the lawyer's advocacy of a claim about family law, so it cannot bear on the argument's merits.

notes.t: Pragma-dialectical view of ad hominem arguments
pts: Ad hominem moves attempt to prevent someone from advancing their view, by denigrating them, questioning impartiality, or claiming inconsistency.
Pragma-dialecticians treat any ad hominem as fallacious, whereas other modern treatments allow it as legitimate under the right conditions.
An ad hominem does not deal with the other's argumentation but attempts to discredit the person by questioning credibility.
A person may both attack credibility and deal with the argument, so the authors add pragma-dialectical concerns to a list of problems rather than deeming all ad hominem fallacious.
Three general problems with fallacious ad hominem arguments are identified, the first being that an arguer concludes a position is false based on material questioning the person.
defs: Ad hominem argument
An argument that attempts to discredit a person by questioning their credibility, impartiality or consistency rather than dealing with their argument.
tips: Do not assume all ad hominem arguments are fallacious; the pragma-dialectical view is a traditional, stricter position, and other treatments allow legitimate uses.
Distinguish attacking the person's credibility from engaging with the argument itself, since one may do both in the same case.
rq: Why do pragma-dialecticians regard every ad hominem as fallacious, and how does this differ from other modern treatments?
They consider its use always fallacious, so no case-by-case assessment is needed; other modern treatments allow it as legitimate if the right conditions are met.
Why can an attack on a person sometimes be appropriate even though it targets credibility?
A person may both attempt to discredit someone and deal with their argument, and attempts to discredit may themselves be appropriate in some cases.

units.name: 4 Critical questions and burden of proof
units.ov: This material covers ad hominem arguments, which shift attention from a position to the character or circumstances of the person advancing it. It sets out critical questions for judging them: is the shift negative, is the character claim relevant, is it true, and who carries the burden of proof. The ideas connect because a personal attack is fallacious only when it replaces engagement with the argument or fails the tests of relevance and evidence, and even a successful attack supports only limited conclusions.
must: Definition: an ad hominem shifts attention negatively from the position or claim to the character or circumstances of the person advancing it, so the person is addressed instead of the argument.
Critical question 1: does the argument draw negative attention to the person delivering the claim rather than to the position itself? The key feature is the negative direction of the appeal.
Ad hominem versus ethotic: ethotic arguments appeal positively to character, authority or expertise, while ad hominem appeals are negative. Do not confuse the two.
An ad hominem need not be a combative 'attack'. Drawing negative attention to character features is enough.
The core problem is irrelevance. A person's flaws do not remove their right to have their argument considered, and ignoring their view in dialogue means ignoring the issue.
Relevance test: the attack is legitimate only if the character claim bears directly on the position, so that a reasonable person would question it. Character features may be wholly irrelevant.
Relevance and truth are separate questions. A relevant claim may be false, and an irrelevant one may be true, and truth is often hard to establish.
Burden of proof: whoever makes the allegations must support them with real evidence. Without it the argument is weak and likely fallacious.

Limited conclusions: even a relevant, true attack only weakens our reasons for believing the position, or shows the person's advocacy is not enough to warrant belief. It does not show the position is false.

Not every personal mention or attack is fallacious. The fallacy arises only when the person replaces engagement with the position. Silencing the other party is often aimed at an on-looking audience, to strengthen the attacker's own standing.
conn: Ethotic versus ad hominem: both appeal to character, but one is positive and the other negative. A question may ask you to classify an appeal and then test its relevance.

Relevance versus truth versus burden of proof: assess whether the character claim is relevant, then whether it is true, then whether the attacker has supplied evidence. Each step can fail independently.
Credibility versus falsity: a successful ad hominem lowers the weight of the person's advocacy but does not refute the conclusion. Rejecting the position outright is an overreach.
Audience and dialogue: in dialogue, ad hominem can ignore the issue and aim at an on-looking audience. This links the fallacy to the aim of silencing and to the question of who is persuaded.
exq: A speaker dismisses a researcher's findings on sustainable agriculture by pointing out that the researcher once worked for an agribusiness firm. Apply the critical questions to decide whether this is a fallacious ad hominem. Consider relevance, truth and burden of proof.
Distinguish an ad hominem argument from an ethotic argument, using one example of each from a sustainable development debate. Why does the direction of the appeal matter?
'Attacking someone's character can never justify doubting their position.' Discuss, explaining what a relevant and well-evidenced personal attack can and cannot establish.

Explain why relevance and truth are separate questions when evaluating an ad hominem, and who bears the burden of proof for the allegation. Illustrate with a case where the claim is relevant but unsupported.
Why might an arguer use an ad hominem aimed at an on-looking audience rather than at the opponent? Evaluate how this affects whether the dialogue addresses the issue.

notes.t: Treatments of Ad Hominem: concerns and Critical Questions
pts: Ad hominem concerns range from complete irrelevance, to doubts about the premises, to doubts about the conclusion.
Attacking a person's character can at most show that their advocacy is not enough to warrant believing the position, not that it is false.
Character features drawn attention to may be irrelevant to the position being advocated.
In dialogue, attacking the person while not addressing their view means ignoring the issue.
Theorists disagree about which concerns are appropriate and how important each is.
defs: Ad hominem
A fallacy in which an arguer attacks the person (character or circumstances) making a claim rather than addressing the argument or position itself.
tips: Do not treat every personal attack as fallacious; check whether the ad hominem material is relevant and factually correct.
Even a relevant personal attack may only justify limited conclusions about credibility, not overall rejection of the position.
rq: Why does attacking someone's character not by itself show their position is false?
Because character flaws only bear on how much credibility the person's advocacy deserves; the position's truth depends on its own premises and support.
What makes ad hominem material legitimately relevant to appraising a claim?
When the material is factually correct and bears on the position or claim, and the conclusion drawn from it is appropriate.

notes.t: Ad hominem arguments: identifying the shift from position to person
pts: The first critical question asks whether an argument draws negative attention to the person delivering the argument or claim, rather than to the position itself.
Ethotic appeals to character or authority are positive, whereas ad hominem appeals are negative; the key issue is the negative direction of the appeal.
An ad hominem need not be an 'attack' in the traditional, combative sense; drawing negative attention to character features is enough.
The core problem is a shift from position to person, which is a serious problem of irrelevance, since a person's flaws do not remove their right to have their argument considered.
Silencing the other party is usually aimed at an on-looking audience, intended to strengthen one's own standing in the eyes of that audience.
defs: Ad hominem argument

An argument in which attention is shifted negatively from the position or claim being defended to the character or circumstances of the person advancing it, so that the person rather than the argument is addressed.
Ethotic argument
An argument that appeals to the character, authority or expertise of others; its appeal is positive, in contrast to the negative direction of an ad hominem.
tips: Do not confuse ad hominem (negative appeal to character) with ethotic appeals to authority or expertise (positive appeal).
Not every mention of a person is fallacious; the fallacy arises only when the person replaces engagement with the position.
rq: Why does drawing attention to someone's character count as a fallacy even when it involves no overt 'attack'?
Because the shift from the position to the person makes the argument irrelevant to the claim at issue, regardless of whether the tone is hostile.
What distinguishes an ad hominem from a legitimate ethotic appeal to authority?

The direction of the appeal: ethotic appeals are positive and rely on expertise or good character, while ad hominem appeals are negative and target character or circumstances to discredit the argument.

notes.t: Relevance and burden of proof in ad hominem arguments
pts: Ad hominem material is only legitimate to dismiss a position if the character claim bears directly on that position, so a reasonable person would question it.
Whether the alleged character claim is true is a separate question from its relevance, and is often hard to determine.
The person making the allegations bears the burden of proof and must support them with real evidence; otherwise the argument is weak and likely fallacious.
An ad hominem argument does not by itself show a position to be wrong; it only weakens our reasons for holding that position.
Proficiency in judging relevance comes from practice working with the ideas and discussing cases with others.
defs: Ad hominem argument
An argument that dismisses or weakens a position by attacking the character or circumstances of the person advancing it; legitimate only when the attack is relevant to the position.
tips: Do not assume an ad hominem attack is fallacious merely because it targets a person; judge whether the character claim is directly relevant to the position.
Remember that relevance and truth are distinct: a relevant claim may still be factually incorrect, and the arguer must still back it with evidence.
rq: Why can a true character flaw still fail to justify rejecting someone's position?
Because the flaw must bear directly on the position; if it is unconnected to the claim, it is irrelevant even if true.
What if the person alleging a character flaw cannot produce evidence for it?
The argument is minimally weak and likely fallacious, since the burden of proof has not been met.

units.name: 5 Types: abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque, guilt by association
units.ov: This material covers the ad hominem family of arguments: abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque and guilt by association. Each attacks the person rather than the position, but each is fallacious only when the personal fact is irrelevant to the claim, or when it diverts attention from the issue. The Critical Questions give a shared framework for deciding relevance case by case, and ethotic reasoning explains when an arguer's credibility legitimately matters.
must: Core definition: an ad hominem attacks a person's character, circumstances or reputation instead of the position they advance; it is fallacious only when it replaces a reasoned response with irrelevant reasons.
Abusive ad hominem: a direct attack on character used in place of answering the argument; it only pretends to be an argument.
Insults and name-calling are counterproductive but not in themselves fallacious; check that real premises and a conclusion exist before labelling a fallacy.

Circumstantial ad hominem (Locke): presses a person with their own circumstances, vested interest or commitments. It is not automatically refuting, so use the Critical Questions to weigh how much the circumstance bears on the reasoning.

Tu quoque ('you too'): alleges inconsistency between the arguer's actions or past statements and their present claim. The inconsistency is pragmatic, not logical, so it does not show the claim is false (the overweight physician's diet advice still stands or falls on its merits).

Evaluating a tu quoque: a change of mind is not inconsistency, so check that the position really changed and that there is no relevant difference between the earlier and present cases. It can also appear as a defence, as in Case 5E, where both sides use it.

Guilt by association: dismisses a person because of a real or alleged link to another person, organisation or way of thinking, assuming guilt transfers. It is fallacious when no genuine transfer is shown, and a real association is necessary but not sufficient.

Three Critical Questions for guilt by association: (1) does the association actually exist? (2) is attention being diverted from the position under discussion? (3) is the association relevant to that position? The Lomborg case fails at the first step because no guilt attached to the cited books.

Ethotic reasoning: the arguer's credibility is a legitimate factor in weighing their conclusion, so consistency of words and deeds can matter. The burden of proof lies with whoever claims past conduct undermines the current claim, and a past record must be a matter of record.

Fallaciousness depends on context: assess both the internal relationships among an argument's components and the external relationships between argument, context and audience. Each case is decided on its merits.
conn: Abusive vs circumstantial vs tu quoque: all target the person, but they differ in what is targeted (character, circumstances or interests, inconsistency). Exam cases often require classifying the type, then judging relevance.

Ethotic reasoning links to the legitimacy of ad hominem: when credibility is genuinely relevant, as with a vested interest or demonstrable inconsistency, the attack may be reasonable rather than fallacious. This is why the Critical Questions and the burden of proof matter.
Tu quoque and guilt by association share the irrelevance test: the critic's inconsistency or the association must be shown to bear on the claim, otherwise attention is diverted from the issue.
Case studies (5E, Lomborg, the press charge) show the same argument can be used by both sides, or can be ad hominem without aiming to dismiss the position, which ties together context and audience.
exq: Define abusive ad hominem and explain why name-calling alone is not necessarily fallacious. What must be present before a case can be labelled a fallacy?

A physician who is overweight advises a patient to diet, and the patient replies 'you don't practise what you preach'. Identify the fallacy, explain the pragmatic vs logical inconsistency, and say when the objection might be legitimate.
Using the three Critical Questions, evaluate a guilt by association argument such as the Lomborg publisher case. At which step does it fail, and why does a real association not suffice?
Distinguish circumstantial ad hominem from abusive ad hominem with examples. How should an evaluator decide how much weight a vested interest should carry?

In Case 5E both sides use a tu quoque. Explain how a tu quoque can be used as a defence, and what you would check (change of position, relevant differences) before accepting the alleged inconsistency.

notes.t: Abusive Ad Hominem fallacy
pts: The abusive ad hominem is a direct attack on an individual's character rather than on a circumstance related to them.
Highly charged, abusive attacks are generally dismissed as an appropriate argumentative strategy because they rarely impress anyone seeking good reasons.
Calling someone names is counterproductive to good communication but is not in itself fallacious; fallacy requires an actual argument.
Before labelling a case abusive ad hominem, check that the person has provided both premises and a conclusion; otherwise no argument can be fairly constructed to attack.
defs: Abusive ad hominem
A fallacy in which a direct attack on an individual's character is used in place of a reasoned response to that person's argument.
tips: Do not treat every insult as a fallacy; verify that a genuine argument with premises and a conclusion is actually present.
Remember that name-calling is counterproductive but not itself fallacious.
rq: Why is name-calling alone not enough to establish an abusive ad hominem fallacy?
Because the fallacy requires an actual argument (premises and a conclusion) that is being avoided by the personal attack; insults without an argument are merely counterproductive, not fallacious.
Why do abusive ad hominem arguments tend to fail the second critical question?
Because the attack targets the person rather than engaging with their argument, so the argument itself is avoided altogether.

notes.t: Abusive Ad Hominem and the Critical Questions
pts: An abusive ad hominem attacks a person's character or circumstances instead of addressing the charge they make; it only pretends to be an argument.
Such an argument draws a conclusion about the person's position but offers reasons that are irrelevant to that conclusion, so it is fallacious.
Each case must be decided on its own merits; past inaccurate claims count only if they are a matter of record.
The burden of proof lies with the arguer to supply support for any claim that the person's past conduct undermines their current claim.
Locke's circumstantial ad hominem differs from the abusive type: it presses a person with consequences of their own commitments.
defs: Abusive ad hominem
A fallacy in which someone's personal characteristics or circumstances (e.g., being a single mother or a known drunk) are used to dismiss their claim, rather than addressing the claim's merits.
Circumstantial ad hominem
A type of ad hominem (identified by John Locke) in which a person is pressed with the consequences of their own circumstances or commitments rather than their character.
tips: Do not call every personal attack fallacious; check whether the personal fact is genuinely relevant to the claim's credibility.
Remember the burden of proof lies with the arguer who cites a person's past record.
rq: Why is the Pelletier argument fallacious even though it uses true facts about Ms. Bédard?
Because the facts (being a single mother, being pitiful) are irrelevant to whether her claims about overbilling are true; the conclusion does not follow from the reasons.
What would make a past-claims-based dismissal legitimate rather than fallacious?
If the past inaccurate claims are a documented matter of record and are relevant to the reliability of the current claim, and the arguer supplies that support.

notes.t: Circumstantial ad hominem and tu quoque arguments
pts: A circumstantial ad hominem questions an arguer's position by pointing to his particular circumstances or vested interest in the issue, not his character.
Circumstantial reasons do not automatically refute an argument; the evaluator must judge how much the circumstantial factor should bear on the reasoning, using the Critical Questions.
Tu quoque means 'you too': the arguer is accused of inconsistency between what he does or said before and what he now proposes or charges.
The inconsistency in a tu quoque is pragmatic rather than logical, so it does not show the arguer's claim is false.
A physician's own weight has no strict bearing on whether your diet advice is sound.
defs: Tu quoque
A fallacious (or pragmatic) response claiming an arguer is inconsistent between his actions/past statements and his present claim, thereby dismissing the argument.
Circumstantial ad hominem
Questioning an individual's argument by pointing to his circumstances or vested interest in the outcome rather than to the argument itself.
tips: Do not treat a circumstantial objection as automatically decisive; weigh its relevance with the Critical Questions.
Distinguish tu quoque (inconsistency between conduct/statements and present claim) from attacks on character alone.
rq: Why does the city planner living on route B not automatically make her route A argument wrong?
Her circumstances only raise a question about bias; the argument must still be evaluated on its merits using the Critical Questions to decide how much weight the circumstance deserves.
Why is a tu quoque charge not a logical refutation?
It identifies pragmatic inconsistency between what someone does or said and what he now proposes, which does not logically establish that his current claim is false.

notes.t: Consistency of character and tu quoque in ethotic arguments
pts: In ethotic reasoning, the arguer's credibility is key to weighing their conclusion, so consistency of actions and words can matter greatly.
People should change their minds, so a change in position is not automatically a violation of consistency; we must check whether the position was really changed.
An alleged inconsistency must be credible: there must be no relevant difference between the earlier case and the present.
In Case 5E both sides use a tu quoque: one attacks the majority member, the other defends him by pointing to a minority member's past expenses.
defs: Tu quoque
A form of ad hominem in which an arguer's claim is dismissed because the person advancing it is accused of inconsistency or of doing the same thing themselves.
Ethotic reasoning
Reasoning in which the credibility of the arguer is a key factor in deciding what weight to give their conclusion.
tips: Do not assume inconsistency just because a person's current view differs from a past one; check for genuine change of position and for relevant differences between cases.
Recognise that a tu quoque can appear on either side of a dispute, including as a defence.
rq: Why does the text say a change of mind is not automatically a violation of consistency?
Because people should change their minds in light of arguments; one must check whether the position has genuinely changed and whether the alleged inconsistency is credible.
Why might the defence in Case 5E still be a fallacy even if the facts about the minority member are true?
Because pointing out the opponent's similar conduct does not address whether the majority member's expenses were justified; it is a tu quoque.

notes.t: Ad Hominem Arguments: Tu Quoque and Guilt by Association
pts: Tu quoque ('you too') defence deflects criticism by pointing to the critics' own past behaviour, which impedes resolution of the actual issue.
Guilt by Association attacks a person based on a real or alleged association with another person, organization, or way of thinking, assuming guilt transfers across that link.
Guilt by Association is only fallacious if no genuine transfer of 'guilt' is shown; the association alone does not establish the claim.
In the Lomborg case, the charge fails at the first step because no guilt attached to the cited books, so nothing could transfer to the publisher.
defs: Guilt by Association

A fallacy in which a person's argument is dismissed because of a real or alleged association with another person, organization or way of thinking, assuming that any 'guilt' of that associate transfers to the person.
Tu quoque (You too)
A response to criticism that points to the critic's own similar behaviour rather than addressing whether the criticised behaviour is acceptable.
tips: Do not confuse a real association with a relevant transfer of guilt: showing an association is necessary but not sufficient to commit or refute the fallacy.
Tu quoque is a fallacy of irrelevance; it does not refute the criticism even if the critic is inconsistent.
rq: Why does the 'You too' reply fail to resolve the original issue?
Because pointing to the critics' own past behaviour does not show whether the behaviour under dispute is justified; it only shifts blame and leaves the issue unaddressed.
What must be shown for Guilt by Association to be a legitimate argument rather than a fallacy?
That the associated party actually carries some 'guilt' (defect) and that a genuine connection exists that justifies transferring it to the person being attacked.

notes.t: Evaluating Guilt by Association and ad hominem arguments
pts: Guilt by Association arguments can be assessed for fallaciousness using the basic Critical Questions: first check the alleged association actually exists.
The second Critical Question asks whether attention is being diverted away from the position under discussion.
The third Critical Question tests whether the association is relevant to the position the person is advancing.
Ad hominem arguments show that fallaciousness must be appraised by exploring the context of argumentation.
Two basic problems with fallacious arguments: internal relationships among components, and external relationships between argument, context and audience.
defs: Ad hominem argument
An argument that attacks the reputation, character or circumstances of a person rather than the position that person advances.
tips: Do not dismiss an argument merely because it attacks a person; check whether the association is real, relevant, and whether attention is diverted from the position.
Remember that the sense of dismissing a position may be absent even when an argument is ad hominem, as with the charge against the press.
rq: Why must the first Critical Question be checked before judging a Guilt by Association argument fallacious?
Because if the alleged association with the guilty party did not actually exist, the charge rests on a false premise and the argument fails regardless of its form.
How does the internal problem differ from the external problem in evaluating an ad hominem argument?
The internal problem asks whether the conclusion follows from the ad hominem material; the external problem asks how the argument relates to its context and audience, e.g. silencing a party.

units.name: 6 When ad hominem is not fallacious
units.ov: This material covers ad hominem arguments, which target the person making a claim rather than the claim, and explains why they are not always fallacious. The key skill is to separate attacks that replace evaluation of the reasons (fallacious) from remarks that bear legitimately on credibility, conflict of interest, qualifications or fitness for a role (potentially non-fallacious). The ideas connect through one test: is the personal point offered as a reason to reject the claim, or only as a reason to weigh the source's testimony differently?
must: Definition: an ad hominem targets the person making a claim rather than the claim itself, and it is fallacious when the attack is offered as a reason to reject the claim.
Core test: does the personal attack replace evaluation of the reasons, or does it only bear on the source's reliability?
Not every personal remark is an ad hominem, and not every ad hominem is fallacious, so avoid labelling all of them as fallacies.
Attacking a writer's motive or stake does not by itself refute the argument, which must still be assessed on its merits.
A stake or conflict of interest can still be relevant to credibility and to how much weight the testimony deserves, as long as it is not treated as proof the claim is false.
Questioning a source's credibility, qualifications or claimed authority can legitimately affect the weight their argument gets.
Abuse or ridicule of an author or book is not a reasoned rebuttal of its content, so it is fallacious when used as a rebuttal.
Character remarks can be relevant when they bear on fitness for a position of responsibility, as in the torture debate.
Distinguish insult or abuse from showing a relevant conflict of interest or lack of qualifications.
conn: Credibility versus truth: a source's stake can lower the weight given to their testimony, but it cannot make their argument invalid. Questions often ask you to separate these.
Relevance of the attack to the issue: personal criticism is legitimate when it bears on the role in question (fitness for office) and fallacious when it is unrelated to the claim.
Abuse versus conflict of interest: the same remark can be fallacious in one context and legitimate in another, so you must analyse the function of the remark in the argument.
Evaluating arguments on their merits links to assessing sources in sustainable development debates, where funders, stakeholders and expertise are often contested.
exq: Define an ad hominem argument and explain, with an example, why it is not always fallacious.

A report on a policy is dismissed because its author is funded by an industry group. Is this fallacious? Distinguish between rejecting the argument and discounting its credibility, and say what further evidence you would need.
Compare ridicule of a book's author with pointing out an author's lack of relevant qualifications. Which is fallacious, and why?
Discuss whether character remarks about a speaker are relevant in the torture debate, with reference to fitness for a position of responsibility.
Give a step-by-step test you would apply to decide whether a personal attack in a given text is a fallacious ad hominem, and apply it to a short example you devise.

notes.t: Ad hominem arguments and when they are not fallacious
pts: Not every case presenting personal attack is a clear ad hominem, and those that are may not be fallacious.
Attacking a writer's motive or stake in the issue does not by itself refute the argument; the argument must be assessed on its merits, though a stake may be relevant to credibility.
Questioning a source's credibility or the representation of their authority can legitimately bear on how much weight their argument deserves.
Ridicule or abuse of a book or author is not a reasoned rebuttal of its content.
Some personal-character remarks are relevant when they bear on a speaker's fitness for a position of responsibility, as in the torture debate.
defs: Ad hominem argument
An argument that targets the person making a claim rather than the claim itself; it is fallacious when the personal attack is offered as a reason to reject the claim.
tips: Do not label every personal remark as fallacious; check whether the attack actually replaces evaluation of the reasons or only bears on the source's reliability.
Distinguish insulting a person or book (abuse) from showing a relevant conflict of interest or lack of qualifications.
rq: Why might attacking a letter writer's financial interest still be a non-fallacious consideration?
Because a stake in the outcome can be relevant evidence of bias, affecting how much credibility the argument deserves, even though it doesn't refute the argument by itself.
What distinguishes a fallacious ad hominem from a legitimate credibility challenge?
Whether the personal attack is offered as a substitute for evaluating the argument's reasons (fallacious) or as relevant information about the source's reliability or qualifications (legitimate).

units.name: 7 Worked examples: letters, Peirce, debate, advertising
units.ov: These worked examples train you to spot and classify ad hominem arguments in letters, a Peirce passage on Hume's argument against miracles, the Bush-Kerry debates, and a ConsumerFreedom.com advertisement against PETA. The central skill is separating the person (character, motives, circumstances, consistency) from the claim and its evidence. You must also recognise when a personal remark is legitimately relevant to reliability and so is not fallacious.
must: Definition: an ad hominem attacks the person's character, motives or circumstances instead of the merits of the claim or argument.
The test: identify what is attacked (the person) versus what should be assessed (the argument and its evidence); the fallacy occurs when the person's attributes replace evidence.
Not every personal remark is ad hominem: remarks on expertise, bias or credibility can be relevant when they bear on the reliability of the claim.
Attributing motives (jealousy, mud-slinging in the Elinor Smith/Amelia Earhart letter) does not show the criticism of Earhart's flying skills is false.

Chiropractic example: dismissing the practitioner for lacking veterinary training targets qualifications, not the evidence for the 'subluxated vertebra'. The vet's own claim that the diagnosis is unfounded is a substantive evidential claim, not a fallacy.
Peirce on Hume: saying the miracles argument was inserted to gain popularity amid English disbelief attacks Hume's motive, not the argument itself (circumstantial type).

Debate examples: Bush calling Kerry a flip-flopper, or saying doubters lack the judgment to be president, targets the person; Kerry citing the president's past false claims on North Korea talks is also credibility-based rather than substantive.
Inconsistency charges are legitimate only if shown with specific contradictory statements, not merely asserted; Kerry distinguishes a consistent threat assessment from choice of method.

Advertising: the ConsumerFreedom.com ad discredits PETA by guilt by association with criminals and by quoting Ingrid Newkirk's extreme statement, rather than engaging PETA's position on animal research.
Classify: abusive (direct personal attack) versus circumstantial (motives or interests), and give reasons for the classification.
conn: Relevance versus fallacy: credibility attacks (expertise, bias, inconsistency) are ad hominem only when they substitute for engaging with the evidence, which links the definition to the TIPs on legitimate criticism.
Motive attacks (Peirce on Hume, jealousy in the Earhart letter) are circumstantial ad hominem, while character insults and the 'lacks judgment' remark are abusive; exam answers should classify each.

Debate and advertising use the same move: discrediting a source (Kerry/Bush, PETA/Newkirk) through association or a representative quote to dismiss the whole position, so link to guilt by association and unfair generalisation.
Distinguish the vet's evidence-based rebuttal from the dismissal of the chiropractor's qualifications: same topic, one legitimate and one fallacious.
exq: Define ad hominem and explain, using the Elinor Smith/Earhart letter, why attributing jealousy to a critic does not refute her claim.
Is Peirce's comment that Hume inserted his argument against miracles to gain popularity an ad hominem? Distinguish it from a legitimate challenge to Hume's reasoning.
In the Bush-Kerry excerpts, identify two ad hominem moves and one legitimate response, justifying each, and say how Kerry's consistency claim could be tested.
Analyse the ConsumerFreedom.com advertisement against PETA: which fallacious moves are present, and how could the ad engage PETA's actual position?
When is a remark about someone's qualifications or credibility not an ad hominem? Illustrate with the chiropractor/veterinarian example.

notes.t: Ad hominem arguments in letters and published commentary
pts: An ad hominem attack targets the person making a claim rather than the claim itself, as in the letter dismissing Elinor Smith's criticism as jealousy.
Attributing a critic's motives (jealousy, mud-slinging) does not show that the criticism of Amelia Earhart's flying skills is false.
Dismissing chiropractic because the practitioner lacks veterinary training is an ad hominem targeting qualifications rather than the evidence for the 'subluxated vertebra'.
The veterinarian's letter argues that the chiropractor's single diagnosis is unfounded, but this is a substantive claim about evidence, not merely an attack on the person.
The jpost.com letter raises an irrelevant point about the nationality of a court president, which bears no logical connection to any conclusion about human rights or justice.
defs: Ad hominem argument
A fallacious argument that attacks or appeals to the character, motives, or circumstances of a person rather than the merits of the claim or argument that person is making.
tips: Do not label every personal remark as ad hominem; a remark about a person's qualifications can be relevant if it bears on the reliability of their claim.
Students often confuse ad hominem with merely criticising someone; the fallacy occurs only when the person's attributes are used in place of evidence against the argument.
rq: Why is the claim that Smith is motivated by jealousy not sufficient to refute her criticism of Earhart?
Motives do not determine truth; the criticism must be evaluated on its evidence, even if the critic is biased.
How does the veterinarian's letter distinguish between a legitimate and an illegitimate criticism of chiropractic?
It criticises the chiropractor's lack of scientific training (ad hominem-like), but also argues the core notion of subluxation is unproven (a substantive evidential point).

notes.t: Ad hominem arguments: examples and Peirce on Hume's argument against miracles
pts: Peirce argues Hume's argument against miracles is loosely connected to the rest of his book and was likely inserted to gain popularity.
Peirce ties the popularity of Hume's anti-miracle view to the prevailing climate of disbelief in England at the time, which Hume may have exploited.
The passage attacks the motive of the author rather than engaging the merits of the argument against miracles, which is the ad hominem move.

The first example challenges the judge's justice by contrasting a country's claimed respect for minorities with the judge's conduct in China, appealing to the judge's record instead of the claim itself.
The Bush example shows a response that targets the opponent's character or statement rather than the substance of the claim about Iraq and bin Laden.
defs: Ad hominem argument
A fallacious move that attacks the person making a claim (their character, motives, or circumstances) instead of addressing the claim or its reasons.
tips: Do not label every criticism of a person as ad hominem; attacks on credibility can be relevant when the person's reliability genuinely bears on the claim.
Distinguish the fallacious ad hominem from legitimate arguments about a speaker's expertise or bias, which bear on evidence.
rq: Why does Peirce's motive-based criticism of Hume not by itself show that Hume's argument against miracles is false?

Because the psychological or popularity motive of an author says nothing about whether the premises and inferences of the argument are sound; evaluating the argument requires assessing its logic and evidence.
How does the judge example differ from simply saying the country's claim is false?
It shifts attention to the judge's past conduct as a reason to doubt the credibility of the claim, which is an attack on the source rather than a direct rebuttal of the claim.

notes.t: Ad hominem and accusations of misleading/inconsistent positions in political debate
pts: Each speaker responds to an accusation of misleading by reasserting their own consistency rather than addressing the substance of the claim.
Bush attacks his opponent's character by claiming he changes positions, which shifts focus from the policy question to the person.
Kerry argues that his position on Saddam Hussein was consistent, distinguishing a consistent threat assessment from the choice of method.
Bush claims the intelligence was the same for both candidates, using shared evidence to defend his decision.
Bush dismisses critics by suggesting doubters lacked judgment to be president, a personal attack rather than a rebuttal of their reasoning.
defs: Ad hominem argument
A fallacious argument that attacks the character, motives, or consistency of a person rather than the merits of the claim they are making.
tips: Do not confuse an ad hominem attack with a legitimate point about contradictory evidence; a genuine inconsistency must be shown with specific statements, not merely asserted.
Identify the fallacy by pointing to what is attacked (the person) versus what should be assessed (the argument).
rq: Why does accusing an opponent of inconsistency fail to refute their policy argument?
Because inconsistency concerns the speaker's character or record, not whether the policy claim itself is true or well-supported; it is an ad hominem move.
How could Kerry have shown that Bush's accusation of inconsistency was irrelevant to the question of Iraq policy?
By separating the question of whether the threat was real from the question of how to respond, and arguing the merits of each on evidence.

notes.t: Ad Hominem Arguments – examples from debate and advertising
pts: The Bush and Kerry excerpt is a debate on whether bilateral talks with North Korea would undermine China's involvement in the six-party talks.
Kerry rebuts Bush's position by attacking the president's credibility (past false claims), rather than only the substance of the bilateral-talks proposal.
The ConsumerFreedom.com advertisement discredits PETA by linking it to criminals who destroyed medical research, instead of directly engaging PETA's position on animal research.
Quoting Ingrid Newkirk's extreme statement is used to portray the whole organization as hostile to medical progress.
defs: Ad hominem argument
A fallacious form of reasoning that attacks the character, motives, or circumstances of a person making a claim, rather than addressing the merits of the claim itself.
tips: Do not label every criticism of a person as ad hominem; it is fallacious only when the attack replaces engagement with the argument's actual reasons.
Distinguish ad hominem circumstantial (motives tied to interest) from abusive (personal attack) when classifying examples.
rq: Why is Kerry's attack on Bush's record not, by itself, a refutation of Bush's claim that bilateral talks will fail?
Because discrediting the speaker's past statements does not show that the present claim is false; the argument must address whether bilateral talks would in fact cause China to withdraw.
How does the advertisement's use of a single quote from one PETA leader differ from a fair representation of PETA's position?
It generalizes an extreme individual statement to the whole organization and shifts focus to the character of the group rather than the substance of its views on research.

units.name: 8 Further reading
units.ov: The supplied notes contain only a single heading, 'Further Reading on ad hominem arguments', from the module's '8 Further reading' section, with no substantive content extracted. This report therefore cannot summarise the module's sustainable development material. It gives a cautious revision framework on ad hominem arguments, which is the only topic named, and flags what to check in the original reading.
must: The source notes are almost empty (one heading on p23), so check the actual reading list and lecture slides before relying on this report.
Definition: an ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim (character, motives, circumstances) rather than the claim's evidence or reasoning.
It is an informal fallacy: a claim's truth or an argument's validity does not depend on who asserts it.
Main forms: abusive (direct personal attack), circumstantial (pointing to the speaker's situation or interests), and tu quoque ('you do it too').
Related to the genetic fallacy: dismissing a claim because of its origin, not its merit.
Not every reference to a person is fallacious: questioning credibility, conflicts of interest or expertise can be legitimate when the claim rests on testimony or authority.
Sustainability relevance: ad hominem attacks are common in debates on climate science, development aid and policy, where critics target scientists, activists or institutions rather than evidence.
Exam skill: identify the fallacy, name its type, explain why it fails, and propose how to engage the evidence instead.
Good practice: separate evaluating the source (e.g. bias, funding) from evaluating the argument, and use both explicitly in critical analysis.
Cite specific authors and examples from the module's further reading; the notes give none, so add them from the source.
conn: Ad hominem and critical evaluation of sources: judging credibility and bias is legitimate, but it should not replace assessing the argument itself.
Ad hominem and sustainability debates: polarised discussions on climate action or the Global North/South often use personal attacks, so questions may ask you to analyse rhetoric in a case study.
Ad hominem alongside other fallacies (straw man, appeal to authority, genetic fallacy): questions often ask you to tell them apart.
exq: Define an ad hominem argument and distinguish abusive, circumstantial and tu quoque forms, giving a sustainable development example of each.
When, if ever, is it reasonable to question a speaker's motives or credibility in a debate on climate policy? Justify your answer.
Read this passage from a climate debate and identify any ad hominem reasoning. Explain why it fails and how you would rebut it using evidence.
Discuss how ad hominem attacks can undermine public discussion of sustainable development goals, and suggest ways to counter them.

units.name: 1 Correlation and causal reasoning
units.ov: This material introduces causal reasoning in argumentation, focusing on when it is legitimate to move from an observed correlation to a causal claim. It frames the Argument from Correlation to Cause as a scheme that is reasonable only when specific conditions are met, and fallacious otherwise. It previews three common errors: inferring cause from correlation or temporal sequence, confusing causal elements, and predicting negative outcomes for proposals. The notes are brief, so the ideas must be supplemented with examples from lectures.
must: Correlation alone does not establish causation: an observed association is not proof that one thing causes the other.
Correlation-based generalizations carry an implicit causal claim, so look for causal conclusions hidden in statements that appear only to report an association.
Definition: the Argument from Correlation to Cause is an argumentation scheme that infers a causal relation from an observed correlation.
The scheme is reasonable only when the correct conditions are met; when they are not, the reasoning is fallacious. Be able to say which is which and why.
Temporal sequence (A before B) is not enough to show A causes B, which is the post hoc type of error.
Three problematic types of causal reasoning: (1) concluding causation from correlation or temporal sequence, (2) confusing causal elements, (3) predicting negative causal outcomes for proposals.
Practical test: before accepting a causal conclusion, check whether the conditions for the scheme hold, and consider alternatives such as reverse causation, a common cause, or coincidence.
Distinguish evaluating an argument as reasonable (scheme with conditions satisfied) from fallacious (scheme misused), rather than simply labelling it right or wrong.
conn: Correlation versus causation links to sustainable development evidence: for example, a link between income growth and emissions or health outcomes may be cited as causal when confounders such as industrialisation or policy are ignored.
Implicit causal claims connect to argumentation schemes: identifying the hidden claim lets you apply the scheme's conditions and critical questions.
Temporal sequence errors connect to predicting outcomes of proposals, since both rely on assuming causal links that may not hold.
exq: Explain why a correlation between two variables (e.g. national GDP and CO2 emissions) does not by itself establish causation, and state what conditions would make an argument from correlation to cause reasonable.
Define the Argument from Correlation to Cause and, using a sustainability example, show how it can become fallacious.
Identify the implicit causal claim in a news headline reporting an association (e.g. 'Cities with more green space have healthier residents') and evaluate whether it is justified.
Outline the three problematic types of causal reasoning introduced in this topic and give one example of each.
A policy report notes that deforestation rose after a new road was built and concludes the road caused it. Assess this reasoning, discussing temporal sequence and alternative explanations.

notes.t: Correlations and Causal Reasoning
pts: Implicit in a correlation-based generalization is a causal claim; the Argument from Correlation to Cause is reasonable only when correct conditions are met.
When the conditions for the Argument from Correlation to Cause are not met, fallacious reasoning occurs.

The chapter focuses on three problematic types of causal reasoning: concluding causation from correlation or temporal sequence, confusing causal elements, and predicting negative causal outcomes for proposals.
A correlation between two things does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
defs: Argument from Correlation to Cause
An argumentation scheme that infers a causal relation from an observed correlation; reasonable only when the correct conditions are satisfied, otherwise fallacious.
tips: Do not treat a correlation or mere temporal sequence as proof of causation; check whether the correct conditions hold.
Watch for implicit causal claims hidden in conclusions that appear to report only an association.
rq: Why does the busy social life example involve an implicit causal claim rather than only a correlation?
Because concluding that avoiding colds is linked to a busy social life implicitly asserts that the social life caused or was a causal factor in avoiding colds, not merely that they co-occur.
What might go wrong if you infer cause simply from a temporal sequence?
The earlier event may not be a cause at all; the sequence could be coincidental or caused by a third factor, so the inference is fallacious.

units.name: 2 The post hoc fallacy
units.ov: This material covers the post hoc fallacy, where a causal claim is inferred from temporal sequence alone (post hoc ergo propter hoc) or from a mere correlation. It traces the idea to Aristotle and shows through the Stone/Houellebecq case that context, background knowledge and plausible mechanisms decide whether such inference is fallacious. The two varieties are linked by one principle: sequence or co-occurrence is necessary but not sufficient evidence for cause, and the burden of proof lies with the person claiming causation.
must: Definition: post hoc ergo propter hoc infers that A caused B because B followed A in time ('after this, therefore because of this').
The second variety infers causation from correlation (regular co-occurrence); both varieties are treated together as post hoc reasoning.
Temporal order and correlation are necessary but never sufficient for causation; always check coincidence, common (third) cause and reverse causation.
Post hoc reasoning is not always fallacious: with plausible context, background knowledge and a warranted connection, correlation or sequence can support a causal hypothesis.
Charity principle: only charge the fallacy if no plausible contextual considerations support the causal link; the onus is on the person inferring cause.

Case 9A: inferring that dining with Houellebecq is perilous because Stone was arrested afterwards treats timing alone as evidence. It becomes plausible only with extra context (e.g. known police surveillance of the novelist).

Credible causal claims need a mechanism suggested by background experience and confirmed by testing (e.g. E. coli and sickness), unlike a bare correlation between trends (church attendance and social mores).

Aristotle (Rhetoric) criticised treating non-causes as causes because they came before or alongside an event, and noted politicians like this (Demades blaming Demosthenes for the war). His 'cause' is logical, not modern scientific.

Pinto: bare temporal-sequence reasoning may fail minimal rationality, so it may not count as reasoning; what matters is the total context of reasoning. Tversky and Kahneman's heuristics explain why people are fooled.

Correlations are still practically useful (e.g. judging whether an area can support a sports franchise) without showing causation; the Stone footnote also shows a separate flaw, hasty generalisation from one case.
conn: Post hoc fallacy and confounding/common cause: correlations in sustainability data (e.g. income and emissions, or aid and development) may arise from a third factor or reverse causation, so causal policy claims need mechanisms and testing.
Pinto's total context versus charitable evaluation: whether an argument is fallacious depends on background knowledge, so the same inference can be weak in one context and reasonable in another.

Heuristics (Tversky and Kahneman) and political rhetoric (Aristotle's Demades example): people accept sequence-based causes because they seem representative, and politicians exploit this when assigning blame or credit.
Single-case sequence versus pattern correlation: one-off events rely on coincidence being plausible, while correlations from studies need independent support such as a mechanism.
exq: Define post hoc ergo propter hoc and distinguish its temporal-sequence and correlation varieties, using Case 9A (Stone and Houellebecq) to illustrate.
'All post hoc reasoning is fallacious.' Discuss, explaining what contextual conditions (e.g. police surveillance of Houellebecq) could make a causal inference warranted.

Two trends rise together over 30 years (e.g. church attendance and changing social mores, or a development indicator and an emissions trend). List the alternative explanations to causation you must rule out and what evidence would support a causal claim.

Explain Pinto's view that temporal-sequence reasoning may fail minimal rationality and the role of total context. How does it differ from the Tversky and Kahneman heuristic explanation of why people are fooled?
Why is correlation necessary but not sufficient for a good causal claim? Use the E. coli example and the sports franchise example to contrast causal and practical uses of correlation.

notes.t: The Post Hoc Fallacy
pts: Post hoc reasoning need not be fallacious: showing an inference from a correlation to a cause can lend support to a causal hypothesis.
Post hoc ergo propter hoc infers cause from temporal sequence alone: 'after this, therefore because of this'.
The second type infers a causal claim from a correlation; both types are treated together under the post hoc heading.
The fallacy is traced to Aristotle's Rhetoric, where representing non-causes as causes merely because they happened before or alongside an event is criticised.
Aristotle notes politicians are especially fond of this line of reasoning, illustrated by Demades blaming Demosthenes for the war.
defs: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
A fallacy inferring that because event B follows event A in time, A caused B; 'after this, therefore because of this'.
tips: Do not assume all post hoc reasoning is fallacious; judge whether the correlation or sequence actually supports the causal claim.
Temporal sequence alone (B after A) does not establish that A caused B.
rq: Why does Pinto argue that post hoc reasoning is not always fallacious?
Because an inference from a correlation to a cause can provide genuine support for a causal hypothesis, even if it does not prove it.
What is the difference between the two interpretations of post hoc reasoning?
The first infers cause from temporal sequence alone; the second infers a causal claim from a correlation.

notes.t: The Post Hoc Fallacy and Causal Reasoning
pts: Aristotle's fallacy is broader than temporal succession: one event may merely accompany another, yet we wrongly infer causation when no justification exists.
The most common route into the error is when one event precedes another, since we have learnt that effect follows cause in time.
In Case 9A, the argument infers that dining with Houellebecq is perilous because Stone was arrested shortly afterwards; the timing alone is treated as evidence of cause.
The implicit assumption is a causal link between the lunch and the arrest, which the report does not establish.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
The error of inferring that because event B followed event A, A caused B, without adequate justification for a causal connection.
tips: Do not equate Aristotle's fallacy with modern causal fallacy: footnote 3 notes his 'cause' is used in a logical rather than scientific sense.
Temporal order is necessary but never sufficient for causation; check for coincidence, common cause, or reverse causation.
rq: Why is temporal succession alone not sufficient evidence that one event caused another?
Because effects follow causes in time, but many events occur in sequence or together by coincidence or common cause; succession does not establish causal connection.
In Case 9A, what additional evidence would be needed to justify the claim that dining with Houellebecq is perilous?
A systematic link, such as a pattern of many dinners followed by arrests versus controls, or a plausible mechanism connecting the lunch to the arrest.

notes.t: Post hoc reasoning and the total context of causal inference
pts: Inferring causation merely from temporal sequence (post hoc reasoning) is a fallacy, since there is no obvious connection between the two events and coincidence explains them equally well.
Pinto argues that such temporal-sequence reasoning may fail to meet a condition of minimal rationality, so it may not count as reasoning at all.
Pinto instead emphasises the total context of reasoning, including background knowledge and past experience, which can implicitly rule out other causal factors.
Contextual background can explain why a causal inference seems plausible: Stone could have blamed his arrest on lunching with Houellebecq if he knew police were surveilling the novelist.
Others being fooled may reflect heuristic thinking (Tversky and Kahneman): people focus on immediate, representative events and avoid critical thinking.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
Concluding a causal connection between two events solely because one temporally precedes the other.
tips: Do not treat mere temporal order as evidence of cause; always check for a plausible mechanism and alternative explanations such as coincidence.
The footnote shows an extra error: generalising from one example ('anyone' would find dining with the author perilous) is a separate flaw.
rq: Why does Pinto think a temporal-sequence inference might not even count as 'reasoning'?
Because it fails to meet a condition of minimal rationality, so Pinto would not call it reasoning at all.
How can background knowledge make a causal inference more defensible?
It can implicitly rule out other causal factors, e.g. knowing police surveillance explains the arrest, so the lunch is not the true cause.

notes.t: The post hoc fallacy: unwarranted inference from correlation to causation
pts: Correlation alone (regular co-occurrence) does not establish a causal relation; inferring cause from it is the second variety of post hoc.
Correlations involve a pattern of occurrences, often found through studies, unlike one-off cases.
A criterion for good causal claims is that they be supported by a clear correlation, but correlation is necessary, not sufficient.
Correlational information is still useful practically, e.g. for deciding whether an area can support a sports franchise, even though it does not show causation.
Judging the fallacy requires charitable review of context: if plausible considerations exist and the connection is warranted, no fallacy is committed.
defs: Post hoc fallacy (correlation variety)
Inferring a causal claim from a mere correlation, i.e. treating a regular co-occurrence of two things as proof that one causes the other, without warrant.
tips: Do not treat correlation as proof of causation; check for a third common cause or reverse causation.
Judge the fallacy charitably: only charge it if no plausible contextual considerations support the causal link.
rq: Why is a correlation between attendance and living nearby not by itself evidence that living nearby causes attendance?
Two things occurring together regularly may both be caused by a third factor, or the causal direction may be reversed or absent; correlation does not establish causation.
If a correlation is useful for deciding about a sports franchise, why is it still not a causal claim?
Usefulness for prediction or planning does not require causation; the correlation can guide decisions without showing that one factor produces the other.

notes.t: Correlation, causation and the post hoc fallacy
pts: Inferring causation from a mere correlation between two trends (e.g. church attendance and social mores) is a post hoc style error unless a causal link is made plausible.
Coincidence can account for two correlations occurring together, so a causal claim needs independent support.
A causal claim is credible when background experience has suggested the mechanism and testing has confirmed it (e.g. E. coli and sickness).
The onus lies on the person inferring causation from correlation; in its absence one can argue coincidence is more likely.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
Assuming that because one event follows or accompanies another, the first caused the second, without adequate causal evidence.
