tips: Do not treat a correlation between two trends as proof that one causes the other; check for coincidence and a plausible mechanism.
Recognising a reasonable causal scheme (E. coli) is not the same as accepting every causal claim; judge by background evidence.
rq: Why is the E. coli–sickness causal claim treated as more legitimate than the church attendance–social mores claim?
Because experience and testing already support a plausible causal mechanism for E. coli, whereas the church claim lacks such background.
What should one do when a causal link is suggested but not yet understood?
Assess whether it is plausible given other experience and look to rule out coincidence before accepting causation.

units.name: 3 Misidentified cause: common cause and reversed cause
units.ov: This material covers the misidentified cause fallacy: a real causal link exists but is wrongly understood, either because a hidden common cause (confounder) drives both correlated factors or because the direction of causation is reversed. It contrasts this with the post hoc fallacy (no causal link at all) and introduces necessary versus sufficient causes as a way to handle complex causation. Case examples (contraception, the shelter and assault reports, Beevor's Nazi Germany case 9D) show how propaganda or hasty conclusions produce these errors.
must: Misidentified cause: a causal relationship is wrongly inferred from a correlation because a common cause or reversed direction has been overlooked
Common cause (confounder): a third factor Z causes both X and Y, so the X-Y link is spurious (e.g. contraception explaining two correlated trends)
Reversed causation: Y actually causes X, not X causing Y (e.g. assaults create the need for a shelter; Germany's attack on the USSR was misread as the effect of Communist expansion)
Post hoc fallacy vs misidentified cause: post hoc asserts a link where none exists; misidentification errs about a real link (wrong direction or hidden third factor)
Necessary cause: if removed, the effect cannot occur; sufficient cause: can produce the effect, but other sufficient causes may also produce it
Do not confuse necessary with sufficient: removing a necessary cause prevents the effect, while removing a sufficient cause may not
Real-world causes are complex, so no single 'the cause' is usually identifiable; analysts look for necessary causes and the full causal picture to avoid missing a hidden agent
Alternative explanations of a correlation: more reported assaults after a shelter opens may reflect greater willingness to report, not more crime
Mechanisms of error differ: deception/propaganda (Case 9D) versus Hasty Conclusion (failing to think through likely causal relations); name the mechanism separately
Always ask critical questions: Is there a third factor? Could the direction be reversed? Is the correlation merely coincidence?
conn: Post hoc vs misidentified cause: both start from a correlation or sequence, but the diagnosis (no link vs wrong direction/hidden factor) determines which fallacy applies
Necessary/sufficient causes link to common cause: finding a hidden confounder shows the apparent cause was not necessary, and complex multi-factor causation explains why single causes mislead
Reversed causation and propaganda in Case 9D: the direction error is the fallacy, while deception or Hasty Conclusion explains why people made it
Shelter example combines reversed causation (assaults cause shelter) with a measurement confounder (reporting rates rise)
exq: Using a named example, explain how a common cause can make two correlated trends appear causally related, and state the critical questions you would ask to expose it.
Case 9D: Identify the reversal of cause and effect in the German reading of the attack on the Soviet Union, and explain how propaganda versus a Hasty Conclusion could each produce it.
Distinguish the post hoc fallacy from the misidentified cause fallacy, giving one example of each and saying which element of the causal claim is wrong.
A city reports more assaults after opening a shelter. Give at least two alternative explanations (reversed causation, increased reporting) and say what evidence would distinguish them.
Define necessary and sufficient cause, and explain why removing a necessary cause prevents an effect while removing a sufficient cause may not.

notes.t: Misidentifying the cause: confounding factors and cause-effect confusion
pts: The post hoc fallacy attributes a causal link where none exists; misidentification errors instead involve mistakes about a real causal link.
A common error is identifying X as the cause of Y when a third factor Z actually causes both X and Y (a confounding common cause).
Another error reverses causation: taking X to cause Y when in fact Y causes X.
Most real-world causes are complex, so we can rarely identify a single thing that counts as the cause; analysts often seek a necessary cause instead.
Overlooking the full causal picture makes it easy to miss a causal agent acting behind others.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
Attributing a causal relationship between two events where none exists, usually because one occurred before or alongside the other.
Necessary cause
A cause that, if removed, would prevent the effect from occurring.
Sufficient cause
A cause that can result in an effect, though the effect could still occur through another sufficient cause if it is absent.
tips: Do not confuse a necessary cause with a sufficient cause: removing a necessary cause prevents the effect, while a sufficient cause may be one of several routes to it.
Distinguish misidentified causes (a real link with the wrong direction or a hidden third factor) from post hoc errors (no link at all).
rq: Why can a third factor Z make us wrongly conclude that X causes Y?
Z causes both X and Y, so X and Y correlate even though neither causes the other; the apparent link is spurious.
Why is it hard to name 'the' cause of an event like the New Orleans flood?
Most effects have many interacting causal factors (hurricane, levee design, political decisions), so no single factor uniquely counts as the cause.

notes.t: Misidentified cause and the common-cause / reversed-cause fallacies
pts: A correlation between two trends does not establish that one causes the other; look for a common cause behind both.
Misidentified Cause fallacy arises when a common cause (e.g. contraception) explains both correlated factors, so the apparent link is spurious.
Reversed causation: the supposed effect may actually be the cause (assaults create the need for the shelter, not the reverse).
Increased reported assaults after a shelter opens may reflect greater willingness to report, not more crime.
defs: Misidentified Cause
A fallacy in which a causal relationship is wrongly inferred from a correlation, typically because a common cause or a reversed direction of causation has been overlooked.
tips: Do not stop at a correlation: always ask whether a third factor or reversed causation explains the pattern.
Remember that reversed causation (Y causing X) is a distinct error from common cause; identify which one applies.
rq: Why might a shelter appear to increase crime even if it does not?
Because the shelter makes reporting easier, so more existing assaults are recorded; the causal arrow runs from assaults to the shelter.
How could you test whether contraception is a common cause of falling birthrates and rising female employment?
Check whether the correlation between employment and birthrate weakens when contraception access is controlled for, or compare regions with differing contraception access.

notes.t: Misidentifying the Cause (Case 9D: Beevor on Nazi Germany and Communism)
pts: A Misidentified Cause fallacy reverses cause and effect, treating the effect as the cause.
In Case 9D, Germans read Nazi Germany's attack on the Soviet Union as the effect of Communist expansion, when the order was actually reversed.
Widespread misidentification here was driven by state propaganda, which explains the reasoning through deception.
Where no deception is involved, a Hasty Conclusion can lead people to fail to think through likely causal relations and reverse them by mistake.
The three causal fallacies discussed so far can be identified and evaluated using certain Critical questions.
defs: Misidentified Cause
A causal fallacy in which the direction of causation is reversed, so an effect is mistakenly identified as the cause of what actually caused it.
tips: Do not confuse a Misidentified Cause (reversed causation) with a deception-based error; identify the mechanism separately.
Check the direction of causation in the case itself: the fallacy is the reversal, not the mere presence of a causal claim.
rq: Why might a propaganda-driven misidentification differ from one caused by a Hasty Conclusion?
Propaganda produces the error through deliberate deception, whereas a Hasty Conclusion produces it through a failure to think through the likely causal relations.
How could you check whether a claimed cause is really the effect?
Ask whether the proposed effect could have occurred before the proposed cause, and whether the supposed cause depends on the supposed effect.

units.name: 4 Critical questions for correlation-based causal claims
units.ov: This material gives a checklist of critical questions for evaluating causal claims that rest on correlation. It moves from whether a real correlation exists, to whether it could be coincidence, to whether the causal direction is right and whether a common cause explains both variables. The post hoc fallacy is the error that results when these checks are skipped.
must: Question 1: does the causal claim rest on an actual correlation? Support weakens from a correlation study, to anecdote, to no correlation at all.
Absence of correlation does not prove absence of causation; it shifts the burden of proof onto the arguer to justify the causal claim.
Question 2: could the correlation be mere coincidence? Look for contextual factors that make a causal inference plausible.
Post hoc fallacy: wrongly inferring that because one event followed or accompanied another, the first caused the second, without adequate causal grounds.
If no plausible inference from correlation to cause can be given, expect the post hoc fallacy.
Question 3: even with evidence of a causal link, check that cause and effect are correctly identified (guard against reversed causation).
Check for a common cause (confounder) that explains both variables, so that neither causes the other.
Correlation is necessary evidence for a causal claim but never sufficient: plausibility, direction and confounders must also be addressed.
Evidence strength ranking: correlation study > anecdote > no correlation. Use it to judge how strongly a claim is supported.
Apply the questions in order, and in an answer name the specific question being used.
conn: Post hoc fallacy and coincidence: a correlation with no plausible mechanism or context is the typical trigger for post hoc reasoning.
Reversed causation and common cause: both are failures to identify cause and effect correctly, even when the causal link is real, so they are often tested together.
Burden of proof and absent correlation: no correlation does not refute the claim, but the arguer must supply other justification.

Sustainable development examples: claims such as 'aid causes growth' or 'growth causes lower emissions' need all the checks, because confounders like income, governance or time trends may drive both variables.
exq: A politician claims that a country's emissions fell because it introduced a green policy, citing only that emissions fell after the policy. Apply the critical questions and identify the fallacy involved.
Explain why absence of correlation does not prove there is no causal link. What is the effect on the burden of proof?
Countries with higher electricity access show higher life expectancy. Discuss how reversed causation and a common cause could each undermine the claim that electricity raises life expectancy.
Rank correlation study, anecdote and no correlation as support for a causal claim, and justify the ranking with an example.
Define the post hoc fallacy, and show with an example how contextual factors can make a causal inference from a correlation plausible rather than coincidental.

notes.t: Critical questions for causal claims based on correlation
pts: First ask whether the causal claim rests on an actual correlation; support weakens from correlation study to anecdote to no correlation at all.
Absence of correlation does not prove no causal link, but it puts the burden on the arguer to justify the causal claim.
Check whether the correlation could be mere coincidence, using contextual factors that make a causal inference plausible.
Without a plausible inference from correlation to cause, expect the post hoc fallacy.
Even with evidence of a causal link, verify the cause and effect are correctly identified and that no common cause explains both.
defs: Post hoc fallacy
Wrongly inferring that because one event followed or accompanied another, the first caused the second, without adequate causal grounds.
tips: Do not treat absence of correlation as proof of no causation; it only shifts the burden of proof to the arguer.
Check that cause and effect are correctly identified before accepting a causal claim, not just that they correlate.
rq: Why does a missing correlation not rule out a causal link, yet still weaken the causal claim?
Causal relations can exist without a detected correlation, but without correlation the arguer bears the burden of showing why the link should be believed, so support is weaker.
What separates a plausible causal inference from a post hoc fallacy?
A plausible inference is supported by contextual factors showing the correlation is unlikely to be coincidence; without them, the inference relies only on temporal or co-occurrence sequence.

units.name: 5 Argument from Consequences
units.ov: This material introduces the Argument from Consequences, a practical reasoning scheme that uses causal reasoning to project a likely outcome of an action or policy. It recommends the action if the outcome is positive and rejects it if negative. Evaluation turns on how likely the consequence is, what evidence supports it, and whether opposite consequences are ignored, as the tuition-fees example shows.
must: Definition: a practical argument projecting a likely consequence of an action/policy, recommending it if the consequence is positive and rejecting it if negative
Two variants: positive (recommend the action) and negative (reject the action); always identify which one is in play
The key evaluative factors are the likelihood that the proposal will cause the consequence and the reasons given for believing it
Never treat a projected consequence as certain; the reasoning is defeasible and open to objection, so the aim is the best available explanation
Causal claims must be checked for reversed direction (B causes A, not A causes B) and for a hidden common cause
Walton's three critical questions: How likely is the consequence? What evidence supports it? Are opposite consequences ignored?
Overgeneralisation weakens likelihood: in the tuition example, claiming that all students face a financial burden when only some plausibly do
Counter-reasons undermine a predicted outcome: parental income, savings plans and future earnings in the tuition case
A matching claim of negative consequences is not evidence against an opposing positive argument; it merely asserts the contrary
Predicting negative outcomes does not make an argument fallacious; it is fallacious only if the consequence is unlikely, unsupported or ignores opposite consequences
conn: Causal reasoning and the scheme: the strength of a consequences argument depends on whether the causal link is sound, including checks for reverse causation and common causes
Critical questions and fallacy diagnosis: an argument is judged fallacious by applying Walton's likelihood, evidence and opposite-consequences questions, not by its negative tone
Positive versus negative variants in rebuttal: one argument from positive consequences can be countered by a negative one, but the rebuttal needs its own evidence, as in the tuition fees debate
Policy evaluation in sustainable development: policy proposals are judged by projected outcomes, so likelihood, evidence and trade-offs between competing consequences must all be weighed
exq: Define the Argument from Consequences and explain how its positive and negative variants lead to recommending or rejecting an action, using a policy example.
Apply Walton's three critical questions to an argument that raising tuition fees will impose financial burdens on all students. Does the argument succeed? Justify your answer.
Explain two ways a causal claim in an argument from consequences might be mistaken (reverse direction and hidden common cause) and give an example of each.
Why is it wrong to call an argument fallacious just because it predicts negative outcomes? State the conditions under which it is fallacious.
Evaluate a rebuttal that answers a positive-consequences argument only by asserting matching negative consequences. What further evidence would strengthen it?

notes.t: The Argument from Consequences
pts: The Argument from Consequences is a scheme with positive and negative variants that draws on causal reasoning to project a likely consequence of an action or policy.
Depending on whether the projected consequence is positive or negative, the action or policy is recommended or rejected.
The crucial factors are the likelihood that the consequences will be caused by the proposal and the reasons given for believing so.
Causal claims may be wrong about direction (B causing A rather than A causing B) or be due to a hidden common cause, so they must be checked.
Such reasoning is open to objection and defeat, so the job is to provide the best explanations available.
defs: Argument from Consequences
A practical argument that projects a consequence likely to follow from an action or policy and recommends or rejects that action according to whether the consequence is positive or negative.
tips: Do not treat a projected consequence as certain; assess the likelihood of causation and the reasons given for it.
Remember that the scheme has both positive and negative variants, which lead to recommending or rejecting the action respectively.
rq: Why must an arguer check whether B causes A rather than A causing B before accepting a consequence claim?
Because the proposed action may not produce the consequence if the causal direction is reversed or a hidden common cause explains both events.
What should be assessed when no contextual evidence is available for a causal claim?
The plausibility of the claim given general background knowledge about the situation.

notes.t: Argument from Consequences: evaluating predicted negative outcomes
pts: The argument predicts negative consequences (financial burdens) from raising tuition, rebutting a positive-consequences argument.
Likelihood of the predicted consequence is weakened because the claim generalizes to all students, while only some are plausibly affected.
Reasons such as parental income, savings plans and future earnings undermine the claim, and no specific reasons favour the negative outcome over others.
The argument offers no evidence against the opposing positive argument beyond a matching claim of negative consequences.
Walton's three critical questions (likelihood, evidence, opposite consequences) show the argument fails.
defs: Argument from Consequences

A reasoning scheme in which an action is accepted or rejected based on its predicted outcomes; it is fallacious when the predicted consequence is unlikely, unsupported, or ignores opposite consequences.
tips: Do not conclude an argument is fallacious merely because it predicts negative outcomes; assess the likelihood and evidence for them.
Check whether opposite consequences are ignored, since this is a key critical question.
rq: Why does generalizing a consequence to all students weaken the argument?
Because only some people are plausibly affected, so a universal prediction is too strong and less likely to hold.
What three critical questions should be asked of a consequence-based argument?
How likely the consequence is, what evidence supports it, and whether consequences of the opposite value should be considered.

units.name: 6 Slippery Slope fallacy and its critical questions
units.ov: This material introduces Slippery Slope reasoning as negative reasoning from consequences. It rests on a causal chain from a proposed action to a bad outcome, and it is not inherently fallacious. Evaluation uses three critical questions (plausibility of each step, whether the slope can be stopped, and how negative the outcome really is), and the final section contrasts causal Slippery Slope reasoning with similarity-based Precedent reasoning.
must: Definition: a Slippery Slope opposes an action because it is claimed to set off a causal chain of further undesirable actions leading to a negative outcome.
Slippery Slope reasoning is NOT inherently fallacious; earlier textbooks were wrong to say so. Assess each case on its merits.
The conclusion is usually implicit (we should not take the first step), so reconstruct it before evaluating.
The core premise is causal: the action will (or probably will) lead to a series of connected steps. Each link must be independently plausible, not merely present in a chain.
Critical Question 1: Is each forward-looking causal step plausible? If any step is clearly unlikely, the argument can be labelled fallacious.
Critical Question 2: Is the slope unstoppable or irreversible? If the chain can be halted or reversed, the next step need not arrive.
Critical Question 3: Is the outcome really negative? Severity is audience-relative, and reversibility can make an outcome less bad.
Strength of causal language matters: 'inevitable' demands far more evidence than 'likely' and is more open to counterinstances.
Variants exist: a single causal step, simultaneous events, or argument from negative consequence with no intervening step. Classify these correctly.

Slippery Slope (causal: one event causes another) differs from Precedent (similarity: it will follow because it is like the case proposed). The two can be combined, so assess each component separately.
Case 9F fails on two counts: the links from legislation to confusion and then to cohabitation are unsupported, and the jump to ending heterosexual traditional marriage is unwarranted.
conn: Plausibility of steps and strength of causal wording: 'inevitable' claims make the first critical question harder to satisfy and invite counterinstances.
Irreversibility and severity: if a slope can be stopped or reversed, the final outcome is less negative, so Critical Questions 2 and 3 interact.
Audience and severity: whether the outcome is bad depends on who judges it, so the arguer's own audience may differ from the wider audience affected by the policy.
Slippery Slope and Precedent reasoning: both warn about future consequences and may appear in one argument, but a causal link and a similarity claim need different fallacy tests.
exq: Reconstruct the argument in Case 9F, including its implicit conclusion, and use the three critical questions to evaluate whether it is a fallacious Slippery Slope.
Why is it a mistake to label every Slippery Slope argument as fallacious? Give the conditions under which one is reasonable and one under which it is fallacious.
Compare the effect of 'inevitably' versus 'probably' in a Slippery Slope argument. What evidence is needed in each case, and how does this relate to counterinstances?
Distinguish Slippery Slope reasoning from Precedent reasoning, using a short example that combines both, and explain how you would assess each component.
Discuss how reversibility and audience affect judgements of how negative a Slippery Slope's final outcome is, using a sustainable development policy as an example.

notes.t: The Fallacy of the Slippery Slope
pts: Slippery Slope reasoning is negative reasoning from consequences, defined by a causal chain from the proposed action to a negative outcome.
Slippery Slope reasoning is not inherently fallacious; earlier textbooks wrongly claimed it was, partly from failing to examine real cases fully.
In its simplest form, the argument rests on a crucial premise that the proposed action will (or probably will) lead to a series of causally connected actions.
Variants may have only one causal step, or simultaneous rather than serial events; argument from negative consequence has no intervening step.
defs: Slippery Slope
A form of negative consequence reasoning in which an action is opposed because it is claimed to set off a causal chain of further undesirable actions leading to a negative outcome.
tips: Do not label every slippery slope argument as fallacious; assess whether the causal links are plausible and supported by evidence.
Distinguish a single-step variant or simultaneous events from a full serial chain when classifying the argument.
rq: Why is the key premise of a slippery slope argument its causal claim rather than the mere listing of bad outcomes?
Because the argument's strength depends on whether each step in the chain is genuinely caused by the previous one; without a credible causal link the reasoning is weak.
What distinguishes a slippery slope from an argument from negative consequence?
A slippery slope contains intervening causal steps in a series, whereas argument from negative consequence goes directly from action to consequence.

notes.t: Evaluating Slippery Slope arguments (Case 9F)
pts: A Slippery Slope argument's conclusion is usually implicit: we should not take the first step because the final consequence is undesirable.
Its core premise is causal, presenting a chain of links; a good Slippery Slope needs each causal link to be plausible (though not guaranteed) and the end consequence clearly negative.
The Case 9F argument fails on both counts: no obvious reason links legislation to a generation's sexual confusion, and the next step to cohabitation is not obvious.
Trends toward cohabitation already exist in some societies, so linking them to state sanctioning requires considerable argumentation that is absent.
The argument implicitly jumps to claiming the proposal would end traditional marriage even among heterosexuals, a step unwarranted by the evidence given.
defs: Slippery Slope argument
An argument that a first step should be avoided because it causes a chain of further steps leading to an undesirable final consequence.
tips: Do not treat a causal chain as valid merely because it is a chain; each link must be independently justified.
Note that the conclusion of a Slippery Slope is often unstated and must be reconstructed from the argument.
rq: Why does the author say the argument in Case 9F is weak even though it has a causal chain?
Because its causal links are not plausible (no obvious reason legislation causes generational confusion) and the final step to cohabitation is not obviously connected to the first step.
What would make a Slippery Slope argument stronger?
Plausible, well-supported causal links at each step and a clearly negative final consequence.

notes.t: Critical Questions for the Slippery Slope fallacy
pts: The negative-outcome factor is assessed by asking whether the consequence is truly undesirable, noting that different audiences may judge it differently.
Three Critical Questions identify and assess potentially fallacious Slippery Slopes: plausibility of steps, possibility of stopping, and whether the outcome is really negative.
The core evaluative question is whether each forward-looking causal step is plausible; if any step is clearly unlikely, the argument can be labelled fallacious.
The strength of causal language matters: claims of inevitability need far more evidence than claims of likelihood, and are more open to counterinstances.
defs: Slippery Slope fallacy
An argument that a proposed action will trigger a chain of causal steps leading to a negative outcome, where the steps are implausible, reversible, or the outcome is not truly negative.
tips: Do not judge the negative outcome only from the immediate audience; consider the wider audience affected by the policy.
Watch for strong causal words like 'inevitable', which demand stronger evidence than 'likely'.
rq: Why does claiming a causal link is 'inevitable' weaken an argument compared with saying it is 'likely'?
Inevitability is a much stronger claim requiring far more evidence and is more easily refuted by a single counterinstance.
Why might a slope fail to be slippery even if the first step seems plausible?
Because one could stop and go back at some point, so the chain of consequences is not automatic.

notes.t: Slippery Slope arguments: causal slopes, irreversibility and severity
pts: Slippery Slope arguments assume that once a causal chain starts, it slides inevitably toward the final consequence.
The second critical question asks whether the causal chain is unstoppable or irreversible; if the slope can be halted, the next step need not arrive.
Critics may argue that effects of a proposal could simply be reversed or positively altered, undermining the claimed irreversibility.
The third critical question asks how really negative the conclusion is; reversibility can make bad outcomes less negative, so a proposal may be worth pursuing.
What an arguer deems negative may not be judged negative by a wider audience, so severity depends on who is judging.
defs: Slippery Slope argument
An argument claiming that a proposed action will set off a causal chain leading inevitably to an undesirable final consequence.
tips: Do not assume a bad end-point is real without checking that each causal link is plausible and irreversible.
Severity is audience-relative: an arguer's view of a negative consequence may not be shared by a wider audience.
rq: Why does showing a causal step is reversible weaken a Slippery Slope argument?
If the slope can be stopped or reversed, the later undesirable steps need not occur, so the inevitability premise fails.
Could a bad consequence still justify rejecting a proposal even if it is reversible?
Only if the consequence is severe enough; if the proposal offers much and can be reversed if it fails, there is reason to proceed.

notes.t: Slippery Slope vs. Precedent reasoning; chapter exercises
pts: Slippery Slope reasoning is causal: it claims one event will likely cause another.
Precedent reasoning claims something will follow because it is like what is being proposed.
The two reasoning types are easy to confuse and can even be combined in one argument.
Fallacious cases of each kind differ, so they must be distinguished when assessing arguments.
defs: Slippery Slope reasoning
An argument that one event will likely cause a chain of further events, typically undesirable, so the initial step should be avoided.
Precedent reasoning
An argument that something will follow, or should be treated alike, because it is similar to a known case or what is being proposed.
tips: Do not confuse causal claims (Slippery Slope) with similarity claims (Precedent); the fallacy conditions differ.
Arguments may mix both strategies, so assess each component separately rather than the argument as one block.
rq: Why is it important to tell Slippery Slope reasoning apart from Precedent reasoning when assessing an argument?
Because the two have different structures (causal chain versus similarity), so the criteria for fallacious cases differ for each.
How can an argument combine both strategies, and what should you check?
It can claim a causal chain while also appealing to similarity; check each claim separately against its own critical questions.

units.name: 7 Exercises, examples and further reading
units.ov: This material is a set of exercises and further reading on critical reasoning, using real argument extracts (NAFTA and Canadian health care, foxhunting, abortion and crime, cheap paperbacks, a moral case against dance). It trains students to separate premises from conclusions, to spot weak analogies, appeals to authority, and correlation-cause and post hoc errors, and it points to key sources on post hoc and slippery slope reasoning.
must: Separate conclusion from premises first: identify what the author is trying to prove before assessing any support.
Correlation is not causation: the Levitt-Donohue link (abortion in the early 1970s, lower crime in the 1990s) needs confounders and alternative explanations considered before it counts as causal.
Post hoc reasoning ('after, therefore because') is the core fallacy; Pinto's essay is the recommended starting point.
Slippery slope arguments are covered by Govier (essay) and Walton (book); do not attribute post hoc to them or slippery slope to Pinto.
Argument by analogy only works if the cases are relevantly similar: the Canadian letter cites European examples, but the binding constraint is NAFTA trade law.
NAFTA's health care exemption covers only fully publicly funded, non-commercial systems; privatizing would trigger 'national treatment' rights for U.S. firms.
Generalising from anecdote is weak: 'many who ended immorally began by dancing' does not show that dancing causes immorality.
An appeal to scripture is an appeal to authority, not evidence of causation.
Inference from an unusual event (Vanessa walking past the office) to a motive is plausible only if the event is genuinely out of the ordinary.
Check whether a speaker actually supports a generalisation such as 'never' before treating it as a causal claim (the Smarties dialogue).
conn: Correlation and cause links the Levitt-Donohue study, the dance argument, and post hoc reasoning: each moves from association or sequence to cause without ruling out confounders.
Analogy and counterexample link the NAFTA letter and the Penguin/Orwell extract: a parallel from a different legal or market setting does not settle the question at hand.

Premise-conclusion analysis underlies every exercise, including the foxhunting argument, where the claim that shooting would maim foxes is a premise needing evidence, and the dance argument, which concedes the sex urge is not sinful but limits its fulfilment to marriage.
Slippery slope and post hoc arguments both claim a causal chain, so both require evidence for each link, as in the argument that cheap reprints cripple libraries and reduce new novels.
exq: Identify the conclusion and premises in the dance extract. Which step commits a correlation-cause error, and why does the concession that not everyone who dances is immoral not rescue the argument?
Critically evaluate the claim that Levitt and Donohue's finding shows abortion caused lower 1990s crime. Which confounding factors would you consider?
Explain why the Canadian letter's analogy to European examples fails, with reference to NAFTA's health care exemption and 'national treatment'.
Distinguish post hoc from slippery slope reasoning, naming the recommended source for each, and give an example of each from the exercises.
Analyse Forsyth's foxhunting argument: which premises are empirical, which are evaluative, and what evidence would the claim that farmers are poor marksmen need?

notes.t: Analysing reasoning in dialogue and argument (correlation and cause)
pts: The second man's reasoning is an inference from an unusual event (Vanessa walking past his office) to a conclusion about her motive, which is only plausible if the event is genuinely out of the ordinary.
The Canadian letter argues by analogy: the Supreme Court's European examples are said to support two-tier care, but the relevant constraint is trade law (NAFTA), not the European precedents.
NAFTA's health care exemption applies only to fully publicly funded, non-commercial systems; privatizing would trigger 'national treatment' rights for U.S. firms.
tips: Don't treat the Smarties dialogue as a causal claim without checking whether the 'never' is a generalisation that the speaker actually supports.
Distinguish the European examples from the binding trade rules; a counterexample in another legal setting does not settle what NAFTA requires.
rq: Why does the second man's conclusion depend on the claim that Vanessa 'never' walks by his office?
Because a rare event is evidence of a special reason; if she walked by often, the morning visit would not support his inference about her intent.
What would the letter's argument need to be missing to be a non-sequitur about Europe?
It would need a premise that the European countries' rules govern Canada's obligations; the letter instead points to NAFTA's different rules.

notes.t: Chapter Exercises: foxhunting, abortion-crime research, and paperback publishing
pts: Exercise 6 presents Frederick Forsyth's defence of foxhunting, arguing culling is necessary and hunting is the most humane method.
The passage argues that ending hunts would push farmers to shoot foxes, but farmers are poor marksmen, so many foxes would be maimed.
Exercise 7 reports Levitt and Donohue's claim that aborting 'unwanted' children in the early 1970s is linked to lower crime rates in the 1990s.
Exercise 8 describes Penguin's 1935 launch of cheap paperbacks and Orwell's mixed response, praising them as a reader but condemning them as a writer.
tips: Distinguish the author's conclusion from the premises supporting it when analysing these extracts.
Do not treat the Levitt and Donohue correlation as established causation without considering confounding factors.
rq: Why might the Levitt and Donohue argument be considered a correlation rather than proof of causation?
Falling crime in the 1990s coincides with the early-1970s abortion pattern, but other factors could explain both; the link is correlational unless alternative explanations are ruled out.
What assumption does Forsyth's argument rely on about farmers' ability to replace hunting?
That farmers can kill foxes efficiently with guns; the passage challenges this by noting they are not marksmen, so the argument's humaneness claim depends on this premise.

notes.t: Excerpts on dance and the book trade: moral argument against dance and a letter on publish
pts: The author argues that bodily contact and dance movements to modern rock music produce sexual arousal, and that modern dance is designed to convey 'love-making'.
The author accepts that the sex urge is God-given and not sinful per se, but holds that its righteous fulfilment is limited to marriage.
The argument concedes that not everyone who dances ends in immorality, yet claims many who came to immoral ends began by dancing, a generalisation from anecdote.
The first passage (item 8) argues that cheap reprints could cripple lending libraries and reduce new novels, pitting art against trade.
tips: Watch for the slide from 'some people who danced ended immorally' to 'dancing causes immorality', a classic correlation-causation error.
Note that the author's appeal to scripture (I Corinthians, Galatians) is an appeal to authority, not evidence of causation.
rq: Why is the argument that dance leads to immorality weak even if many immoral people once danced?
Because it infers cause from correlation: many people who ended immorally had danced, but this does not show dancing caused their immorality, and the author admits most dancers are not immoral.

notes.t: Further Reading: post hoc and slippery slope sources
pts: Robert Pinto's essay is a recommended starting point for exploring the complexities of post hoc reasoning.
Trudy Govier's essay is a recommended source on slippery slope arguments.
Douglas Walton's book is a recommended full-length treatment of slippery slope arguments.
tips: Note the difference in sources: Pinto addresses post hoc, while Govier and Walton address slippery slope arguments; don't attribute one topic to the other's author.
rq: Why does the page point to Pinto's essay on post hoc reasoning as a place to begin, rather than treating post hoc as a simple error?
Because post hoc reasoning (inferring causation from temporal sequence) involves complexities that merit careful study, not just a simple label of fallacy.

units.name: 1 What the appeal to authority is and why we rely on experts
units.ov: This material introduces ad verecundiam (appeal to authority or expertise) as an argument form that is often rational, since nobody can verify everything personally, but becomes fallacious when status, prestige or power is mistaken for relevant expertise. It traces the idea from Locke's coercive 'awe and shame' version, through status-based authority, to the modern restriction to genuine expertise, and grounds it in testimony as a weaker kind of evidence that is presumed honest but is checked against other testimony and common experience.
must: Definition: ad verecundiam supports a claim by appealing to the status or testimony of an authority or expert rather than to direct evidence or reasons.

Not every appeal to authority is a fallacy: it is rational when we lack direct evidence and cannot practically acquire the expert's knowledge (e.g. physician, mechanic, scientists building on earlier results).
The key test is whether the authority is genuinely expert in the relevant field and whether the appeal suits the situation, so that trust is well founded.
The fallacy arises when an audience mistakes status as an authority for expertise in the relevant field (status or position is present, expertise is merely assumed).

Locke's original ad verecundiam: citing an eminent person's word to pressure the audience through awe or shame into accepting a claim without challenge. This is coercive, and Locke is vague about what makes an authority legitimate.

Authority can come from social standing, prestige or political power, not only knowledge. A sovereign's word gives a reason to act as if true, even if it gives no reason to believe it. Medieval deference to Aristotle is the historical example.

Modern treatments stress the cognitive element: the ad verecundiam is restricted to appeals to genuine expertise unavailable otherwise, so the 'argument of authority' is now usually an appeal to experts.

Testimony, including expert testimony, is a principal source of belief. It is presumed honest by default (presumption in favour of testimony) and is doubted only when it conflicts with common experience or other evidence.

Testimony is a weaker kind of evidence: reliable for an individual's own states or experiences, but giving little compelling evidence across a wide domain. It is checked against other testimony and wider experience.
Distinguish ad verecundiam from other 'ad' arguments such as ad populum (the crowd) and ad baculum (force).
conn: Reliance on experts links to the presumption in favour of testimony: both rest on trust that is rational by default but defeasible when the testimony conflicts with other evidence or experience.
The status vs expertise distinction links Locke's coercive version, political authority and the modern expert-based version, and shows how a legitimate appeal becomes a fallacy.
Ad verecundiam sits in a series with the other 'ad' arguments (ad populum, ad baculum), so exam answers should contrast what each appeals to (authority, popularity, force).

In Global Sustainable Development, citing scientists or policymakers on climate or development tests whether authority rests on relevant expertise, and how far testimony counts as evidence across a wide domain.
exq: Is the appeal to authority always a fallacy? Use the examples of a physician or mechanic and of scientists building on earlier results to justify your answer.
Explain Locke's argumentum ad verecundiam. Why is it coercive and why is his account of authority vague?
How does a legitimate appeal to expertise differ from a fallacious appeal to status or prestige? Use the example of medieval deference to Aristotle or a political sovereign.
Why is testimony a weaker kind of evidence over a wide domain, and when is the presumption in favour of testimony overridden?
Describe a sustainability-related case where a person is cited as an authority outside their field of expertise, and say how you would assess whether the appeal is acceptable.

notes.t: Ad verecundiam: the Appeal to Authority or Expertise
pts: The Appeal to Authority (ad verecundiam) uses the status of an authority or expert to support a claim; it is a strategy few can avoid, and it is often reasonable when direct knowledge is impractical to acquire.
Relying on an expert's testimony is rational when we lack direct evidence and cannot practically acquire the expert's knowledge and experience ourselves.
The chapter treats ad verecundiam as the third 'ad' argument, following the appeals to components of experience studied in the previous two chapters.
defs: Ad verecundiam (Appeal to Authority or Expertise)
An argument form in which a claim is supported by appealing to the status or testimony of an authority or expert, rather than to direct evidence or reasons.
tips: Do not assume every appeal to authority is fallacious; the question is whether the authority is genuinely expert and the appeal is appropriate to the situation.
Distinguish the appeal to authority (ad verecundiam) from other 'ad' arguments such as ad populum or ad baculum.
rq: Why is appealing to a doctor's authority not automatically a fallacy, given that it is an 'ad' argument?
Because the doctor has knowledge and experience the patient lacks and cannot practically acquire; relying on expert testimony is reasonable when direct evidence is impractical to obtain.

notes.t: Appeal to authority and the reliance on experts
pts: Nobody can know everything affecting them, so we must rely on and trust other people's say-so; the real issue is when that trust is well placed.
Scientists build on previous teams' results and accept them on the authority of those who conducted them, since replicating everything is impractical.
Trusting a physician or mechanic does not make subsequent deliberation fallacious, yet the appeal to authority is often dismissed as a fallacy.
Locke's original argumentum ad verecundiam uses an eminent person's word to back a claim, pressuring the audience through awe and shame; this is coercive and problematic.
Locke is vague about the nature of the authority involved; it involves more than just knowledge.
defs: Argumentum ad verecundiam (appeal to authority)
Persuasion by invoking an eminent person's word as backing for a claim, so that the audience, feeling awe or shame, accepts the claim without challenge.
tips: Do not dismiss all appeals to authority as fallacies; the question is whether the trust placed in the authority is well founded.
Locke's account is vague about what makes an authority legitimate, so distinguish genuine expertise from mere eminence.
rq: Why is relying on a physician not automatically fallacious, while the appeal to authority is often called one?
Relying on a competent, relevant expert whose trust is well placed is reasonable; the fallacy arises when authority is used to coerce acceptance through awe or shame rather than genuine expertise.
What distinguishes the scientists' reliance on prior results from a fallacious appeal?
They rely on experts who conducted work according to professional standards and procedures, which justifies trust.

notes.t: Authority arguments (ad verecundiam) and the appeal to experts
pts: Authority can derive from social standing, prestige or political power, not only knowledge; deference to such status is the 'argument of authority'.
Modern treatments stress the cognitive element, restricting the ad verecundiam to appeals to genuine expertise unavailable otherwise, so modern authority appeals are often appeals to experts.
A fallacy arises when an audience mistakes a person's status as an authority for expertise in the relevant field.
A political sovereign's saying something gives a reason to act on it as if true, even when it is not a reason to believe it.
Medieval deference to Aristotle is a historical example of status-based authority, contrasted with this book's critical evaluation of his ideas.
defs: ad verecundiam
Fallacy of appealing to authority, prestige or status (rather than sound evidence or genuine expertise) as a reason to accept a claim.
Argument of authority
Reasoning that relies on a person's position or status to support a claim; in modern treatments restricted to appeals to expertise.
Appeal to experts
Modern form of authority appeal in which a person with specialised knowledge not generally available is cited as evidence.
tips: Do not treat all appeals to authority as fallacious; legitimate appeals to genuine experts are acceptable.
Distinguish status/position from expertise: the error occurs when only the first exists but the second is assumed.
rq: Why might an appeal to a sovereign's statement be a legitimate reason to act, yet a fallacy as a reason to believe?
Political power gives practical reasons for action (compliance) regardless of truth; using it as evidence for belief confuses status with knowledge.
What distinguishes an appeal to an expert from a fallacious appeal to authority?
Whether the authority's status reflects genuine expertise in the relevant field, rather than prestige or position alone.

notes.t: Testimony as evidence in argument
pts: Testimony (including an expert's word) is one of the principal sources of the beliefs we hold.
Judging a particular person's testimony means comparing it against our wider experience, so testimony is effectively checked against testimony.
Claims about someone's own state of mind or specific experiences are accepted on her say-so, because of the presumption of honesty in communication.
Testimony is a weaker kind of evidence: reliable for an individual, but providing little compelling evidence across a wider domain.
Testimony is doubted when it falls outside common experience or is contradicted by other evidence.
defs: Presumption in favour of testimony
Default acceptance of a person's report, based on expectation of honesty in communication, unless there is reason to doubt her trustworthiness.
tips: Do not treat testimony as strong evidence in wide domains; it is a weaker kind of evidence than broad experience.
Testimony is doubted only when it conflicts with common experience or other evidence; the presumption of honesty otherwise applies.
rq: Why does the text say that comparing a report with common experience is really comparing testimony with testimony?

Our knowledge of how the world is comes from others' reports, so checking one report against what we know means checking it against other testimony, which we assume is more reliable when based on wide experience.
Why can we accept someone's report of her own feelings without independent evidence, but not a claim about a wider subject?
Honesty is presumed in communication, and she is the reliable source on her own mind; for wider claims, testimony alone offers weaker support than broader evidence.

units.name: 2 Legitimate appeal to expertise, Locke and Salmon
units.ov: This material examines when appeal to expertise is legitimate. It starts with the general expert-appeal form, which is valid only if it assumes the source is infallible, and so is unsound. It then covers Locke's ad verecundiam (deference out of respect or shame) and Salmon's inductive version, which rests on the expert's track record and gives only probable support. The common thread is that the strong 'always correct' premise is what makes the argument either valid but unsound or fallacious, and that a weaker inductive premise makes it reasonable but fallible.
must: General expert-appeal form: 'Someone (X) asserts S, therefore S is true'. As stated it is not valid, because nothing links assertion to truth.
Hamblin's repair: add the premise 'everything X says is true'. This makes the form deductively valid, but the premise is the problem.
The premise claims too much. Unless the source is a divine being, 'everything X says is true' is unverifiable and controversial, so the argument is valid but unsound.
Case 7A: 'everything the president says is true' is unverifiable and controversial, so it illustrates the problem.
Appeal to expertise is a legitimate exception: expert experience stands above general experience, but only if the argument meets criteria of expertise. Asserting authority is not enough.
Locke's ad verecundiam: fallacy of appealing to respect for, or shame before, an authority (e.g. a high office holder) instead of genuine evidence. People defer to avoid the shame of challenging him.
The 'expert is always correct' premise works as immunization: it blocks criticism in advance and shuts down dialogue. That is why it is both implausible and problematic.
Salmon's inductive version: appeal to authority is not always fallacious. If the expert has a good track record, the generalization 'experts like this are usually right' supports the claim.
Salmon's version gives only probable support. Any particular assertion could be wrong, so contextual critical questions must still be asked.
Key contrast: deductive (infallibility premise, valid but unsound) versus inductive (reliability premise, plausible but fallible). Say which one an example uses.
conn: Hamblin's validity fix versus soundness: a valid form with an implausible premise is still unsound. Link this to the infallibility premise and Case 7A.

Locke's ad verecundiam versus Salmon's inductive version: both involve deference to authority, but one rests on shame or respect and the other on evidence of track record. Questions often ask you to tell them apart.

Immunizing premises and critical questioning: 'always correct' blocks challenge, while the inductive version invites contextual questions about expertise, so legitimacy depends on whether the argument stays open to criticism.
Legitimate exception and criteria of expertise: general appeal is generally weak, but expert claims deserve consideration when criteria are met, which leads to Salmon's probabilistic standard.
exq: Explain why the general expert-appeal form 'X asserts S, therefore S is true' is invalid. How does Hamblin's added premise make it valid, and why does it remain unsound?
Using Case 7A (the president), assess whether the premise 'everything the president says is true' can be defended. What would verifying it require?
Distinguish Locke's ad verecundiam from Salmon's inductive appeal to authority. Give one example of each and say which is fallacious.
'Appeal to authority is always a fallacy.' Discuss with reference to Salmon's track-record argument and the idea that conclusions are only probable.
Why does the 'expert is always correct' premise immunize an argument from criticism, and what critical questions should replace it when assessing an expert's claim?

notes.t: The General Appeal to an Expert
pts: Appeal to expertise is a legitimate exception: experts' experience stands above general experience, so their claims deserve consideration if the argument meets criteria.
The general expert-appeal argument form is: someone asserts S, therefore S is true.
Hamblin's version makes the crucial premise 'everything X says is true', which renders the form valid.
Unless the premise appeals to a divine being, it claims too much, more than could be verified.
Case 7A shows the problem: the premise that everything the president says is true is unverifiable and controversial.
defs: General appeal to an expert
An argument form in which a claim is accepted as true because an expert or source asserts it; valid only if a strong, usually unverifiable, premise about the source's infallibility is included.
tips: Do not treat any expert's claim as automatically true; the argument must satisfy criteria of expertise, not just assert authority.
Recognise that validity here comes from an overly strong premise, so a valid form can still be unsound.
rq: Why does Hamblin's form make the argument valid, and why is that a problem?
The premise 'everything X says is true' guarantees the conclusion, but it is too strong to be verified unless X is divine.
What distinguishes a legitimate expert appeal from a fallacious one?
Legitimate appeals meet correct criteria about the expert's relevant experience; fallacious ones rely on unverifiable blanket claims of reliability.

notes.t: Locke's ad verecundiam and Salmon's inductive version of appeal to authority
pts: Locke's treatment suggests people may defer to a high office holder out of shame at challenging him, giving him the benefit of the doubt.
The first premise (an expert is always correct) functions as an attempt to immunize the argument from criticism, blocking challenges in advance.
Appeal to authority is not always fallacious; Salmon gives an inductively correct version based on the expert's track record.
Salmon's version yields only probable grounds: any particular assertion by the expert could be wrong, so contextual questions remain to be asked.
defs: Ad verecundiam
Fallacy of appealing to respect for, or shame before, an authority figure rather than to genuine evidence or expertise.
tips: Do not treat every appeal to authority as fallacious; check whether the premise is an inductive generalization about expert reliability.
Note that the always-correct premise is the problematic element, since it is implausible and blocks dialogue.
rq: Why does Salmon's version avoid the fallacy that Locke's first premise commits?

Salmon's premise is inductive and about a majority of statements being true, so it admits that any particular assertion may be wrong, rather than claiming the expert is always correct, which immunizes the argument from criticism.
What contextual questions should be asked even when the inductive version is used?
Questions about the expert in question, the subject area involved, and related matters, since the conclusion is only probable.

units.name: 3 Critical questions for expert appeals
units.ov: This material covers how to evaluate appeals to expert authority (argument from expert opinion, ad verecundiam) using critical questions. These ask whether the source is a genuine authority with cognitive expertise, whether the claim was actually made and can be traced, and whether the expertise is relevant to the claim. Appeals are not fallacious in themselves. They become fallacious when these conditions fail, and the ideas link through burden of proof, testimony and dialectical exchange.
must: Three basic critical questions: (1) is the source a genuine authority/expert, (2) did the expert actually make the claim (attribution), (3) is the expertise relevant to the subject matter
Cognitive authority = authority grounded in genuine field-specific expertise, as opposed to mere status, office or fame
Argument of Authority (status/office treated as expertise, no relevant credentials) is typically fallacious, so do not equate celebrity with expertise
Appeals to expert opinion are not automatically fallacious: they are legitimate when all critical questions are satisfied
Burden of proof lies with the arguer: show the expert said it or give a clear reference so the source can be checked
Relevance: an expert outside their own field carries no more weight than a nonexpert unless a relevant link is shown
Ad verecundiam criteria: expert identified, credible track record, field suited to genuine expert knowledge, statement relevant to the question
Expert appeals reduce to testimony, so scepticism about experts mirrors scepticism about testimony, and some testimonies rightly count for more than others
Check vested interest/motives (e.g. Bono linking himself to a high-profile health issue) as grounds for scrutiny
Case 7B's premise allows dialectical exchange so a critic can challenge the authority, and real appeals are more complex than three questions capture
conn: Cognitive authority vs mere authority links question 1 (genuineness) to the fallacy of the argument of authority, and to the celebrity example (Bono)
Burden of proof links attribution (question 2) to dialectical exchange: the arguer must supply a traceable source so the critic can challenge it
Expert opinion as testimony links track record and field suitability to deciding which testimonies deserve more weight
Relevance (question 3) combines with vested interest: an expert may be genuine yet speak outside their field or have motives needing scrutiny
exq: State and explain the three basic critical questions for appeals to expert authority, applying each to a celebrity such as Bono endorsing a health policy.
Distinguish cognitive authority from an argument of authority. Why is the latter typically fallacious, and when is an appeal to authority still legitimate?
Discuss the burden of proof in appeals to experts. What must an arguer do to meet it, and how does this enable dialectical exchange?
Using the criteria for ad verecundiam, evaluate a case where a respected physicist comments on climate policy economics. Which criteria are met or fail?
'Scepticism about experts is just scepticism about testimony.' Assess this claim and explain how criteria separate legitimate from fallacious expert appeals.

notes.t: The General Appeal to an Expert: Critical Questions
pts: The Case 7B first premise avoids the fault of the previous example, allowing a dialectical exchange where a critic can challenge the authority's word.
Key questions arise: what constitutes an expert in the subject area, and whether a popular singer qualifies as one.
Possible vested interest: it may benefit Bono to associate with a high-profile health issue, which warrants scrutiny.
Basic critical questions help deal with general types of appeal to authority: identify the source, confirm the claim was made, and check relevance.
The first critical question ensures we are dealing with cognitive authority associated with expertise rather than mere authority.
defs: Appeal to authority (argument from expert opinion)
An argument that accepts a claim because a person or source regarded as an authority asserted it; evaluated by critical questions about genuineness, attribution, and relevance.
Cognitive authority
Authority grounded in genuine expertise and knowledge of a field, as opposed to authority based merely on status or fame.
tips: Do not treat celebrity or fame as genuine expertise; always check whether the authority has cognitive, field-specific knowledge.
Remember the three basic critical questions: genuine authority, the claim was actually made, and relevance to the subject matter.
rq: Why does Case 7B avoid the fault of the previous example, and why does that matter?
Its first premise attributes a checkable, specific reliability to Bono's statements, so a critic can challenge the authority's word in dialectical exchange.
Why might a popular singer's claim about a health issue still fail as expert evidence?
Fame does not confer expertise; the singer may lack a body of specialized knowledge and may have a vested interest in the issue.

notes.t: Three critical questions for appeals to expert authority
pts: A genuine authority must have credentials supporting expertise in a recognized field; appeals to status alone, treated as if it were expertise, are likely fallacious.
The arguer bears the burden of proof: either show the expert actually said the claim, or give a clear reference so a critical appraiser can check the source.
Expertise must be relevant to the claim; an expert's statements outside their field carry no more weight than a nonexpert's unless a relevant relationship is shown.
Appeals to expert authority can involve greater complexities than these three questions reveal.
defs: Argument of Authority
An appeal to a person's status or office as if it were a cognitive claim to expertise, with no genuine credentials relevant to the field; typically fallacious.
Burden of proof (in appeals to experts)
The obligation of the arguer to either support the claim that an expert said something or provide a clear reference to the source so it can be investigated.
tips: Do not treat holding an office or high status as equivalent to genuine expertise in the relevant field.
Check relevance: a credible expert in one area may be no more authoritative than a layperson on a question outside their field.
rq: Why does the arguer, rather than the critical listener, have the burden of proof when citing an expert?
Laypeople rarely have immediate access to the sources, so the arguer must support the attribution or provide a checkable reference.
Why isn't a criminal psychologist's opinion on capital punishment automatically authoritative?
Their expertise is not strictly relevant to the moral question; standing equals a nonexpert's unless the arguer shows a relevant relationship.

notes.t: Appeals to expertise (ad verecundiam) and Critical Questions
pts: Skepticism toward expert authority mirrors skepticism toward testimony, since an expert's claim often reduces to a conflict between testimonies or experiences.
Some testimonies rightly count for more than others, so we need clear criteria to separate legitimate expert appeals from fallacious ones.
The authority or expert must be identified and have a track record that makes their statements more reliable than those of non-experts.
The field must be one that lends itself to genuine expert knowledge; otherwise the appeal is fallacious.
The expert's statements must relate to their field of expertise and be relevant to the question at hand.
defs: ad verecundiam

The fallacy of appealing to an authority or expert who is not identified, lacks a credible track record, speaks outside a field suited to expert knowledge, or whose statements are irrelevant to the question.
Critical Questions
A set of conditions used to assess whether an appeal to expertise is legitimate or fallacious.
tips: Do not assume that any appeal to authority is fallacious; the appeal is legitimate when all Critical Questions are satisfied.
Check both that the expert's field suits expert knowledge and that the specific statement is relevant to the question.
rq: Why might an appeal to a well-known expert still be fallacious?
Because the expert may be speaking outside their field, or their statements may be irrelevant to the question at hand, failing Critical Questions 2 or 3.
Why is an unidentified expert a problem even if the claim sounds authoritative?
Without an identified source and track record, there is no way to judge whether their statements are more reliable than a non-expert's.

units.name: 4 Applying the questions: verifiability, field, relevance and testability
units.ov: This material covers how to evaluate appeals to expert authority (ad verecundiam) using a set of critical questions: verifiability/identity, vested interest and consensus, the field question, the relevance question and the testability question. An appeal is legitimate only if the source is named and checkable, unbiased, in a credible field, speaking within its expertise, and making a claim that can be followed up. The questions work together as a checklist: credentials alone never suffice.
must: Ad verecundiam is a fallacy when the authority is not legitimate or relevant on the claim at issue, or the claim is unsupported or biased; credentials alone are never sufficient.
Verifiability and identity: the expert must be clearly named, with credentials and track record identified, so the source can be researched and the claim checked.
Unidentified studies cannot be corroborated and work like hearsay evidence, which courts are reluctant to accept; whistleblower anonymity is a legitimate reason but the appeal is still weak evidence.
Vested interest: clear illegitimate bias weakens an appeal to the point of fallacy.
Consensus is preferred; where none exists, the claim should at least be consistent with other knowledge in the field. When experts disagree, check consistency rather than assuming one is right.

Field question: is there a genuine body of knowledge with general acceptance, so that real experts can exist? Massive disagreement among credentialed scientists (clinical ecology, Case 7D) undermines this; fame, sales and credentials do not prove legitimacy.
Relevance question: the expert must speak within their own field and the statement must bear on the claim (e.g. evolutionary theory misapplied to global terrorism).
Testability question: there must be some way in principle to follow up and verify what the authority says; opinion or speculation beyond their knowledge does not justify appeal.
Promissory reason: an expert's name is treated as a guarantee that supporting evidence exists but is too difficult to present; it is acceptable only if the evidence can be checked.

Claims with more serious consequences deserve greater weight; in new fields laypeople may have to judge appeals weak and seek other evidence. Judge the authority claim, not whether the conclusion seems right.
conn: Verifiability and testability overlap: a named, researchable source (identity) makes a claim followable, while unidentified sources fail both and resemble hearsay.
The field and relevance questions form a sequence: first is the field legitimate (clinical ecology), then is this expert speaking within it (evolution applied to terrorism).
Vested interest and consensus combine: a biased lone expert contradicting field consensus is a typical weak appeal, and seriousness of consequences raises the standard of scrutiny.
Promissory reasoning links to verifiability: trust in the expert's name is acceptable only if the promised evidence can in principle be checked.
exq: Using the five criteria for legitimate appeals to experts, evaluate an argument that cites 'studies show' with no source named. Is it fallacious, and does whistleblower anonymity change this?
Explain the difference between the field question and the relevance question, using clinical ecology and evolutionary theory applied to terrorism as examples.

A well-credentialed scientist with funding from a company makes a claim about that company's product while other experts disagree. Assess the appeal in terms of vested interest, consensus and consistency with other knowledge.
Define the testability question and promissory reason. When is relying on an expert's name as a guarantee of evidence acceptable?
Why should claims with serious consequences be weighed more heavily, and how should laypeople judge expert appeals in new or developing fields?

notes.t: Ad Verecundiam: criteria for legitimate appeals to experts
pts: A legitimate appeal to experts requires that the claim could in principle be tested or verified by the person making the appeal.
The expert should have no vested interest in the claim; clear illegitimate bias weakens the appeal to the point of fallacy.
Consensus in the field is preferred; where none exists, claims should at least be consistent with other knowledge in the relevant field.
The identity question: the expert source must be clearly named and its credentials and track record identified so the source can be researched.
Claims with more serious consequences should be given greater weight than those with less.
defs: Ad verecundiam
A fallacy of appealing to an authority or expert who is not a legitimate or relevant source of expertise on the claim at issue, or whose claim is unsupported or biased.
Promissory reason
An appeal to an expert treated as a promise that supporting evidence exists, though it is too difficult to present in the argument itself; the expert's name guarantees the evidence exists.
tips: Do not treat credentials alone as sufficient; the appeal must also be checkable and free of illegitimate bias.
When experts disagree, check consistency with other knowledge in the field rather than assuming one expert is correct.
rq: Why must the expert be named rather than cited anonymously?
So someone could in principle follow up by researching the source and checking the evidence, which is what makes the promissory reason credible.
What if an expert has a strong financial stake in the outcome of a claim?
The appeal is weakened, possibly to the point of being fallacious, because the illegitimate bias undermines reliability.

notes.t: Appeal to authority: unverifiable sources and the 'field question'
pts: An appeal to unidentified studies cannot be corroborated or verified, so it is fallacious as evidence.
Unverifiable appeals work like hearsay evidence, which courts are disinclined to accept.
Protecting a whistleblower's identity is a legitimate reason for anonymity, yet such appeals remain weak evidence in argument.
The field question asks what makes a body of knowledge credible enough that genuine experts can exist in it.
Clinical ecology illustrates the problem: credentialed scientists disagree massively within the field.
defs: Hearsay evidence
Evidence reported secondhand or from unidentified sources that cannot be checked, and so is given little weight in argument or law.
tips: Do not judge the argument by whether the conclusion seems right; the question is whether the authority claim gives good grounds.
Massive disagreement within a field, as with clinical ecology, undermines claims that the field has genuine experts.
rq: Why is the Aspartame argument's appeal to 'recent scientific studies' fallacious even if the conclusion may be true?
Because the studies are unidentified, so they cannot be corroborated or verified; the authority claim gives no good grounds for the conclusion.
Why might anonymity still be justified for whistleblowers, yet still weak as argument evidence?
Protecting a source's identity has good reason, but unverifiable claims cannot be checked, so they remain weak evidence.

notes.t: Ad verecundiam: legitimacy of fields and the relevance question
pts: In new or developing fields, laypeople may have no option but to judge expert appeals weak and seek other evidence.
An appeal to an expert needs a genuine field with a body of knowledge and general acceptance; the Case 7D appeal fails this because the evidence tells against it.
The relevance question: the expert must speak within their field of expertise and the statement must bear on the claim being advanced.
Recognized experts can be misleadingly cited on issues outside their expertise, such as evolutionary theory applied to global terrorism.
defs: Relevance question
The requirement that an expert speaks within their own field of expertise and that what they say is relevant to the claim being advanced; failure makes the appeal fallacious.
tips: Do not treat fame, sales or credentials as proof that a field is legitimate; check for general acceptance and evidence.
Watch for experts speaking outside their field; a strong credential does not make an off-topic claim relevant.
rq: Why does the credibility of a large book-sales figure fail to establish an expert's authority in Case 7D?
Sales and popularity do not establish a legitimate field with a body of knowledge or general acceptance; the field's standing and evidence matter instead.
What is the difference between an expert's authority in a field and their authority on a related issue?
Authority applies only within the field of expertise; speaking outside it, even on a related topic, makes the appeal irrelevant and fallacious.

notes.t: Appeal to Authority: the testability question and expertise limits
pts: An Appeal to Authority is fallacious when the authority's expertise does not extend to the claim being made, especially when it goes beyond their field.
The testability question checks whether the authority's claim can be followed up or verified; if not, the authority claim is weakened.
Claims that are opinion or speculation rather than directly tied to the authority's knowledge do not justify appeal to that authority.
defs: Appeal to Authority
A fallacious argument in which a claim is accepted merely because a source is claimed to be an expert, when that expertise does not properly cover the claim.
Testability question
A criterion for evaluating authority claims: there must be some way in principle to follow up on and verify what the authority says.
tips: Do not conclude that an expert is always wrong; the issue is whether the claim falls within their area of expertise and is verifiable.
Distinguish a genuine expert statement from opinion or speculation outside their field, which is the key test in these cases.
rq: Why does Spock's expertise in pediatrics not justify his remarks on government behaviour?
Because his expertise concerns child health and rearing, not government policy or adult nutrition/politics, so his authority does not extend to those claims.
What would it mean for a claim by an authority to fail the testability question?
There would be no way in principle to verify it, so the grounds for accepting the authority's claim are called into question and the authority claim is weakened.

units.name: 5 Bias, consensus and consequences questions
units.ov: This material covers critical questions for evaluating appeals to authority (ad verecundiam): whether the authority is biased, whether the claim fits a field consensus, and what the consequences of accepting or ignoring it would be. Bias and vested interest test the source's credibility, consensus tests the claim against the field, and consequences weigh a decision when the other questions are unresolved. Case 7H (Wall Street Journal editors versus the scientific consensus) shows the questions applied together.
must: Appeal to authority (ad verecundiam) is fallacious when the authority is irrelevant, unidentified, biased by a vested interest, or contradicted by a consensus; otherwise it can be a bona fide argument
Bias question: ask whether the authority has an illegitimate bias, i.e. a vested interest or stake in the outcome
Vested interest = personal gain from the case (e.g. paid celebrity endorsers, industry funding); it undermines credibility even within the authority's own field
Not all bias is illegitimate: open biases rooted in real beliefs do not automatically undermine reasoning; only vested interests do
Consensus question: a claim contrary to a clear field consensus deserves doubt; mavericks can be right, but one expert's word is not enough
Distinguish expert disagreement (hard for laypeople to judge, but does not mean no one is right) from a claim against a clear consensus (warrants doubt)
Case 7H: Wall Street Journal editors are not credible authorities, and the US National Academy of Sciences plus ten other bodies oppose their view, so the appeal is fallacious

Consequences question (the seventh critical question): what follows from accepting or ignoring the claim? It is a weighing consideration, not proof of fallacy, and can decide cases when other questions are unresolved
Identification of the expert allows traceability and independent checking, but does not remove a vested interest

Guilt by association is fallacious unless the link is real and relevant to the reliability of the source's findings; a consultant who later sells the recommended property creates a second interest that taints earlier advice
conn: Bias and consensus: a vested-interest expert (e.g. industry-funded) who contradicts a clear consensus fails two critical questions, as in Case 7H
Bias versus guilt by association: a relevant vested interest legitimately undermines an authority, but an irrelevant association is itself a fallacy, so check relevance to reliability
Consensus and consequences: when expert disagreement leaves the consensus question unresolved, the consequences of acting wrongly (e.g. in sustainability or climate policy) can tip the decision
Identification and bias: traceability lets you investigate funding and later interests, such as the consultant who sells property after advising
